text:
Preface
Draft placeholder.
This book accompanies Econ/Demog C175. Each chapter takes up one topic from the course’s lectures; the parts group related topics, and the optional chapters at the end cover topics taught in earlier years. It explains the economic model behind that week’s lectures in plain language, reads the classic texts alongside you, and shows how the model can be confronted with data. The labs are where you do that confrontation yourself. The book is meant to prepare you for them, not to do them for you.
How to use each chapter:

Before lecture, read the opening sections and the “In their own words” boxes, which quote the assigned classic reading.
After lecture, work through the model sections and the “Check your understanding” questions.
Before the lab, read the “Data in action” section. It uses the same data you will use, but leaves the lab’s questions for you.

The R code that makes each figure is folded away under “Show the R code.” You don’t need it to follow the text, but it is there if you’re curious how a figure was made.

title: 1  Ten Thousand Years of Population
text:
1.1 What is economic demography?
Economic demography asks two kinds of questions. The first half of this course is about the consequences of population: how the number of people, and how fast that number changes, affects human welfare. The second half is about the causes of population change: the economic forces behind births, deaths, migration, marriage, and divorce.
Two news stories show what this looks like.
crumbs: Population and the economy: big theories

title: 1  Ten Thousand Years of Population
text:
1.1.1 Example 1: China’s “looming crisis”
In January 2019, the New York Times ran the headline “China’s Looming Crisis: A Shrinking Population.” Four years later it reported that “China’s Population Falls, Heralding a Demographic Crisis”: deaths had outnumbered births for the first time in six decades.
If you grew up hearing that the world’s problem was too many people, this should raise some questions:

What’s wrong with a shrinking population?
What is the best population size? Best for whom?
Why did population grow so much after 1950?
What limited growth in earlier centuries?
What will population change do to the environment?
And to inequality?

These questions run through the whole course. Note also that China’s falling fertility is not just a story about the one-child policy. Population growth was slowing long before that policy, and has kept slowing since it ended. We return to China in Chapter 11.


1.1.2 Example 2: The immigration surge
In July 2024, the Congressional Budget Office (CBO), the nonpartisan agency that scores the federal budget for Congress, published an analysis of the recent surge in immigration to the United States.


Added · from readings Figures in this subsection are from the CBO report (2024), Summary and pp. 6, 19–21. The slides show CBO’s Figures 1–2 and Table 2.
CBO compared two scenarios. In its baseline, net immigration of the category it calls “other foreign nationals” averages 1.7 million a year from 2021 to 2026. In a counterfactual, it stays at the pre-2020 trend of 200,000 a year. The difference, the “surge,” is 8.7 million people. Counting their U.S.-born children, the U.S. population in 2034 is about 10 million people, or nearly 3 percent, larger with the surge than without it.
CBO’s headline findings:

The federal budget. The surge lowers federal deficits by $0.9 trillion over 2024–2034. Immigrants in the surge pay $788 billion in income and payroll taxes. Benefits to them and their children add $177 billion to mandatory spending. The broader effects on the economy add more revenue than spending.
The economy. Nominal GDP is $8.9 trillion higher over the decade. Most of that, $7.8 trillion, comes simply from having more people.

Should we conclude that the surge is “good for the economy”? Economic demography teaches us to ask for whom, and measured how. A few things to notice:


Added · new The per-capita comparison is my calculation from CBO’s numbers (real GDP +2.9% vs. population “nearly 3 percent” in 2034). It answers one of the discussion questions in your course calendar.

Totals versus per capita. In 2034, real GDP is 2.9 percent higher because of the surge, and the population is nearly 3 percent larger. So GDP per person is roughly unchanged. A bigger economy is not the same as a richer population. Notice that CBO reports almost everything in totals.
Short run versus long run. Through 2026, wage growth slows for workers with 12 or fewer years of education, because there are more workers with similar skills. Later, wage growth speeds up slightly for all groups, as overall productivity rises.
Productivity can go both ways. At first, the surge lowers average productivity, because the new arrivals have, on average, less education and work experience. Over time, the 3 percent of surge adults who work in science and engineering are expected to raise productivity through innovation, with the biggest effect 5 to 15 years after arrival. By 2034, CBO estimates, the two effects roughly cancel out.
Federal versus local. CBO’s estimates cover the federal budget only. It notes that research generally finds immigration raises state and local costs, especially for schools, more than state and local revenues.

The point is not that CBO is wrong. The report is careful and full of caveats. The point is that “Is immigration good for the economy?” breaks into many questions. There are perspectives to weigh: short term or long term, federal or local government, the whole economy or per capita, capital or labor, rich or poor, skilled or unskilled, producer or consumer. We take up immigration directly at the end of the course.

1.2 Measuring population growth

1.2.1 Absolute or proportional change?
Table 1.1 shows estimates of world population over the last 10,000 years.

There are two ways to describe change. We could count the absolute change, in persons per year. Or we could measure the proportional change, in percent per year. Demographers usually prefer proportional change, for several reasons:

It is more constant over time.
It connects naturally to individual behavior. Each person’s chance of having a child or dying produces a growth rate, not a fixed number of new people.
The underlying process is multiplicative. (The Bible says “be fruitful and multiply,” not “be fruitful and add.”)
It connects to the other models we’ll use, such as the Solow growth model.

But absolute change sometimes matters more. For the environment, for example, what counts may be the total number of people burning fuel, not the rate at which that number grows.


1.2.2 The exponential model
The standard model of proportional growth is exponential growth:
\[
N(t) = N(0)\, e^{Rt},
\]
where \(N(t)\) is the population at time \(t\) and \(R\) is the annual growth rate. Taking natural logarithms of both sides and rearranging gives a formula for the growth rate between any two dates:
\[
R = \frac{\log N(t) - \log N(0)}{t}.
\]
(Throughout this book, “log” means the natural logarithm, which is what R’s log() function computes.) This formula has a simple picture: \(R\) is the slope of the graph of log population against time, its “rise over run.” For example, world population grew from 6,080 million in 2000 to 7,218 million in 2015, so
\[
R = \frac{\log(7218) - \log(6080)}{15} = 0.0114,
\]
about 1.1 percent per year.


Added · new The “rule of 70” is not in your slides.
A handy rule of thumb: a population growing at \(R\) percent per year doubles in about \(70/R\) years. At 1 percent per year, it doubles in about 70 years. At 0.1 percent, it takes about 700 years.


1.2.3 Seeing growth
Figure 1.1 shows world population on the original scale and on a log scale, using the data from Lab 1.


Show the R code
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4.2, 2, 1))
plot(world$year, world$pop / 1000, type = "o", pch = 19, cex = 0.45, xaxt = "n",
     xlab = "Year", ylab = "Population (billions)", main = "Original scale",
     font.main = 1)
axis(1, at = seq(-8000, 2000, 2000))
plot(world$year, log(world$pop), type = "o", pch = 19, cex = 0.45, xaxt = "n",
     xlab = "Year", ylab = "log of population (millions)", main = "Log scale",
     font.main = 1)
axis(1, at = seq(-8000, 2000, 2000))
par(op)








Figure 1.1: World population, 8000 BCE to 2024, on the original scale (left) and a log scale (right). Data: Lab 1 file (Wikipedia; 2024 from the UN).





On the original scale, nothing happens for ten thousand years and then population explodes. The log scale shows proportional change, and it tells a subtler story. For eight thousand years before the Common Era, log population rose by about 4, a slope of about 4/8000 = 0.0005: growth of about 0.05 percent per year. Since then, the slope has steepened again and again. Even the proportional rate of growth has accelerated.


Added · from readings Livi-Bacci 2017, pp. 6–7 and Table 1.1.
Livi-Bacci makes the same point with slightly different estimates. If world population was 252 million at the start of the Common Era and 771 million in 1750, average growth was only 0.06 percent per year. If the death rate averaged 40 per thousand, then the birth rate must have averaged about 40.6: births exceeded deaths by just 1.5 percent. For most of human history, he writes, “fertility and mortality must have remained in virtual equilibrium.” Since the 1960s, by contrast, births have exceeded deaths by 200 percent.
Figure 1.2 plots the growth rate in each interval.


Show the R code
R_world <- 100 * diff(log(world$pop)) / diff(world$year)
end_year <- world$year[-1]
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4.2, 2, 1))
plot(end_year, R_world, type = "s", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "Year", ylab = "Growth rate (% per year)", main = "All periods",
     font.main = 1)
s <- end_year >= 1900
plot(end_year[s], R_world[s], type = "o", pch = 19, cex = 0.7, lwd = 2,
     xlab = "Year", ylab = "Growth rate (% per year)", main = "Since 1900",
     font.main = 1)
par(op)








Figure 1.2: Average annual growth rate of world population in each interval between the dates in the Lab 1 data, plotted at the end of each interval. Left: 8000 BCE to 2024. Right: since 1900.





The history of human population thus has three phases:

For most of human history, near-zero population growth.
Then a period of accelerating growth.
Most recently, slowing growth. The future of humanity may depend on how fast this slowing proceeds.

Explaining each phase is one of the goals of this course. Near-zero growth is the subject of Chapter 3. Accelerating and then slowing growth is the subject of the demographic transition, below.






In the lab



In Lab 1 you compute these growth rates yourself from the world population data, and use the exponential model to ask “what if” questions about the past and the future. The lab ends with an exercise on Sauvy’s optimum populations (Chapter 2).




Added · from readings Livi-Bacci 2017, pp. 26–27 and Table 1.1.
One more striking number from Livi-Bacci. Making “courageous” assumptions, demographers estimate that about 82 billion people had been born by the year 2000. The 6 billion alive in 2000 were thus about 7 percent of all the humans who have ever lived.

title: 1  Ten Thousand Years of Population
text:
1.3 Generations, reproduction, and survival

1.3.1 Paying the “demographic debt”
Population growth is ultimately a matter of generations. Does each generation of parents raise enough children to replace itself?


Added · from readings The Bichi family and French Canadian examples are from Livi-Bacci 2017, pp. 7–9.
Livi-Bacci illustrates this with the descendants of Jacopo Bichi, a sharecropper near Florence who married Domenica Del Buono in 1667. Over three generations, five married couples of the family, ten spouses in all, raised nine children who in turn married. Ten breeders brought nine offspring to reproduction: a 10 percent decline per generation that, if repeated for long enough, would lead to the family’s extinction. Other families did better. The pioneers of French Canada, who settled the St. Lawrence Valley in the seventeenth century, raised an average of 4.2 married children per couple. That is a doubling in a single generation. Two pioneers, Jean Guyon and Mathurine Robin, had 2,150 descendants by 1730.
A population grows, shrinks, or stays the same depending on whether, on average, each generation more than replaces, fails to replace, or exactly replaces itself.






Try this (from class)



In lecture we simulate generational growth with the class itself. Each row is a generation. Each person computes the “per parent” growth implied by their own family (number of children in their parents’ family, divided by two), and the first row multiplies these together, row by row. Afterward, ask yourself: Is this a good estimate of the growth rate of your parents’ generation? What might be wrong with it?




1.3.2 Two measures: fertility and survival


Added · from readings The components of fertility in this subsection are from Livi-Bacci 2017, pp. 9–12.
Two summary measures capture reproduction and survival:

The total fertility rate (TFR) is the average number of children a woman would have over her reproductive life at current birth rates, in the absence of mortality. It is the most common summary measure of fertility. Before the demographic transition it exceeded 6. In the United States it has recently fallen to about 1.6, and in South Korea in 2023 it was 0.72.
Life expectancy at birth, \(e_0\), is the average number of years a newborn would live at current death rates.

What limits fertility in a society without birth control? Livi-Bacci breaks it into two parts. The first is the interval between births, which is made up of a period of infertility after each birth (longer when mothers breastfeed longer), the waiting time to conceive, nine months of pregnancy, and time lost to miscarriage. Together these give intervals of 1.5 to 3.5 years, usually 2 to 3. The second is the span of the reproductive period actually used. That runs from marriage, which may be as early as 15 or later than 25, to the end of fecundity, with mothers’ average age at last birth around 38 to 41. Combining the extremes gives between 4.3 and 16.7 children per woman. In practice, averages below 5 or above 8 are rare. The two biggest levers are the age at marriage and the length of breastfeeding. Hold onto the first: it is Malthus’s preventive check.
Survival matters too, because a woman who dies young cannot have her children. Livi-Bacci shows that when life expectancy at birth is 20 years, only about 29 percent of a generation’s potential reproductive life is actually lived. At an \(e_0\) of 50 it is 71 percent, and at 83 it is 98 percent. If women would have 6 children each in the absence of mortality, high mortality cuts that to about 1.8 children per woman born.


1.3.3 From TFR to growth rate
To turn the TFR into a growth rate, we need three adjustments:

Sex. Only daughters go on to have children. About 48.86 percent of births are girls.
Mortality. Only daughters who survive to childbearing age have children. Survival to about age 30 is a good summary.
Generation length. Growth per generation must be converted to growth per year. A generation is about 30 years.

A good approximation is
\[
R \approx \frac{\log\left[\text{TFR} \times 0.4886 \times \text{survival to age 30}\right]}{30}.
\]
For example, with a TFR of 4 and survival to age 30 of 0.7, each woman is replaced by 4 × 0.4886 × 0.7 = 1.37 surviving daughters, and \(R \approx \log(1.37)/30 \approx 0.01\), or 1 percent per year.


1.3.4 The space of growth


Added · new The figure is my construction, after your slide 02-31 and Livi-Bacci’s Figure 1.8. I approximate survival to 30 from \(e_0\) with a smooth curve through Livi-Bacci’s three values (29%, 71%, 98%), plus endpoints I chose at \(e_0\) = 15 and 95, and use your growth formula. The discussion of age structure in the last paragraph is mine.

surv_of_e0 <- splinefun(c(15, 20.7, 50.8, 83, 95), c(0.20, 0.292, 0.708, 0.982, 0.995),
                        method = "monoH.FC")

     pos = c(2, 4, 3, 3, 4, 1, 1))

Figure 1.3: Isogrowth curves: combinations of life expectancy and TFR that imply the same long-run growth rate (labels are annual rates). Red: the world, 1700–2100 (Lee). Survival to age 30 is approximated from life expectancy using Livi-Bacci’s figures.





The thick curve is zero growth. Before 1900, the world sat in a narrow band just above it, with low life expectancy and high fertility. Livi-Bacci notes that pre-modern populations nearly all lived in the band between 0 and 1 percent growth, though they got there in different ways. Denmark at the end of the eighteenth century combined a life expectancy of about 40 with just over four children per woman. India a century later combined a life expectancy of about 25 with just under seven. During the twentieth century, life expectancy rose first, carrying the world far above the zero line, before fertility fell and brought it back down.
One caution. The curves show the long-run growth rate that a combination of fertility and mortality would eventually produce. Actual growth in a given year also depends on the population’s age structure. In 2000, the world’s TFR of 2.7 implies long-run growth of only a few tenths of a percent per year. Actual growth was 1.2 percent, because the world’s population was young, with many people of childbearing age. That momentum takes decades to work itself out.


1.3.5 Environmental constraints


Added · from readings This subsection summarizes Livi-Bacci 2017, pp. 2–5 and 19–24. Your slides don’t cover it.
Why did population grow so slowly for so long? Livi-Bacci begins with biology. Species follow different reproductive “strategies.” r-strategists (insects, fish, small mammals) have many offspring and invest little in each, and their numbers swing violently. K-strategists (large mammals, including humans) have few offspring, invest heavily in each, and stay in more stable balance with their environment. Humans are an extreme K-strategy species.
Within that biology, the environment sets limits. Hunter-gatherers lived at densities of about 0.1 to 1 person per square kilometer, limited by the plants and animals available within a day’s walk. Agriculture raised the limit enormously. By the mid-eighteenth century, the major European countries had 40 to 60 people per square kilometer, about 100 times the density of hunter-gatherers. But farming still depended on plants and animals for energy, and so ultimately on land. Hunter-gatherers used about 5,000 calories of energy per person per day, and farming societies never more than about 12,000 to 26,000. The industrial revolution broke the link between energy and land: early industrial societies used about 70,000 calories per person per day, and some today use more than 200,000.
So each great technological era, hunting and gathering, agriculture, and industry, raised the ceiling on human numbers. Population then grew toward the new ceiling and slowed as it approached it. This is the idea, common to animal biology and to Malthus, that growth slows as density rises. We develop it in the next chapter.

title: 1  Ten Thousand Years of Population
text:
1.4 The demographic transition

1.4.1 Crude rates
The simplest measures of births and deaths are the crude birth rate, annual births divided by population, written \(b\), and the crude death rate, annual deaths divided by population, written \(d\). (“Crude” because the denominator is everyone, men and women, young and old.) Without migration, the growth rate is just
\[
R = b - d.
\]
Typical values: about 40 deaths per thousand per year in ancient Rome, about 10 in modern Japan, and about 8 in the modern United States. (Is it really more dangerous to be born in Japan than in the United States? Think about age structure.)


1.4.2 A puzzle, seen from the 1970s
Today the demographic transition can seem obvious: birth and death rates used to be high, and now both are low. But put yourself in the position of an observer in the 1970s. World population growth had been accelerating for centuries. Energy prices were skyrocketing, environmental worries were rising, and economic growth was slowing. If you saw the sequence 1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 3, what number would you predict next?
Predicting the future requires understanding the system that produces births and deaths. Perhaps both depend on income: \(b(y)\) and \(d(y)\). Perhaps both depend on population size: \(b(N)\) and \(d(N)\). Perhaps mortality changes for its own reasons, and fertility responds to mortality: \(b(d)\). The next several chapters explore these possibilities.


1.4.3 An idealized picture
Figure 1.4 shows the demographic transition in its idealized form.








Figure 1.4: An idealized demographic transition. Left: crude birth and death rates. Right: the growth rate, R = b − d. High growth is just a phase.






Before the transition: high fertility and high mortality. Mortality fluctuates with random shocks such as epidemics and harvest failures.
During the transition: mortality falls first, and the decline in fertility lags behind. The gap between them produces transitional growth.
After the transition: fertility finally falls too. Now the fluctuations in growth come from fertility, and fertility may fall below replacement.

Some typical numbers. Before the transition, the TFR exceeds 6, and life expectancy is about 40 to 50 years or less. In Korea in 1950, the crude birth rate was 37 per thousand and the death rate 32, for growth of half a percent. During the transition, growth rates reached 1 to 2 percent in historical Europe and 3 to 4 percent in Africa. In Iraq in 1985, the birth rate was 42 per thousand and the death rate 8, for growth of 3.4 percent. After the transition, the TFR is around 2 (or 2.5, or 1.5), life expectancy is 70 or 80, and growth is near zero. Belgium in 1984 had a birth rate of 12 per thousand and a death rate of 11.


1.4.4 Sweden
Figure 1.5 shows the transition in Sweden, using the Human Mortality Database data we use in Lab 2. (In lecture we compare Sweden with Mexico, where the transition came later and was much faster.)


Show the R code
op <- par(mar = c(4, 4.2, 1, 1))
plot(swe$year, swe$cbr, type = "n", ylim = c(0, 55),
     xlab = "Year", ylab = "Per 1,000 population")
s <- swe$year %in% 1800:1900
polygon(c(swe$year[s], rev(swe$year[s])), c(swe$cbr[s], rev(swe$cdr[s])),
        col = adjustcolor(col_b, 0.18), border = NA)
lines(swe$year, swe$cbr, col = col_b, lwd = 1.5)
lines(swe$year, swe$cdr, col = col_d, lwd = 1.5)
legend("topright", c("Crude birth rate", "Crude death rate"),
       col = c(col_b, col_d), lwd = 2, bty = "n")
par(op)
area <- sum((swe$B[swe$year %in% 1800:1899] - swe$D[swe$year %in% 1800:1899]) /
            swe$N[swe$year %in% 1800:1899])
ratio <- swe$N[swe$year == 1900] / swe$N[swe$year == 1800]








Figure 1.5: The demographic transition in Sweden: crude birth and death rates, 1751–2014. The shaded area between the curves from 1800 to 1900 is the sum of annual growth rates over the century. Source: Human Mortality Database.





Sweden’s death rate began a long, slow decline in the late eighteenth century. The birth rate stayed high until the 1870s and then fell, reaching death-rate levels by the 1930s. The gap between them, the shaded area, is transitional growth.
There is a neat way to use such a picture. Because growth rates add up on the log scale, the total growth over a period is \(e\) raised to the sum of the annual growth rates, which is the area between the birth and death curves. For Sweden from 1800 to 1900, that area is about 0.97, which implies the population should have multiplied by \(e^{0.97} \approx 2.65\).


Added · new The emigration explanation is my addition. The numbers are computed from the HMD data. Note: slide 02-27 lists “Sweden 1900 2.3 million, 2000 5 million.” The HMD has 2.35 million in 1800 and 5.10 million in 1900, so the slide’s years look like they should be 1800 and 1900.
In fact, Sweden grew from 2.35 million in 1800 to 5.1 million in 1900, a factor of only 2.17. Where did the missing growth go? Births minus deaths leaves out migration, and nineteenth-century Sweden sent large numbers of emigrants to the United States. The formula \(R = b - d\) holds only for a closed population.


1.4.5 The world
Return to Table 1.2. World life expectancy rose from 27 years in 1800 to 65 in 2000, and is projected to reach 81 by 2100. The TFR fell from 6 to 2.7 and is projected to reach 2. Growth peaked at about 1.8 percent per year around 1950 and is projected to approach zero by 2100. On Figure 1.3 you can see the transitional growth as the excursion above the zero-growth line, and you can see how growth depends jointly on life expectancy and fertility.
The stylized facts we want to explain, then, are stationarity → transitional growth → stationarity (?). The next chapter asks a normative question: what population size is optimal, and for whom? Chapter 3 then turns to Malthus, his “trap,” and why neither population nor the economy grew much for thousands of years.

title: 1  Ten Thousand Years of Population
text:
1.5 Key ideas

Economic demography studies the consequences of population for welfare and the causes of population change. Totals and per-capita measures can tell very different stories.
Population growth is best measured proportionally. In the exponential model, the growth rate is the slope of log population: \(R = [\log N(t) - \log N(0)]/t\).
Human history has three phases: near-zero growth for millennia, accelerating growth, and recently slowing growth.
Growth depends on fertility (TFR) and survival: \(R \approx \log(\text{TFR} \times 0.4886 \times \text{survival to 30})/30\).
In the demographic transition, mortality falls first and fertility follows, producing a temporary burst of growth.

text:
1.6 Check your understanding


Added · new Q3 comes from your slide 02-18. The rest are new and avoid the Lab 1 graded questions.

Doubling times. Use Table 1.1 to compute how long it took world population to double at the growth rates of 1000–1500 and of 1750–2000.
Absolute versus proportional. World population grew by more people per year from 1750 to 2000 than in any earlier period, and it will likely continue adding tens of millions a year even as the growth rate falls. Give one question for which the absolute number matters more than the rate, and one for which the rate matters more.
Nigeria. In 2010, Nigeria’s TFR was about 6 and survival to age 30 about 0.8. Use the approximation to estimate its growth rate. How long would it take to double?
Per capita. CBO projects that the immigration surge raises GDP by 2.9 percent in 2034. What other number do you need to judge whether the average U.S. resident is better off, and where in the report would you find it?
Migration and growth. Explain why the area between Sweden’s birth and death curves overstates its population growth in the nineteenth century. Would the same be true for the United States in the same period? Why or why not?

text:
1.7 Further reading

Livi-Bacci, Massimo. 2017. “The Space and Strategy of Demographic Growth.” Chapter 1 of A Concise History of World Population, 6th ed. Wiley. Pages 1–27. A broad overview mixing biology, economics, and demography. It sets the stage for Malthusian constraints and the growth theories later in the course.

1  Ten Thousand Years of Population

title: 2  The Optimum Population
text:
2.1 Not too big, not too small
What size population is best? It is a slippery question, because the answer depends on who is asking (a peasant, a worker, a voter, a king, a president, a capitalist, “society”) and what they want to maximize (average welfare, longevity, cultural power, military power, the sum of everyone’s welfare).
The French demographer Alfred Sauvy, whose General Theory of Population is our guide here, insisted that “optimum” is an innocent word, a synonym for “best.” “The most violent opponents can agree on such a premise, even if they disagree on what they hold to be ‘best’.” He listed nine possible aims: individual welfare; the fastest increase of wealth; employment; power; long life and health; culture and knowledge; total welfare; the “sum of life” (population times average lifespan); and sheer numbers, where the optimum is the same as the maximum. Different aims give different optima. So we should really speak of optima, plural.
Sauvy also pointed out a contradiction in phrases like “the population arrived at its greatest strength and comfort.” Strength and comfort are generally maximized at different sizes. The same problem afflicts Jeremy Bentham’s “greatest amount of good for the greatest number.” There is usually a trade-off.
To isolate the effect of numbers alone, Sauvy held everything else constant: natural resources and past investment, technology, the age structure and the productivity of individuals, the distribution of income, working hours, and trade and migration. This is an abstraction, he admitted, since in practice “numbers rarely vary without changing (or being changed by) some other factor.” But it lets us think clearly.
Two more warnings from Sauvy. First, an optimum is a pointer, not a target. In his example, to say that India’s 500 million people “would be more at ease if there were only 300 million” is not to say “that 200 million should be shot.” Second, choosing an aim is an ethical matter, not a scientific one. Sauvy recounts the economist Sismondi’s challenge. Suppose technology allowed the king of England to live alone on his island, with machines doing all the work, at an extremely high standard of living. Would that be an optimum? Most people find the idea distasteful. Still, Sauvy observed, in Western societies the aim of individual welfare had come to dominate. So he concentrated on two optima: the economic optimum and the power optimum.

title: 2  The Optimum Population
text:
2.2 Total, average, and marginal product
We need three concepts that will reappear throughout the course.

The total product, \(TP(N)\), is the output of a population of \(N\) people.
The average product, \(AP(N) = TP(N)/N\), is output per person. With equal sharing, it is the standard of living.
The marginal product, \(MP(N)\), is the additional output from adding the \(N\)th person. Total product is the sum of the marginal products of everyone so far: \(TP(N) = MP(1) + MP(2) + \dots + MP(N)\).

Figure 2.1 shows how the three fit together, following Sauvy’s own diagrams.








Figure 2.1: Total, average, and marginal product (after Sauvy’s Figures 13–14). Top: total product. The marginal product is the slope of the TP curve; the average product is the slope of a ray from the origin to the curve. The steepest ray just touches TP at the economic optimum. Bottom: the marginal product peaks where TP is steepest (K), and crosses the average product at its maximum (the economic optimum).





Three facts to read off the figure:

Marginal product is the slope of total product. Where TP rises steeply, each extra person adds a lot. Where it flattens, they add little. The marginal product peaks at K, where total output grows fastest.
Average product is the slope of a ray from the origin. The ray to any point on the TP curve rises \(TP(N)\) over a run of \(N\), so its slope is \(TP(N)/N\).
At the economic optimum, the two slopes are equal. The steepest possible ray just touches the TP curve, so there the ray’s slope (AP) equals the curve’s slope (MP). In the bottom panel, this is where the MP curve crosses the AP curve at the top of the AP curve.
crumbs: Population and the economy: big theories
2  The Optimum Population

title: 2  The Optimum Population
text:
2.3 The economic optimum
Sauvy’s economic optimum is the population that maximizes the average standard of living, \(AP\). It takes an individual perspective. Size benefits not “society” but each person through their standard of living, and inequality is not part of the objective.
Why is there an optimum at all? Sauvy’s illustration: imagine England with only 50 to 100 people. Even with advanced technology, they could not run railways or steel foundries, and would live as craftsmen or shepherds. Now imagine 200 to 500 million people on the same island, cultivating even the poorest soils by hand. In both cases the standard of living would be very low. Somewhere in between lies the best size. (A smaller example from lecture: what is the optimum size for a freshman English seminar?)

2.3.1 Why a population can be too small: increasing returns
The lecture lists three reasons a population can be too small:

No specialization. Adam Smith’s pin factory: dividing tasks among workers multiplies their output.
No complementarity. Some tasks need more than one person, like holding a ladder while someone changes a light bulb.
Fixed costs. Roads, machines, and teachers are only worthwhile if enough people share them.



Added · from readings The examples in the next three paragraphs are from Sauvy 1966, pp. 45–46 and 48–49, and Livi-Bacci 2017, pp. 1 and 21.
Sauvy fills these out with examples. Specialization, he stresses, is not a matter of new technology. It lets a population use tools it already knows about but couldn’t use without enough people to specialize. “For ten readers one uses a typewriter, for one thousand a printing press.” Even without machines, much work gets cheaper per unit as it is shared: “it does not, for instance, take ten times as long to wash ten plates as to wash one.” Increasing returns of this kind, he notes, show up mostly in activities that transform uniform materials, such as manufacturing.
His second source of increasing returns is communal expenses, or “overheads.” Some costs barely depend on the number of people who share them: the upkeep of a bridge that isn’t crowded, the ruler’s house, a radio programme. The more people there are, the smaller each person’s share. Sauvy is careful to give the objection. Sooner or later one more user will make the bridge too crowded and it will have to be widened, so these costs are only fixed up to a point. But, he concludes, “the fact remains that returns are increased by a rise in the number of men.”
Size matters for settlement too. Sauvy observes that the first Europeans in America “would have been ill-advised to spread out too much.” They needed each other, and trade required people concentrated at a few coastal points. Livi-Bacci adds two more reasons from the deep past. A very small group cannot survive at all: groups must be large enough “to ensure a reasonable choice of partners and to survive catastrophic events.” And only a large population can mobilize the labor to build houses, cities, roads, bridges, ports, and canals. That is why, for most of history, a densely settled landscape was read as a sign of prosperity, and deserted land as a sign of decline.


2.3.2 Why a population can be too big: diminishing returns
The lecture’s reasons a population can be too big:

Diminishing marginal returns. Adding workers to a fixed amount of land adds less and less output.
Variable quality of inputs. The best land is farmed first, so later acres are less productive.
The neoclassical version. Each additional unit of capital, even if identical, adds less to productivity than the one before.



Added · from readings Sauvy 1966, pp. 44–46.
Sauvy’s examples come from natural resources. “The reserves in mines vary; game does not increase proportionally to the number of hunters; fishing grounds have to be moved.” The same holds for hydroelectric dams, forests, and tidal energy. In each case the resource is limited, and more people means less for each.
Sauvy also answers a common objection: isn’t every activity subject to increasing and then decreasing returns? A factory, after all, first becomes more productive as workers are added, and then less so once they get in each other’s way. His answer turns on whether the fixed input can be copied. When a factory is full, you can build a second or third one at about the same cost. But “a mine, a farm, a fishing ground may have decreasing returns because it is difficult to build or find a second similar to the first.” Manufacturing can be replicated, but land and natural resources cannot. That is why diminishing returns bite hardest in agriculture, and why they are central to Malthus, the subject of the next chapter.


2.3.3 Finding the optimum
The relationship between the curves is the key to finding the optimum. When the marginal product is above the average, adding a person pulls the average up. When it is below, adding a person pulls the average down. So the average product is at its maximum exactly where the marginal product crosses it. Sauvy put it as “when the marginal output equals the average output, the latter is not changing.”

title: 2  The Optimum Population
text:
2.4 The power optimum


Added · from readings Cathedrals and interplanetary travel are from Sauvy 1966, p. 59. The variable subsistence level (below) is from pp. 55–56.
Now take the point of view of the ruler, or of society as a whole (“La France”). Sauvy defines power as total production beyond what is needed for subsistence. It is the surplus available for pyramids, armies, cathedrals, or space programs. Power need not be military. Sauvy’s examples include national prestige and culture. “In building cathedrals collectively,” he writes, “the Middle Ages were seeking the power optimum rather than the economic optimum. The same applies to interplanetary travel.” Each person adds their marginal product to output but must be fed, so
\[
\text{power}(N) = TP(N) - N \times \text{subsistence} = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \left[ MP(i) - \text{subsistence} \right].
\]
Do more people always mean more power? No. A person whose marginal product exceeds subsistence adds to the surplus. A person whose marginal product falls short of subsistence is a net cost, and must be fed from others’ output. So power is maximized at the population where the marginal product equals subsistence.
What counts as “subsistence”? Sauvy first treats it as fixed, the bare minimum to keep people alive and working. Then he loosens the assumption. People produce more when better fed, and they get used to a way of life. He reports that commanders claimed soldiers or workers deprived of tobacco would produce less. So the subsistence level that maximizes power depends on the country and the times. In wartime, Sauvy notes, it was higher in the United States than in Germany, and higher in Germany than in the Soviet Union.

title: 2  The Optimum Population
text:
2.5 Ordering the optima
Figure 2.2 puts these together with two more reference points: the minimum population (the smallest that can feed itself, where the average product first reaches subsistence) and the maximum population (the largest that can feed itself, where the average product falls back to subsistence).








Figure 2.2: Sauvy’s optima. The marginal product (orange) rises and then falls. The average product (red) peaks where the marginal product crosses it: the economic optimum. The power optimum is where the marginal product falls to subsistence. The minimum and maximum populations are where the average product equals subsistence.





Sauvy shows that, in general,
\[
O_{\min} < O_{\text{econ}} < O_{\text{pow}} < O_{\max}.
\]
The power optimum is larger than the economic optimum, because past the economic optimum each extra person still produces more than they need to subsist, adding to the ruler’s surplus while lowering everyone’s average. The power optimum is smaller than the maximum, because between the two each extra person produces less than subsistence and must be fed by others.
How can people survive when their marginal product is below subsistence? Because output is shared. As long as the average product is above subsistence, the group as a whole can feed everyone.

title: 2  The Optimum Population
text:
2.8 Extensions from Sauvy


Added · from readings Overheads and military power are from Sauvy 1966, pp. 47–48 and 53–55 (the military discussion is just past the assigned pages).
Overheads raise the optimum. Suppose a population suddenly has to pay a fixed cost, such as tribute to a foreign power or a long-postponed public work. Total output available for consumption falls by a fixed amount at every population size. Because the burden can be shared, more people now help. In Sauvy’s words: “The greater the load men have to bear, the greater their advantage is in being numerous to bear it; so that when a country gets into debt with the outside world, its wealth decreases but its optimum population rises.”
Military power raises the power optimum further. Soldiers produce nothing but must be fed. A state that wants an army as well as weapons needs a population even larger than the power optimum, to feed the soldiers out of the surplus.


Added · from readings Quotes in the next three paragraphs are from Sauvy 1966, pp. 62–63, which are past the assigned pages. The “French intellectual tradition” framing follows lecture.
Rulers and the economic optimum. Why did it take so long for anyone to ask which population makes the average person best off? Sauvy’s answer is that the people whose views counted generally preferred the power optimum. “As a general rule,” he writes, “whoever holds or seeks power wishes to increase numbers.” The patriarch welcomes every birth in his tribe, because his power “is almost identical with his wealth.” The absolute monarch wants more subjects, and his wealth too “coincides with his power because it is separate from the rest of the population.” Under a dominant class with absolute power, “the more slaves, labourers, or workers, the more stable its power.” Then comes the passage quoted in lecture:

“Before the nineteenth century this desire for power used to be so predominant that it hampered for a long time the understanding of the economic optimum. At about the time when this was understood, regal authority began to decline.” (p. 62)

Notice the order in that second sentence: first an idea is understood, and then authority declines. This fits a long French intellectual tradition that treats ideas as real forces in history, so that how people understand their situation shapes what they do next. Once people could see that a larger population might serve the king’s power at the expense of their own standard of living, the case for royal authority weakened.
But Sauvy’s own examples show that the causation can run the other way too. The same contrast between power and welfare appears inside the family. “As long as children remained under the narrow and direct authority of the father, power was by far the main objective. With the emancipation of children the birth rate has decreased because economic considerations have taken the upper hand.” Here a change in conditions, the father’s weakening authority, comes first, and the economic way of thinking follows. Sauvy finds the same pattern in organizations. Senior civil servants want bigger staffs, because staff is power. A private firm, or an efficiency-minded public agency, wants as few people as possible on each task. Which optimum you favour depends on where you stand.
So did the idea of the economic optimum bring down kings, or did the decline of kings make the idea thinkable? Most likely both. New ideas made the old order look less legitimate, and a changing world made the new ideas more persuasive. It is hard to say which was cause and which was effect. Keep that question in mind throughout the course: when behaviour and ideas about behaviour change together, which one is driving?

section: 2.10 Critiques, and why the framework is still useful
text:
2.10 Critiques, and why the framework is still useful


Added · from readings The camel-shaped curve and Gini are from Sauvy 1966, p. 42. Gini’s first name is from general knowledge.
The optimum population has obvious limits:

It assumes fixed technology. Perhaps each population density has its own appropriate technology. We’ll read Ester Boserup on this (Chapter 5).
The optimum may not be a single point. The objective could have many peaks, or a wide, flat top, so that a broad range of sizes is about equally good. Sauvy himself mentions a “camel-shaped curve with two humps.” The Italian statistician Corrado Gini argued for two optima, one at the agricultural stage of development and one at the industrial stage. That example also shows how closely this critique is tied to the first one, about technology.
It ignores feedback between population size and technological level.

And the optimum is a theoretical idea, not a requirement. It doesn’t mean we should get rid of people if we are above it.
Still, the framework is very useful. It shows how the optima are ordered in general, and it shows that the “best” population depends on the objective, which means on whose perspective we take. The tools will also come back. The total product picture will be useful for the Solow growth model, and the marginal product picture for Malthus (next chapter) and for migration.

title: 3  The World According to Malthus
text:
3.1 The puzzle of stationarity
Here is a puzzle to start. For almost all of human history, the world’s population grew so slowly that it was very nearly stationary. Over long stretches, the average woman left behind about one surviving daughter, who replaced her. How did we manage that?
It is harder than it sounds. Suppose instead that each woman had raised, on average, 1.10 surviving daughters instead of 1.00. That seems like a small difference. But with a generation length of about 29 years, it implies a growth rate of about 0.33 percent per year. Sustained for 10,000 years, the time since the beginning of agriculture, that growth would multiply a population by roughly 200,000,000,000,000. Start with a few million people and you end up with far more humans than there are grains of sand on Earth. Go the other way, to 0.90 daughters, and humanity goes extinct.
So the near-stationarity of the past calls for an explanation. There are two kinds of answer:
The accident story has a problem. Random ups and downs don’t cancel out on their own. Left alone, a population whose growth rate wanders randomly will eventually either explode or die out. The near-stationarity of human numbers over millennia suggests a system. Malthus’s great contribution was to describe what that system might be.
A good theory of the pre-industrial world needs to explain three things:
I. Why populations were roughly stationary, neither exploding nor going extinct. II. Why there were nonetheless oscillations, periods of growth followed by periods of decline. III. Why the standard of living of ordinary people didn’t improve much over the long run, even as technology slowly advanced.
Keep these three in mind. We’ll come back to see how well Malthus does on each.

3  The World According to Malthus

title: 3  The World According to Malthus
text:
Added · new Your slide 05-03 poses the 1.10-daughters question. The 29-year generation and the worked numbers are mine.




Accident. The population of, say, England in 1801 (about 9 million) was the cumulative result of a long string of chance events: plagues, good harvests, wars, invasions. Growth and decline happened to cancel out.
System. Something pushed population back toward a particular level whenever it drifted away. On this view, the population of 1801 was an equilibrium, the outcome of a self-correcting system.

title: 3  The World According to Malthus
text:
3.2 A pamphlet against optimism

3.2.1 Context


Added · new Dates, anonymous publication, and the 1803 edition are from general knowledge. Slide 05-12 has only the short biography.
Thomas Robert Malthus (1766–1834) was a young English clergyman when, in 1798, he anonymously published An Essay on the Principle of Population, as it Affects the Future Improvement of Society. He later became one of the first professors of political economy, at the East India Company’s college, and spent the rest of his life revising and expanding the Essay. The second edition (1803) was nearly a new book, packed with data from around the world.


Added · new The Godwin/Condorcet context comes from Malthus 1798 (Preface; Chs. 8–15). That the “friend” was his father is from general knowledge.
The first edition was not written as a dispassionate study of demography. It was a reply to an argument. The 1790s were years of revolutionary optimism. The French Revolution, the spread of printing, and the discoveries of science had convinced writers like William Godwin in England and the Marquis de Condorcet in France that humanity was on the verge of limitless improvement. Godwin imagined a society of equality and reason, in which property would be shared, crime would vanish, and each person would need to work only half an hour a day. Malthus’s Preface says the Essay began in a conversation with “a friend” about one of Godwin’s essays (the friend was his own father, an admirer of Godwin).
Malthus’s answer was that no reform of institutions, however wise, could overcome a more basic problem: the tendency of population to outrun food. He didn’t enjoy this conclusion, or at least he said he didn’t:






In his own words



“The view which he has given of human life has a melancholy hue, but he feels conscious that he has drawn these dark tints from a conviction that they are really in the picture, and not from a jaundiced eye or an inherent spleen of disposition.” (Preface, 1798)




Added · from readings Ostrich passage: Malthus 1798, Ch. 1 (assigned). The comment about the irony is mine.
Malthus also insisted on a rule of evidence that is still a good one. He refused to argue with predictions that had no basis in past experience:

“A writer may tell me that he thinks man will ultimately become an ostrich. I cannot properly contradict him. But before he can expect to bring any reasonable person over to his opinion, he ought to shew that the necks of mankind have been gradually elongating…” (Chapter 1)

In other words: if you claim the future will be different, show me a trend. Keep this rule in mind. It is ironic, because the trend that would overturn Malthus’s own predictions, the industrial revolution, was getting under way in England as he wrote.


Added · from readings Postulates and the geometric vs. arithmetic ratios come from Malthus 1798, Chs. 1–2 (assigned). They are not in your slides or lab. The table and the commentary on it are mine.


3.2.2 The argument in two postulates
Malthus builds his case on two assumptions, which he calls postulata:

“First, That food is necessary to the existence of man. Secondly, That the passion between the sexes is necessary and will remain nearly in its present state.” (Chapter 1)

From these he draws his famous contrast:

“Population, when unchecked, increases in a geometrical ratio. Subsistence increases only in an arithmetical ratio. A slight acquaintance with numbers will shew the immensity of the first power in comparison of the second.” (Chapter 1)

“Geometrical” means growth by multiplication: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. “Arithmetical” means growth by addition: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Malthus took the doubling time of population from the American colonies, where land was plentiful and the population doubled about every 25 years. For food, he made what he considered an extremely generous assumption: Britain’s food supply could be increased every 25 years by an amount equal to the entire current harvest. Table 3.1 reproduces his worked example for Britain.

Two things about this table. First, the numbers aren’t a forecast. Malthus didn’t think Britain would ever have 77 million starving people. His point was that this gap could never actually open up. Something has to stop population growth long before it does. The interesting question is what.


Added · from readings Reservoir metaphor: Malthus 1798, Ch. 6 (not assigned). Calling the ratios rhetorical is my framing.
Second, the specific “ratios” are rhetorical. Modern readers often fixate on whether food really grows arithmetically (it doesn’t, exactly). But nothing in Malthus’s argument depends on the exact form. What matters is that land is fixed, so each additional worker adds less food than the one before. Malthus put this more vividly in Chapter 6. A country with abundant empty land is like “a great reservoir of water, supplied by a moderate stream.” A growing population can draw on the reservoir for a while, “but the sooner, undoubtedly, will the reservoir be exhausted, and the streams only remain.”


3.2.3 Checks: preventive and positive
If population can’t actually grow geometrically for long, something must be checking it. Malthus identifies two kinds of check:






In his own words



“…a foresight of the difficulties attending the rearing of a family acts as a preventive check, and the actual distresses of some of the lower classes, by which they are disabled from giving the proper food and attention to their children, act as a positive check to the natural increase of population.” (Chapter 4)




Added · new The point about late marriage (women in their mid-twenties) as the main fertility lever is from general knowledge. Slide 05-13 makes the marriage link.
In modern terms:

The preventive check works through fertility. People foresee the cost of supporting a family and delay marriage, or don’t marry at all. In pre-industrial Europe, where nearly all births happened within marriage and people married late (mid-twenties for women) or not at all, the age at marriage was the main lever controlling the birth rate.
The positive check works through mortality. When food is scarce, more people die, especially infants and children of the poor.



Added · from readings Slide 05-11 poses the “vice” question. This answer is mine, drawn from Malthus 1798, Chs. 1 and 5.
Malthus summed up all the checks with a phrase that shocks modern readers: “All these checks may be fairly resolved into misery and vice” (Chapter 5). Misery is the positive check: hunger, disease, early death. Vice is harder for us to interpret. For Malthus, a clergyman, it included prostitution, sex outside marriage, and what he called “vicious customs with respect to women.” That category takes in contraception and abortion, which he regarded as immoral. It also included war. (The list in Chapter 5 is “vicious customs with respect to women, great cities, unwholesome manufactures, luxury, pestilence, and war.”) So when Malthus writes about “even the most vicious societies,” he doesn’t mean societies where people are cruel. He means societies where the birth rate is held down by practices he disapproved of.


Added · new Moral restraint (added in 1803) is from general knowledge, not the assigned texts.
In the second edition, Malthus softened his position a little. He added a third category, moral restraint: delaying marriage without vice. This was the preventive check he approved of, and as we’ll see, it is the one hope he held out for improving the lot of the poor.


Added · new My caveat. The claim that Chinese families controlled fertility is from general knowledge, not your materials.
A note on reading Malthus. He wrote with the assumptions of an English gentleman of the 1790s. His descriptions of “savages,” of China, and of the English poor draw on travelers’ tales and the prejudices of his class. Historians have since overturned many of his specific claims. For example, later research has found that pre-industrial Chinese families controlled their fertility in ways Malthus didn’t recognize. Read him for the structure of the argument, which has proven remarkably durable, not for his ethnography.


3.2.4 Oscillation
Malthus didn’t think population sat quietly at its limit. He described a cycle, and this passage from Chapter 2 is the heart of the model:






In his own words



“The constant effort towards population, which is found to act even in the most vicious societies, increases the number of people before the means of subsistence are increased. The food therefore which before supported seven millions must now be divided among seven millions and a half or eight millions. The poor consequently must live much worse, and many of them be reduced to severe distress. The number of labourers also being above the proportion of the work in the market, the price of labour must tend toward a decrease, while the price of provisions would at the same time tend to rise. … During this season of distress, the discouragements to marriage, and the difficulty of rearing a family are so great that population is at a stand. In the mean time the cheapness of labour, the plenty of labourers, and the necessity of an increased industry amongst them, encourage cultivators to employ more labour upon their land, to turn up fresh soil, and to manure and improve more completely what is already in tillage, till ultimately the means of subsistence become in the same proportion to the population as at the period from which we set out. The situation of the labourer being then again tolerably comfortable, the restraints to population are in some degree loosened, and the same retrograde and progressive movements with respect to happiness are repeated.” (Chapter 2)


We can boil this down to a cycle:

Population increases.
Laborers suffer: wages fall and food prices rise.
People marry later and have fewer children; more die.
Farmers, with cheap labor available, cultivate more intensively.
“Tolerable comfort” is re-established.
Restraints loosen. Go back to step 1.



Added · from readings “Histories of the higher classes”: Malthus 1798, Ch. 2 (assigned). The link to historical demography is mine.
Malthus admitted that this oscillation would be hard to see. One reason he gave is especially interesting for a course that works with data. “The histories of mankind that we possess are histories only of the higher classes.” To detect the cycle, he wrote, you would need to know the number of marriages relative to the number of adults, the comparative mortality among the children of the poor and the comfortable, and “the variations in the real price of labour.” He was describing, almost exactly, the research program of historical demography, which 150 years later reconstructed births, deaths, marriages, and real wages from parish registers. We’ll meet some of its results in Section 3.6.

title: 3  The World According to Malthus
text:
3.3 Turning Malthus into a model
Malthus never drew a diagram, but his argument fits neatly into one. The version we use here was popularized by the economic demographer Ronald Lee (1980), and it is the diagram you’ll draw in lecture and in the lab. It combines three relationships, each a function of the real wage, w. Think of the wage as the standard of living of ordinary working people: how much food a day’s labor can buy.

3.3.1 Relationship 1: more people, lower wages
Malthus’s economy has one fixed resource (land) and one variable resource (labor). There is no capital accumulation. When more workers farm the same land, each additional worker adds less to output than the one before. This is the law of diminishing returns. In a competitive labor market, the wage equals what the last worker adds (the marginal product of labor). So more people means lower wages.






Why does the wage equal the marginal product?





Two forces push the wage toward the marginal product. An employer won’t hire an extra worker if that worker would cost more than they add to output, so wages can’t stay above the marginal product. And in a competitive market, a worker paid less than their marginal product could be hired away by another employer, so wages can’t stay below it either. Malthus’s world wasn’t perfectly competitive, as he himself complained about the “combination among the rich” that kept wages down. But the basic logic, that crowding more labor onto fixed land lowers its reward, doesn’t depend on perfect competition.



We draw this as a downward-sloping curve, w(N). One unusual feature: we put population on the vertical axis and the wage on the horizontal axis. That is backwards from the usual labor-demand picture, but it lets us line this curve up with the next two, which also have the wage on the horizontal axis.


3.3.2 Relationships 2 and 3: births and deaths respond to wages
The birth rate rises with wages, b(w). When times are good, more people can afford to marry, and they marry younger. That is the preventive check loosening. The curve flattens at high wages, because there are biological and social limits to how high fertility can go.
The death rate falls with wages, d(w). When times are good, fewer people die of hunger and hunger-related disease. That is the positive check relaxing.
We measure both as crude rates: births or deaths per year, divided by the population. (Demographers call them “crude” because the denominator is everyone, not just the people actually at risk, such as women of childbearing age.) The growth rate of the population is then simply
\[
\text{growth rate} = b(w) - d(w).
\]


3.3.3 Putting it together
Figure 3.1 stacks the pieces. The top panel shows births and deaths as functions of the wage. Where the curves cross, at the wage w*, births equal deaths and the population neither grows nor shrinks. The bottom panel shows the population size that produces each wage. Reading down from w* to the w(N) curve gives the equilibrium population, N*.








Figure 3.1: The Malthusian model. Top: birth and death rates depend on the wage. Bottom: the wage depends on population size. The equilibrium wage w* is where births equal deaths; N* is the population that produces that wage.







Added · new My framing (“division of labor” between the two panels). It isn’t stated this way in your slides.
Notice what sets each equilibrium value. The equilibrium wage w* is determined entirely by the top panel: by demographic behavior, the birth and death schedules. Technology and land, the bottom panel, play no role in setting it. The equilibrium population N* is then whatever size of population drives the wage to w*. This division of labor between the two panels turns out to drive almost every “dismal” result in the next section.


3.3.4 Why the equilibrium is stable


Added · new The year-by-year simulation figure is new. Your slides make this point with the diagram and the app.
Suppose the population starts above N*, at N′. Because there are too many people for the land, the wage is below w*. At that low wage, the top panel shows the death rate above the birth rate, so the population shrinks. As it shrinks, the wage rises, and the gap between deaths and births narrows. The process continues until the population is back at N* and the wage back at w*. Figure 3.2 simulates this year by year.








Figure 3.2: Return to equilibrium from a population that starts 50 percent too large. Simulated with the model of the previous figure.





This self-correction answers puzzle I from the start of the chapter. Population was roughly stationary not by accident but because any departure from N* set off forces that pushed it back. (What happens if population starts below N*? Work it out yourself. It’s the first “Check your understanding” question at the end of the chapter.)


Added · new The explanation of oscillations as shocks plus lags is my addition.
What about puzzle II, the oscillations? In the simple model above, population glides smoothly back to equilibrium. Real populations are hit by constant shocks: good and bad harvests, epidemics, wars. Each shock knocks the population off its equilibrium, and the system then works to pull it back. The result is the kind of irregular “retrograde and progressive movements” that Malthus described. Some economists also think that delays in the system (it takes twenty years to raise a new worker) can produce genuine cycles that overshoot the equilibrium.

3  The World According to Malthus

title: 3  The World According to Malthus
text:
3.4 Dismal conclusions


Added · new “Dismal science” aside is from general knowledge.
Economics was nicknamed “the dismal science” in the nineteenth century, and Malthus is much of the reason. The diagram shows why. Let’s use it to ask what happens when something good happens.

3.4.1 Case 1: A new technology
Suppose farmers discover a better plough, a new crop rotation, or a more productive crop. At every population size, the land now produces more food, so the wage is higher. In the diagram, the w(N) curve shifts outward (Figure 3.3).








Figure 3.3: A technological improvement shifts w(N) outward (dashed). The birth and death curves are unchanged, so the long-run wage is unchanged. Only population is larger.





In the short run, life gets better. With the same number of people and more food, wages rise above w*. But at the higher wage, births exceed deaths and the population grows. It keeps growing until the wage has been pushed back down to w*, which hasn’t changed, because nothing in the top panel has changed. The long-run result: more people, living at exactly the old standard of living. Technology raises population, not living standards.


Added · from readings Quote from Malthus 1798, Ch. 7 (not assigned).
This is the core of Malthus’s case against Godwin and Condorcet. Any improvement is eventually “eaten” by population growth. As Malthus put it, countries are “populous according to the quantity of human food which they produce, and happy according to the liberality with which that food is divided” (Chapter 7). More food makes a country more populous, not happier.
This also answers puzzle III. Pre-industrial technology did improve, slowly, over the centuries. But the improvement showed up as larger populations, not as higher wages.


3.4.2 Case 2: Lower mortality
Malthus was writing just as Edward Jenner was introducing vaccination against smallpox (1796). Surely saving lives is good? Suppose a medical advance lowers the death rate at every wage, shifting d(w) down (Figure 3.4).








Figure 3.4: A decline in mortality shifts d(w) down (dashed). The new equilibrium has a lower wage (w’) and a larger population (N’).







Added · new The point that the death rate’s gain is mostly “clawed back” comes from the model simulation, not your slides.
At the old wage, births now exceed deaths, so the population grows. Growth pushes the wage down until births and deaths are equal again, at a new, lower equilibrium wage w′. The new equilibrium has a larger population, a lower standard of living, and a lower birth rate. And the death rate? It ends up only modestly below where it started: much of the gain is clawed back as the lower wage raises hunger-related mortality.


Added · from readings Lee 1980, p. 543 (in the assigned pages). Not in your slides.
This is Lee’s (1980) key point about the model: the equilibrium wage isn’t a fixed biological “subsistence” level. It depends on mortality, and mortality could change for reasons that had nothing to do with the economy. Epidemic diseases came and went largely on their own schedule. So disease environments could change the long-run standard of living even if nothing else changed.
Malthus pressed this logic to an extreme in a notorious passage in his later editions:

“To act consistently therefore, we should facilitate, instead of foolishly and vainly endeavouring to impede, the operations of nature in producing this mortality… Instead of recommending cleanliness to the poor, we should encourage contrary habits. In our towns we should make the streets narrower, crowd more people into the houses, and court the return of the plague.” (Book IV, Chapter V)



Added · new Your slide 06-08 quotes the passage. Reading it as sarcasm is my interpretation, checked against its context in the 1817 edition, Bk. IV, Ch. V.
Read this passage carefully: it is sarcasm, not a policy proposal. Malthus is attacking people who wanted to encourage early marriage. His point is that if society encourages more births without more food, it is implicitly choosing more deaths, so it might as well be honest about it. The passage is a reductio ad absurdum, meant to push readers toward the preventive check. The fact that it is so often quoted as Malthus’s sincere view tells you something about his reputation.


3.4.3 Case 3: The preventive check, Malthus’s hope
Is there anything that can raise the standard of living in the long run? The diagram says yes: anything that shifts the top panel in the right direction. In particular, suppose people marry later and have fewer children at every wage level, so the b(w) curve shifts down (Figure 3.5).








Figure 3.5: A stronger preventive check shifts b(w) down (dashed). The equilibrium wage rises (w’), the equilibrium death rate falls, and the population is smaller (N’).





Now births fall short of deaths at the old wage, the population shrinks, the wage rises, and the new equilibrium has a higher wage, lower mortality, and a smaller population. This is why Malthus favored “moral restraint.” It was the one route to a permanently better life for ordinary people. Notice that it works by changing behavior, the top panel, not technology, the bottom panel.


Added · from readings Malthus’s Norway and Sweden chapters (lab reading): the 1799 visit and the mortality figures.
Malthus saw the preventive check at its strongest in Norway, which he visited in 1799. Norway’s death rate was remarkably low, about 1 death per 48 people per year (21 per thousand). Sweden’s, next door, was about 1 in 35 (29 per thousand). Malthus credited the difference not to Norway’s climate but to its institutions, which made it hard for young people to marry before they could support a family. Read his account of how those institutions worked in the chapters assigned with the lab. Lab 2 asks you about it.


Added · from readings Slide 06-15 raises the poor laws. The argument and quote are from Malthus 1798, Ch. 5 (not assigned).
The same logic is behind Malthus’s best-known policy position, his opposition to the English Poor Laws, the parish system of relief for the poor. He argued that by promising support to families who couldn’t support themselves, the Poor Laws encouraged early marriage without increasing the food supply, and so “may be said therefore in some measure to create the poor which they maintain” (Chapter 5).


3.4.4 A ruler’s point of view
Not everyone wants a high wage. In Chapter 2 we met Alfred Sauvy’s distinction between the economic optimum (the population that maximizes output per person) and the power optimum (the population that maximizes the surplus available to the state, for armies, monuments, or tribute). A ruler interested in power may prefer a large population at a low wage. Malthus saw this clearly:


Added · from readings Malthus 1798, Ch. 7 (not assigned). Sauvy link is from your slide 06-15/16.

“It may appear to be the interest of the rulers, and the rich of a state, to force population, and thereby lower the price of labour, and consequently the expense of fleets and armies, and the cost of manufactures for foreign sale…” (Chapter 7)



Added · from readings From Malthus’s Sweden chapter (lab reading, a paragraph after the assigned ones). The 2013 population aside is mine.
He found a real example in Sweden, whose government was trying to raise its population through hospitals and other encouragements. “Strange to say!” he wrote, “the government and the political economists of Sweden are continually calling out for population! population!” If Sweden wanted nine or ten million people, Malthus said, it simply needed to produce enough food for them, “and they may rest perfectly assured that they will not want mouths to eat it.” (Sweden’s population passed 9.5 million in 2013, though not for Malthusian reasons.)


3.4.5 Subsistence versus equilibrium
People often summarize Malthus as saying that the poor are always kept at “subsistence,” the bare biological minimum needed to survive. The diagram shows why that is not quite right. The equilibrium wage w* is set by the birth and death schedules, and those reflect behavior and institutions, such as how late people marry and how a society shares food in bad years, as well as biology. Lee calls w* the “conventional standard of living.” Two societies with the same land and technology could settle at quite different living standards if one had a stronger preventive check than the other. Malthus believed that this was exactly the difference between northwestern Europe, with its late marriage, and the places he thought married early and universally.


3.4.6 Try it: the Malthus app


Added · new The app is the course’s own Malthus app (ShinyApps/new-malthus in the 2025 course repo), exported with Shinylive so it runs in the browser, in its own tab. The three questions are mine; they use only a change in starting population, the speed of adjustment, and a rise in the death level, to stay clear of the Lab 2 graded scenarios (a shift in the wage curve, a higher birth rate, an expulsion, and the ruler’s policy options).
The app simulates the two-panel model from this chapter. The top-left panel is the demography (birth and death rates against the wage), the bottom-left is the economy (population against the wage), and the right-hand panels trace population and wages over time. The economy starts in equilibrium; new conditions take effect at time 0, and you press the small “play” triangle under the time slider to watch what happens. It opens in a new tab, so you can make it full screen and keep this page open alongside it. (The first load can take a few seconds while R starts up in your browser.)



The Malthus app at its starting values. Click to open it in a new tab.


Open the Malthus app in a new tab ↗
Before you move each slider, write down what you expect to happen. Then check.

Too many people. Set “Population N at time t=0” to 8 and press play. Before you do: will wages start above or below their equilibrium level? Which will be higher at first, the birth rate or the death rate?
How fast? Using the same run, step through time with the arrow keys. About how many periods does it take for population to close half the gap between 8 and its equilibrium of 5? Does it ever overshoot?
A harsher disease environment. Return N to 5 and raise “death level d’(w)” from 0.10 to 0.13, as if a new disease arrived. Predict the new long-run wage and population before you press play. Who ends up better off: the people living before or after the change?

Lab 2 asks you to use the app to trace the short- and long-run effects of a change in the economy.

title: 3  The World According to Malthus
section: 3.5 Data in action: Malthus in Sweden
text:
3.5 Data in action: Malthus in Sweden


Added · new Tabellverket (1749) is from general knowledge. The HMD/Berkeley line is from your lab.
Malthus wasn’t only a theorist. In later editions he became an avid collector of data, and some of the best data he found came from Sweden. Sweden began a national system of population statistics, the Tabellverket, in 1749, so it has the longest continuous national series of births, deaths, and population in the world. Those records are the source of the Swedish series in the Human Mortality Database (HMD), founded at Berkeley and the Max Planck Institute for Demographic Research, which we use in Lab 2.

3.5.1 What Malthus saw


Added · from readings Bark bread and Wargentin’s table come from Malthus’s Sweden chapter (lab reading). Putting them next to the HMD numbers is my addition.
When Malthus traveled through Sweden in the summer of 1799, he found a country in crisis after a bad harvest. In the provinces near Norway, “a considerable portion of the people was living upon bread made of the inner bark of the fir, and of dried sorrel, absolutely without any mixture of meal.” He also found the Swedish statistician Pehr Wargentin’s analysis of the registers, which made a striking claim: “the births, marriages and deaths increase and decrease according to the state of the harvests.” Malthus reproduced Wargentin’s figures for two bad and two good harvest years. Table 3.2 puts them next to the corresponding HMD numbers.




Table 3.2: Swedish vital events in bad and good harvest years: Wargentin’s figures (as quoted by Malthus) and the Human Mortality Database.
