Added · new Attributing the gap to Finland is my inference. Neither source says so.
The two sources disagree on the level. Wargentin’s counts are about a third higher, most likely because his tables covered the whole Swedish realm, which then included Finland, while the HMD uses Sweden’s present-day borders. But they tell the same story. In the barren years 1757–58, deaths were high and births low. In the abundant years 1759–60, deaths fell and births rose. That is the signature of a Malthusian economy: good times raise births and lower deaths; bad times do the reverse.


3.5.2 The long view
Figure 3.6 shows Swedish crude birth and death rates from 1751 to 2014.


Show the R code
op <- par(mar = c(4, 4.2, 1, 1))
plot(swe$year, swe$cdr, type = "l", col = col_d, lwd = 1.5,
     ylim = c(0, max(swe$cdr)), xlab = "Year", ylab = "Per 1,000 population")
lines(swe$year, swe$cbr, col = col_b, lwd = 1.5)
legend("topright", c("Crude birth rate", "Crude death rate"),
       col = c(col_b, col_d), lwd = 2, bty = "n")
text(1773, swe$cdr[swe$year == 1773], "1773", pos = 4, cex = 0.8)
par(op)








Figure 3.6: Crude birth and death rates, Sweden, 1751–2014. Source: Human Mortality Database.





Two features stand out. The first is the very large year-to-year volatility in the eighteenth century, especially in deaths. The tallest spike, in 1773, came after harvest failures in 1771–72 brought famine and epidemic disease: the crude death rate reached 52 per thousand, nearly twice its usual level. Births that year fell to 25 per thousand. The second feature is the long-run decline of both rates, deaths first and then births. This is the demographic transition, which we met in Chapter 1. It is precisely what Malthus’s model does not anticipate.


3.5.3 Births against deaths
If Malthusian forces were at work, years with high death rates (bad times) should also be years with low birth rates. Figure 3.7 plots each year’s birth rate against its death rate for 1751–1800, the half-century in which Malthus was writing.


Show the R code
s <- swe$year %in% 1751:1800
r <- cor(swe$cbr[s], swe$cdr[s])
op <- par(mar = c(4, 4.2, 1, 1))
plot(swe$cdr[s], swe$cbr[s], pch = 19, col = "grey30", cex = 0.8,
     xlab = "Crude death rate (per 1,000)", ylab = "Crude birth rate (per 1,000)")
abline(lm(cbr ~ cdr, data = swe, subset = s), lwd = 2)
## highlight Wargentin's four years (see the table above)
wy <- swe$year %in% 1757:1760
points(swe$cdr[wy], swe$cbr[wy], pch = 19, col = "#e66101", cex = 1.1)
lab <- swe$year %in% c(1757, 1758, 1760, 1772, 1773)
text(swe$cdr[lab], swe$cbr[lab], swe$year[lab], pos = c(2, 4, 2, 3, 2), cex = 0.8)
## 1759 sits in the densest part of the cloud: label it with a leader line
x59 <- swe$cdr[swe$year == 1759]; y59 <- swe$cbr[swe$year == 1759]
segments(x59, y59, 23.1, 32.5, col = "grey50")
text(23.1, 32.5, "1759", pos = 2, cex = 0.8)
legend("topright", c(paste("Correlation:", round(r, 2)), "Wargentin's years, 1757–60"),
       pch = c(NA, 19), col = c(NA, "#e66101"), bty = "n")
par(op)








Figure 3.7: Crude birth rate against crude death rate, Sweden, 1751–1800. Each point is one year; the line is a least-squares fit. Source: Human Mortality Database.





The relationship is clearly negative: the correlation is -0.58. Even setting aside the catastrophe of 1772–73, years of high mortality tend to be years of low fertility. This is what Malthus and Wargentin predicted.


Added · from readings “Half the system” caution is from your lab (Part 3). Malthus’s short-period warning is from 1798, Ch. 7 (not assigned).
Two cautions. First, a scatter plot of births against deaths tests only half of the Malthusian system. It shows that births and deaths move in opposite directions, as if both were responding to good and bad times. But we have no wage series here. We are inferring the good and bad times from the pattern itself. The other half of the system, that population size drives wages, needs other data. Second, Malthus himself warned that a few years of data can mislead. He wrote that the ratio of births to deaths “for a period of five to ten years, will hence appear to be a very inadequate criterion by which to judge of its real progress in population” (Chapter 7). A run of good years is typically followed by a correction.






In the lab



In Lab 2 you’ll make this scatter plot yourself and then extend it to later periods of Swedish history. The question to keep in mind as you do: if the Malthusian system broke down, what would that look like in the data, and what might be causing it?

title: 3  The World According to Malthus
text:
3.6 Was Malthus right?

3.6.1 About the past: largely yes


Added · from readings Table and the 60% wage fall: Lee 1980, pp. 519–522 (p. 522 is just past the assigned pages). The 15% figure is p. 541 (assigned).
For the world Malthus lived in and the centuries before it, the evidence has been surprisingly kind to him. Using the reconstruction of English population from parish registers by the Cambridge Group for the History of Population and Social Structure, Lee (1980) compared population growth with real wages in England. Table 3.3 shows his summary.




Table 3.3: Population growth and real wages in England, 1535–1795. Source: Lee (1980), p. 522.











Period

When population grew quickly, real wages fell. When population growth slowed, wages rose. Over the sixteenth century, Lee writes, wage earners went from being “comfortably off” to a situation that was “desperate,” with wages falling about 60 percent after a century of population growth. This is the bottom panel of our diagram, in the data. Like Wargentin, Lee also found that births and deaths responded to wages in the short run, in the direction Malthus predicted.
But Lee also found that wages explained only about 15 percent of the year-to-year variation in population growth. Most of the variation in mortality was exogenous: plague and other epidemics came and went for reasons that had little to do with living standards. The Malthusian feedback was real, but it was weak and slow, operating over decades and centuries against a background of constant shocks.


3.6.2 About the future: spectacularly wrong


Added · new Rising real wages after ~1820 are from general knowledge. The list that follows is from your slides 06-22 to 06-28.
Malthus predicted that no lasting improvement in the condition of ordinary people was possible. Within a few decades of the Essay, England’s real wages began a sustained rise that has continued, with interruptions, for two centuries. And population grew at the same time. Both populations and living standards rose together, which Malthus’s model says can’t happen in the long run.
What did he miss? The diagram suggests where to look:

The bottom panel may keep shifting. If technology improves fast enough, and keeps improving, the wage curve can stay ahead of population. Malthus treated improvement as slow and bounded, the “moderate stream.” The industrial revolution turned the stream into a flood.
Capital. Malthus’s economy has one fixed factor (land) and one variable one (labor). Add a second variable factor, capital, that can grow alongside population, and diminishing returns to labor are much less binding. This is the subject of the next chapter, on the Solow growth model.
More people may mean more ideas. Perhaps productivity rises with population density. Ester Boserup argued that population pressure drives agricultural innovation. We’ll take up her argument in a later chapter.
The top panel may change shape. In modern societies, higher incomes are associated with fewer children, not more. Once the birth rate stops rising with the wage, the Malthusian feedback that pulls wages back down is broken.

Or perhaps we should ask: who says Malthus was wrong? Maybe we’ve simply been lucky for two hundred years, and population and consumption are still pressing on resource limits that will eventually bind, as Malthus predicted. That is the debate between David Lam and his critics that we read later in the course.

3  The World According to Malthus

title: 3  The World According to Malthus
text:
3.7 Key ideas

Pre-industrial populations were roughly stationary because of a feedback system: more people → lower wages → fewer births and more deaths → fewer people.
Malthus distinguished the preventive check (lower fertility, mainly through later marriage) from the positive check (higher mortality).
In the two-panel model, the equilibrium wage is set by the birth and death schedules (behavior and biology), and the equilibrium population by technology and resources.
Dismal conclusions: better technology raises population but not wages in the long run, and lower mortality lowers the equilibrium wage. Only a stronger preventive check raises living standards permanently.
Eighteenth-century Swedish data show the predicted negative correlation between birth and death rates. English data show wages falling when population grew.
Malthus described the pre-industrial past well and the industrial future badly. Explaining his failure is the subject of much of the rest of this course.

Added · new Q1 and Q4 come from your slides (05-28, 06-25). Q2, Q3, and Q5–Q8 are new. (The former Q6, a ruler’s policy choice from slide 06-16, was replaced because it nearly duplicates 2025 Lab 2 graded Q8.)

Starting too small. Suppose a population starts below its equilibrium size N*. Using both panels of the diagram, explain what happens to the wage, the birth rate, the death rate, and population size. Does the population return to N*?
Doubling times. Malthus took a 25-year doubling time from the American colonies. What annual growth rate does that imply? (Hint: a population growing at rate r doubles in about 70/r years when r is in percent.) Compare it with the Swedish growth rate from 1751 to 1800, which you can compute from the HMD data as about 0.59 percent per year.
A flat death curve. Lee found that mortality was mostly unrelated to wages. Redraw the top panel with a horizontal d(w). Is there still an equilibrium? Is it still stable? Which check is now doing all the work?
Multiple equilibria. Suppose that at very high wages, the birth rate starts to fall as wages rise. Sketch a b(w) curve like this. How many times can it cross d(w)? For each crossing, decide whether the equilibrium is stable. What might this have to do with how countries escaped the Malthusian trap?
Real versus nominal wages. Malthus argued that the oscillation was hidden partly because employers kept money wages unchanged while food prices rose. Why does the model use the real wage? What would go wrong if we used the money wage?
How easy is it to see Malthus in the data? Lee found that wages explained only about 15 percent of the year-to-year variation in population growth in pre-industrial England. If you had only 20 years of births, deaths, and wages for one village, how confident could you be about whether Malthusian feedback was at work? What would make the feedback easier to detect?
Reading the evidence. In Table 3.2, Wargentin’s counts are much higher than the HMD’s, yet both show the same pattern. Why can two sources disagree on levels but agree on a correlation? What kinds of measurement error would not leave the pattern intact?
Sarcasm. Reread the “court the return of the plague” passage. In one or two sentences, state the argument Malthus is actually making, and explain how it follows from the model.

title: 4  Capital to the Rescue? The Solow Model and Inequality
text:
4.1.1 Technology in Malthus, once more
Start with a review. In the Malthusian model of the last chapter, an exogenous improvement in technology shifts the \(w(N)\) curve outward. Wages rise at first. But higher wages raise population growth, and the larger population drives wages back down. The end result is a bigger population living at the same standard of living as before. Can wages stay higher? Not in Malthus’s world, where the gains from technology disappear.
Two features of that world drive the result. Land is a fixed factor and labor a variable one. And there is no capital accumulation, just land and people. So: what happens if we add savings and productive capital? That is the question of this chapter.


4.1.2 What growth models ask
Growth models are usually framed very generally: “What determines the long-run rate of economic growth?” Our interest is more specific: “What effect does population change have on economic growth and on individual welfare?”


Show the R code
weil <- read.csv("data/weil_2011_growth_subset.csv")
weil <- weil[complete.cases(weil$gpop, weil$rgdpch2009), ]
op <- par(mar = c(4, 6, 1, 1))
plot(weil$gpop, weil$rgdpch2009, log = "y", pch = 19, cex = 0.6,
     col = adjustcolor("black", 0.55),
     xlab = "Average annual population growth, 1975–2009 (%)",
     ylab = "", yaxt = "n")
axis(2, at = c(200, 1000, 5000, 25000, 100000),
     labels = c("200", "1,000", "5,000", "25,000", "100,000"), las = 1)
abline(lm(log10(rgdpch2009) ~ gpop, data = weil), lwd = 2)
lab_c <- c("Japan", "United States", "Nigeria", "Pakistan", "Germany", "Qatar",
           "United Arab Emirates", "India", "China", "Niger", "Ukraine")
lab_pos <- c(1, 4, 1, 4, 3, 4, 2, 1, 4, 4, 4)
i <- match(lab_c, weil$Country)
text(weil$gpop[i], weil$rgdpch2009[i], sub("United Arab Emirates", "UAE", lab_c),
     cex = 0.7, pos = lab_pos, col = "grey20")
mtext("Real GDP per person, 2009 (log scale)", side = 2, line = 4.5)
r_weil <- cor(weil$gpop, log(weil$rgdpch2009))
par(op)








Figure 4.1: Real GDP per person in 2009 (log scale) against average annual population growth, 1975–2009, for 187 countries, with a least-squares line. Data: Weil’s Economic Growth dataset (Penn World Table), which lecture code uses.







Added · new The slide uses World Bank data. I’ve redrawn it with the Weil dataset found in your eco175 folder (used by solow.R). The remarks on the Gulf states are mine.
Do high population growth rates hurt the economy? Figure 4.1 suggests a pattern: countries whose populations grew fastest tend to be poorer. The correlation between population growth and log income is about -0.42. But causality could go either way. Rapid population growth might make countries poor. Or being poor might keep fertility high. And notice the exceptions in the upper right: rich Gulf states such as Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, where population grew fast because of immigration drawn by oil wealth. This chapter develops one causal theory of how population growth could hurt income per person.
Other theories come in later lectures. Ester Boserup argued that population growth induces technological change, and so raises income per person. Environmentalists such as Paul Ehrlich argued that population growth depletes natural resources and reduces income per person, perhaps catastrophically.

title: 4  Capital to the Rescue? The Solow Model and Inequality
text:
4.2 Solow’s neoclassical growth model

4.2.1 Assumptions
Robert Solow’s growth model (developed in the 1950s, at about the same time as Trevor Swan’s) makes four main assumptions:

Labor and capital are fully employed.
All savings get invested.
Labor is a constant proportion of the population.
Output depends only on the ratio of capital to labor. There are no natural resources, and the absolute amounts of capital or population don’t matter.



Added · from readings Dornbusch and Fischer, p. 726.
Dornbusch and Fischer state the model’s goal: to explain “the determinants of growth rates within a country and the reasons for differences in per capita incomes across countries.” And they put its central population result up front: “between two countries with the same technology and saving rates the one that has the higher rate of population growth will eventually have lower per capita income.”
Other assumptions could be made instead, and some come up later in the course:

The savings rate rises with population growth, because there are fewer old people dissaving (Modigliani).
Technological progress is constant (easy to add).
Technological progress depends on population size (harder; Boserup).
Natural resources constrain growth (harder; environmentalists, Samuelson).
Demography depends on the economy (harder).



4.2.2 Notation

Capital per person: \(k = K/L\)
Output per person: \(y = Y/L = f(k)\)
\(s\) = the savings rate, so savings per person are \(s \times y\)
\(d\) = the depreciation rate (the fraction of capital that wears out each year)
\(n\) = the population growth rate (what we called \(R\) in the first chapter)



Added · from readings From the calendar note on the reading: Dornbusch and Fischer write output per head as \(x\). We use \(y\).
(Dornbusch and Fischer write output per head as \(x\) rather than \(y\). Otherwise the notation is the same.)


4.2.3 The production function
Total output depends on capital and labor, \(Y = F(K, L)\), with two properties:

Diminishing returns in \(K\) or \(L\) if the other is held constant.
Constant returns to scale: if we double both \(K\) and \(L\), we double \(Y\).

Size doesn’t matter, because there are no fixed resources. That is the big difference from Malthus.
A common example is the Cobb-Douglas production function,
\[
Y = K^a L^{1-a}, \qquad 0 < a < 1.
\]
Dividing both sides by \(L\) gives output per person as a function of capital per person alone: \(y = (K/L)^a = k^a\). More generally, constant returns let us write \(y = f(k)\).


Added · from readings Dornbusch and Fischer, p. 727.
As Dornbusch and Fischer put it: “As capital per head increases, so that workers use increasing amounts of machinery, output per head increases, but at a diminishing rate.”


4.2.4 Savings, depreciation, and the investment needed to stay even
What happens to capital per person over time? Without new investment, two things erode it:

Population growth dilutes capital per person at rate \(n\) per year. New workers arrive with no machines.
Depreciation reduces the capital stock at rate \(d\) per year.

To keep \(k\) constant, then, we need to invest \((n + d) \times K\) in total, or \((n + d) \times k\) per person. This is the investment requirement.
An example from lecture: suppose an economy has $1 million of capital and 1,000 workers, so \(k\) = $1,000 per worker. Population grows 3 percent a year, and capital depreciates 7 percent a year. Without new investment, next year capital per worker will be about \(\$1{,}000 \times e^{-0.10} \approx\) $905. So the economy must buy about $100 of capital per worker just to stay even. If a worker with $1,000 of capital produces $400 of output, a savings rate of 0.25 provides exactly that $100.


Added · from readings The machines example is from Dornbusch and Fischer, pp. 734–735.
Dornbusch and Fischer give a similar example. With 10 machines per head, 1 percent population growth, and 10 percent depreciation, “we require per year 11 percent times 10 machines, or 1.1 machines, just to offset population growth and depreciation.” If population growth rises to 2 percent, the requirement rises to 12 percent, or 1.2 machines per head.


4.2.5 The steady state
Figure 4.2 puts the pieces together, following the lecture picture. The production function \(y = f(k)\) is the top curve. Savings per person, \(s\,y(k)\), are a fixed fraction of it. The gap between the two is consumption per person. The straight line \((n + d)\,k\) is the investment requirement.








Figure 4.2: The Solow model. Output per worker y = f(k) rises with capital per worker at a diminishing rate. Saving per worker s·y(k) is a fixed fraction of output. The investment requirement (n + d)k is what must be invested just to keep k constant. The steady state k* is where saving exactly meets the requirement.





The steady state is where the saving curve crosses the investment requirement, at capital per worker \(k^*\) and output per worker \(y^*\). There, saving is exactly enough to replace worn-out machines and to equip the new workers. Dornbusch and Fischer describe it as a state in which “current saving and additions to the capital stock would be just enough to equip new entrants into the labor force with the same amount of capital as the average worker uses.”
Is this equilibrium stable? Suppose \(k\) starts below \(k^*\). Then saving exceeds the investment requirement, so \(k\) grows. As it grows, the gap shrinks, and \(k\) approaches \(k^*\) more and more slowly. If \(k\) starts above \(k^*\), the requirement exceeds saving, and \(k\) falls back. Either way, the economy converges to the steady state. Figure 4.3 simulates the path from a low starting point.








Figure 4.3: Convergence to the steady state from a low initial capital per worker, simulated with the parameters of the previous figure. Output per worker rises quickly at first and then levels off at y*.





The lecture calls this “Malthus-like dynamics in a single picture.” Think of \(s\,y(k)\) as the “birth rate of capital” and \((n + d)\,k\) as its “death rate.” Where births and deaths of capital balance, capital per worker is stationary, just as population was stationary where births and deaths balanced in Malthus.


Added · from readings Dornbusch and Fischer, p. 732.
Dornbusch and Fischer draw out one striking implication: “if two countries have the same capital stock and the same rate of population growth and have access to the same production function, they will eventually reach the same level of income.” On this view, poor countries are poor because they start further from \(k^*\), “but if the former save at the same rate, and can get the same technology, they will eventually catch up.”


4.2.6 What happens to the size of the economy?
In the steady state, output per worker doesn’t change. But the population keeps growing at rate \(n\), so capital and total output must also grow at rate \(n\). The economy as a whole grows, just fast enough to keep everyone’s share constant.
This is the first big difference from Malthus. A Malthusian economy can’t accommodate steady population growth without driving wages down. A Solow economy can: capital grows alongside population.

title: 4  Capital to the Rescue? The Solow Model and Inequality
section: 4.3 Saving, population growth, and the price of growth
text:
4.3 Saving, population growth, and the price of growth

4.3.1 A higher saving rate
What happens if people save more? The saving curve shifts up. At the old \(k^*\), saving now exceeds the investment requirement, so capital per worker grows until it reaches a new, higher steady state. Capital per worker and output per worker are both higher. What about consumption, and the long-run growth rate?


Added · from readings Dornbusch and Fischer, pp. 732–733 and their Figure 19-5.
Dornbusch and Fischer pose the puzzle directly: “If people save 10 percent of their income, as opposed to 5 percent, should we not expect this to make a difference in the growth rate of output?” Their answer: “In the short run, it raises the growth rate of output. It does not affect the long-run growth rate of output, but it raises the long-run level of capital and output per head.” Figure 4.4 shows the two effects over time, following their Figure 19-5.








Figure 4.4: A permanent rise in the saving rate at year 20 (after Dornbusch and Fischer, Figure 19-5). Left: output per worker rises to a new, higher steady-state level. Right: the growth rate of total output rises temporarily, then falls back to the population growth rate n.





The growth rate rises only during the transition, while capital per worker is being built up. Once the new steady state is reached, total output again grows at the rate of population growth.
Consumption is a subtler question. Saving more means consuming a larger share of a bigger pie. Whether the pie grows enough to raise consumption depends on how much more is saved. In lecture we’ll look at what happens to the level of consumption.


Added · from readings Dornbusch and Fischer, p. 726.
How much should a society save? Saving more now means more for future generations and less for the present one. Dornbusch and Fischer note that the people who will consume in the future “are not here to vote because they have not yet been born,” and they quote the economist Joan Robinson’s question: “What did posterity ever do for us?” Ultimately, they conclude, “the policy decisions that affect growth are settled politically.”


4.3.2 Try it: the Solow app


Added · new The app is the course’s own Solow app (ShinyApps/solow in the 2025 course repo), exported with Shinylive so it runs in the browser, in its own tab. The three questions are mine; they use only the saving rate and the capital share, to stay clear of the Lab 3 graded questions (a technology shift in the app, slower or negative population growth, and immigrants who change capital per worker).
The app simulates the Solow model. The top-left panel shows saving, sy, and the investment needed to stay even, (d + n)k; the bottom-left shows the production function; and the right-hand panels trace capital and output per person over time. New conditions take effect at time 0; press the “play” triangle under the time slider to run the simulation. It opens in a new tab, so you can make it full screen and keep this page open alongside it. (The first load can take a few seconds while R starts up in your browser.)



The Solow app at its starting values. Click to open it in a new tab.


Open the Solow app in a new tab ↗
Before you move each slider, write down what you expect to happen. Then check.

Save more. Raise “savings level s’” from 0.20 to 0.25 and press play. Before you do: will output per person grow faster forever, or rise to a new, higher level and stop?
Watch the gap close. In the same run, how does the speed of growth change as capital per person approaches its new steady state? Why does growth slow down even though people keep saving 25 percent of their income?
A bigger capital share. Return s to 0.20 and raise “alpha” from 0.4 to 0.5. Predict whether the steady-state capital and output per person will be higher or lower. Why does a larger capital share make capital accumulation matter more?

Lab 3 asks you to use the app to follow an economy through a technological change.


4.3.3 Faster population growth
Now the central question for economic demography. What happens if population growth rises from \(n\) to \(n'\)? Faster growth means more new workers to equip, so the investment requirement line rotates upward, from \((n + d)k\) to \((n' + d)k\) (Figure 4.5, left).








Figure 4.5: Faster population growth (left) rotates the investment requirement upward, lowering steady-state capital per worker (k′) and output per worker (y′). Right: saving more (dotted s′y(k)) could restore the old capital per worker, but at the cost of consumption.





If saving stays the same, capital doesn’t grow fast enough to keep up with the new workers. Capital per worker falls until it reaches a new, lower steady state \(k^{*\prime}\), and output per worker falls to \(y^{*\prime}\). Dornbusch and Fischer:






In their own words



“The decline in output per head as a consequence of increased population growth points up the problem faced by many developing countries. Fast growth in population, given the saving rate, means low levels of income per head. … With high population growth, saving will typically be too small to allow capital to rise relative to labor and thus to build up the capital-labor ratio to achieve a satisfactory level of income per head.” (Dornbusch and Fischer, pp. 735–736)


Is there anything we could do to keep the old level of output per person? Yes: save more and consume less (Figure 4.5, right). A higher saving rate \(s'\) can restore the old capital per worker. So population growth has a price:

If we compensate for faster growth by saving more, consumption falls.
If we don’t save more, the new steady state has lower capital and output per worker, and consumption is still hurt.

4  Capital to the Rescue? The Solow Model and Inequality

title: 4  Capital to the Rescue? The Solow Model and Inequality
text:
4.4 Technology: the Solow ratchet

4.4.1 Can technology save us?
Let’s include a factor \(A\) for technology: \(Y = A\,F(K, L)\). With constant returns to scale, output per worker is \(y = A\,f(k)\), so \(y\) rises with \(A\). A new technology lets us produce more output at every capital-labor ratio (Figure 4.6).








Figure 4.6: A technological improvement raises output at every capital-labor ratio, from A f(k) to A′f(k). Saving rises with output, so the steady state moves from k* to k*′: technology raises output directly and then through capital deepening.





Technology works in two steps:

Higher productivity with the original capital. At the old \(k^*\), output jumps from \(y(k^*)\) to \(y'(k^*)\).
Capital deepening. Because output is higher, so is saving. Capital per worker grows from \(k^*\) to a new steady state \(k^{*\prime}\), raising output further.

You can watch both steps with the “Solow” app in the lab.


4.4.2 Ratchet, not hamster wheel
Do we stay at the new, higher steady state? Or do we slip back, as in Malthus? In Solow’s model, we stay. Each improvement in technology gives a new equilibrium, not just a temporary gain. If technology keeps improving, \(A(t) = A_0 e^{gt}\), then:

population \(N\) grows at rate \(n\);
the economy \(Y\) grows at rate \(n + g\);
output per person \(y\) grows at rate \(g\).

The lecture calls this the difference between a Solow ratchet and a Malthusian hamster in a wheel. In Malthus, population growth eats away any technological improvement. In Solow, the economy needs more capital to keep up, but it can support that capital with its higher output.


Added · from readings Dornbusch and Fischer, p. 736.
Dornbusch and Fischer list three reasons growth per person could continue in the steady state. The “most important is technical progress, which empirical work has identified as the prime source of growth.” The others are increasing returns to scale and investment in human capital as well as physical capital. They add a hopeful caveat: “There can be little doubt that human ingenuity will produce technical progress that will allow growth to continue if that same human ingenuity can maintain peace and political stability.”


4.4.3 Malthus and Solow compared




Table 4.1: Malthus and Solow compared (from lecture).












Malthus
Solow

To sum up: the Solow model retells the Malthusian story with a different steady state.

Good news. It can accommodate constant population growth without lowering wages, which is impossible in Malthus. And technological change brings permanent improvement, not the temporary gain of Malthus.
Bad news. Faster population growth means lower income, unless people give up consumption and keep saving up. More capital alone, such as a one-time foreign investment or aid, won’t change steady-state output. The key to long-term growth in income per person is technology, not savings.

What does Solow leave unexplained? The model takes technology, population growth, and the saving rate as given from outside (exogenous). The great take-off of population and income per person since about 1800 (shown in lecture with Maddison’s data for the United Kingdom) is driven by exactly the things the model doesn’t explain.


Added · from readings Dornbusch and Fischer, p. 737 and their Box 19-2. “Limits to growth” is the reading’s own box. Slide 07-10 mentions the environmentalists as a coming topic.
Writing in the late 1980s, Dornbusch and Fischer added two further notes. Newer growth theories, which let investment in research and human capital affect the long-run growth rate, “do not predict a convergence of income levels among countries that start from different initial capital stocks.” And they flagged, in a box titled “Limits to Growth,” the worry that “growing populations put pressure on resources and cause environmental degradation,” mentioning tropical forests and “some evidence that the global climate may be warming.”

4  Capital to the Rescue? The Solow Model and Inequality

title: 4  Capital to the Rescue? The Solow Model and Inequality
text:
4.5 Growth and inequality: Piketty’s argument

4.5.1 A stylized fact: inequality’s fall and rise


Added · from readings Figures and quotes in this section are from Piketty and Saez (2014), pp. 838–842. The slide shows their Figure 1.
Thomas Piketty and Emmanuel Saez (an economist at Berkeley) assembled a century of tax records to measure the share of income going to the richest tenth of the population. Their first fact is a “great inequality reversal” between Europe and the United States. On the eve of World War I, the top tenth received 45 to 50 percent of total income in most European countries, and slightly above 40 percent in the United States. In Europe, the share then fell sharply, to about 30 percent by the 1950s and 1960s, and it is now close to 35 percent. In the United States, it fell to 30 to 35 percent in the 1950s and 1960s, then “rose at an unprecedented pace since the 1970s–1980s, and is now close to 50%.”
Wealth is far more unequal than income. The richest tenth typically owns 60 to 90 percent of all wealth, but receives 30 to 50 percent of income. The bottom half of the population owns less than 5 percent of wealth, but earns 20 to 30 percent of income. “The bottom half of the population hardly owns any wealth, but it does earn appreciable income.” In pre-WWI Europe, the top tenth owned close to 90 percent of all wealth, so that “there was basically no wealth middle class.”


4.5.2 The Solow model as a tool for studying inequality
The Solow model can help us think about inequality in two ways:

We can decompose income into the share that goes to capital and the share that goes to labor.
We can see how this division changes with capital intensity, \(k\).

Some accounting. Total income is labor income plus capital income: \(Y = Y_\ell + Y_k\). In perfectly competitive markets, each factor is paid its marginal product. So capital income per worker is \(y_k = MP(k) \times k\), and labor gets the rest: \(y_\ell = y - y_k\). In our model, the marginal product of capital is just the slope of the production function (Figure 4.7).








Figure 4.7: Splitting output between capital and labor at capital per worker k. The tangent to the production function has slope MP(k), the return on capital. Capital’s income per worker is k × MP(k) (orange); labor’s is the rest, y − k × MP(k) (green), which is where the tangent meets the vertical axis.







4.5.3 Does slower population growth increase inequality?
We know from the Solow model that a smaller \(n\) raises \(k^*\) and \(y^*\). Who gets the increase in income: the owners of capital, or the workers? The proportion going to capital is
\[
\text{capital share} = \frac{k \times MP(k)}{y(k)}.
\]
But the answer isn’t obvious. If we increase \(k\), there are offsetting effects. Does more capital per person increase capital’s share of income? Yes, because there is more capital. No, because the rate of return on capital falls as capital becomes more plentiful. Which effect is stronger depends on how quickly the marginal product declines.

Cobb-Douglas: the two effects cancel. With \(y = k^a\), the marginal product is \(MP(k) = a\,k^{a-1}\), and the capital share is \((a\,k^{a-1}) \times k / k^a = a\), a constant. Capital intensification is exactly balanced by diminishing returns.
If \(MP(k)\) declines more slowly, we still have diminishing returns, but an increase in capital is no longer fully offset by the fall in its return. The result is an increasing share of national income going to capital owners. This is what Piketty highlights as possible. He thinks it might get worse, because new technologies like robots and automation may have slowly declining marginal products.



Added · from readings Piketty and Saez, p. 842.
Piketty and Saez put the technical point in terms of the “elasticity of substitution” between capital and labor. If it equals 1 (the Cobb-Douglas case), “the capital share … is a technological constant.” But in rich countries in recent decades, both the amount of capital relative to income and capital’s share of income have risen, “which suggests that [the elasticity] is somewhat larger than 1.” Intuitively, they write, there are more and more ways to substitute capital for labor, “e.g., replacing delivery workers by drones or self-driving trucks.”
And capital income is much more unequally distributed than labor income. Table 4.2 shows estimates of the share of labor income and of asset income received by the top tenth under different inequality regimes.




Table 4.2: Share of labor and asset income received by the top decile in different inequality regimes, and the effect of a unit increase in the capital/income ratio β on the top decile’s share of total income. Source: Goldstein and Lee (2014), using Piketty’s estimates (as shown in lecture).

Medium inequality (Europe, 2010)
High inequality (US 2010, Europe 1910)
Very high inequality (US 2030?)

4.5.4 Piketty’s argument in three steps
Put together, Piketty’s argument goes like this:

Slower growth → more capital per person. This is the neoclassical Solow result.
More capital per person increases capital’s share of the economy. This is an empirical claim.
Capital income is more unequally distributed than labor income. Also an empirical claim.

Therefore: slower growth increases income inequality.


4.5.5 “Capital is back because low growth is back”


Added · from readings Piketty and Saez, pp. 840–841. The calendar note asks students to look for “the Solow equilibrium on page 840 and the role of population growth.”
Piketty and Saez make step 1 concrete with what they call the Harrod-Domar-Solow formula. In the long run, the ratio of wealth to income, \(\beta = K/Y\), converges to
\[
\beta = \frac{s}{g},
\]
where \(s\) is the saving rate and \(g\) is the growth rate of total income. And “the growth rate \(g\) is the sum of the population growth rate (including immigration) and the productivity growth rate.” With a saving rate of 10 percent and growth of 3 percent, \(\beta \approx 300\%\): wealth equals about three years of income. “But if the growth rate drops to \(g\) = 1.5%, then \(\beta \approx 600\%\). In short: Capital is back because low growth is back.”


Added · new Connecting \(\beta = s/g\) to the Solow steady state (\(s\,y = (n+d)k\)) is my explanation. It follows from the model, but neither the slides nor the reading spell it out this way.
Where does this come from? It’s the Solow steady state seen from another angle. In steady state, capital must grow as fast as income, so each year’s saving, \(s\,Y\), must add \(g \times K\) to the stock. Setting \(s\,Y = g\,K\) gives \(K/Y = s/g\). Slow growth means each year’s saving piles up relative to income. “In the extreme case of a society with zero population and productivity growth,” Piketty and Saez write, “the wealth-income ratio … would rise indefinitely.” And capital accumulation is slow: “With a saving rate of 10% per year, it takes 50 years to accumulate the equivalent of 5 years of income.”








Figure 4.8: The long-run wealth-to-income ratio β = s/g for a saving rate of 10%, as total growth g varies. Shaded bands show Piketty and Saez’s ranges for total growth in Europe and Japan (about 1–1.5% a year, with population growth near zero) and in the United States (at least 2–2.5%, with population growth above 1% thanks to immigration).





This logic, they argue, explains why the United States holds less capital relative to its income than Europe and Japan. “U.S. population growth rates exceed 1% per year, thanks to large immigration flows,” so total U.S. growth is at least 2 to 2.5 percent a year. In Europe and Japan, population growth is now close to zero, so total growth is about 1 to 1.5 percent. Historically, European wealth was worth about 6 to 7 years of national income before World War I, fell to 2 to 3 years in the 1950s, and is back to 5 to 6 years today. U.S. wealth has generally equalled about 4 to 5 years of income.


4.5.6 r > g
The final piece concerns how wealth is distributed. Piketty and Saez model individual fortunes as growing at the rate of return on wealth, \(r\), while the economy grows at \(g\). The larger the gap \(r - g\), the more unequal wealth becomes. This is the “dramatic reading” from lecture:






In their own words



“Intuitively, a higher r – g tends to amplify initial wealth inequalities: It implies that past wealth is capitalized at a faster pace, and that it is less likely to be overtaken by the general growth of the economy.” (Piketty and Saez, p. 841)


History, they argue, mostly had a large gap. Before the industrial revolution, growth was “much less than 1% per year,” while land typically earned rents of about 4 to 5 percent of its value. “This large gap between r and g explains why wealth concentration was so large until World War I and why wealth concentration was smaller in the United States, where population growth was faster.” In the twentieth century, growth was exceptionally high, “in particular due to very high population growth, which even today represents about half of global gross domestic product growth.” Meanwhile, wars, depression, and taxation cut the return on capital. If population growth slows in the twenty-first century, \(r - g\) is likely to widen again.
Notice how central population is to the whole argument. Population growth is half of \(g\), so a demographic slowdown pushes up both the wealth-income ratio and the gap \(r - g\).


4.5.7 Is it destiny?
Piketty and Saez end on a note of caution, not determinism. High capital intensity is “not bad in itself. After all, it would be good to have an infinite quantity of robots producing most of the output, so that we can devote more time to leisure activities. The problem is twofold: Can we all find jobs as a robot designer (or in leisure-related activities), and who owns the robots?” And their final judgment: “Inequality does not follow a deterministic process. In a sense, both Marx and Kuznets were wrong. There are powerful forces pushing alternately in the direction of rising or shrinking inequality. Which one dominates depends on the institutions and policies that societies choose to adopt.”






In the lab



In Lab 3 you calculate the investment an economy needs to stay even, derive the steady state for a Cobb-Douglas economy (including one with a shrinking population), use the “Solow” app to watch an economy respond to a technological change, and calculate capital’s share of income under different production functions to see when capital intensification does, and doesn’t, raise capital’s share. The lab ends by asking you to think through what one-time waves of immigrants would do to income per person.

title: 4  Capital to the Rescue? The Solow Model and Inequality
text:
4.6 Key ideas

In the Solow model, capital per worker is in steady state when saving exactly covers the investment requirement: \(s\,y(k) = (n + d)\,k\).
In steady state, output per worker is constant, and capital and total output grow at the rate of population growth. Unlike Malthus, the economy can support steady population growth without lowering incomes.
A higher saving rate raises the level of output per worker but only temporarily raises its growth rate.
Faster population growth lowers steady-state capital and output per worker, unless people give up consumption to save more.
Technology is the key to long-run growth in income per person. Its gains are preserved (a ratchet), not eaten away as in Malthus.
Piketty’s argument: slower growth raises capital per person (Solow), which may raise capital’s share of income, and capital income is very unequally distributed. So slower growth can increase inequality. The wealth-income ratio tends toward \(\beta = s/g\), and population growth is a large part of \(g\).

title: 5  Boserup: Population Pushes Technology
text:
5.1 When is a digging stick better than a plow?
Start with a question from lecture. As a pre-industrial human, which would you rather have: a plow, a digging stick, or a bow and arrow?
The plow seems like the obvious answer. It is the more “advanced” technology. But the best answer is: it depends on how many people live around you. By the end of this chapter you should be able to explain why. The answer says something important about how population and technology are related.
crumbs: Population and the economy: big theories
5  Boserup: Population Pushes Technology

title: 5  Boserup: Population Pushes Technology
text:
5.2 Technology pull and population push

5.2.1 Malthus: technology pulls population along
In the Malthusian model of Chapter 3, technology is exogenous. It changes for reasons outside the model, and population follows. A new technology shifts the wage curve outward, wages rise for a while, and then population grows until the wage is back at its old equilibrium level. Population ends up larger, but no richer. Call this the technology-pull theory of population history.
Figure 5.1 shows what this means over the long sweep of history. Each great technological regime (hunting and gathering, settled agriculture, industry) supports a larger equilibrium population at the same equilibrium wage.








Figure 5.1: The technology-pull (Malthusian) view of population history, after a diagram by Ronald Lee. The birth and death curves (top) fix the equilibrium wage w*. Each technological regime has its own wage curve (bottom), so each supports a larger equilibrium population at the same wage.





Plotted against time, this gives the staircase you met in Chapter 1 (Livi-Bacci’s version of Deevey’s diagram): long plateaus of near-zero growth, broken by bursts of growth after each technological revolution, with perhaps another revolution to come.


5.2.2 Boserup: population pushes technology
The Danish economist Ester Boserup (1910–1999) proposed the reverse. Not technological change → population growth, but population growth → technological change. In her view, population grows for its own reasons. It is a kind of natural tendency. Growing numbers then force people to change how they produce food, and much else. This is the population-push theory.


Added · from readings The quotations in this subsection are from Boserup (1976), pp. 21–23 (original Population and Development Review pagination): carrying capacity and the “two main weaknesses,” p. 21; transport and administrative technology, p. 22; zero growth, p. 23.
Boserup began her 1976 article by describing the classical theory she was attacking. It treats population as passive: it “assumes that a given environment has a certain carrying capacity for human populations, defined as the number of persons who can be accommodated in that region under the prevailing system of subsistence.” Population stays at that limit until better food technology raises it. Boserup’s objection:






In her own words



“This reasoning suffers from two main weaknesses: first, the theory focuses exclusively on the technology of food production, ignoring the effects of technological changes in other areas and the effects of the environment; secondly, the theory ignores the effects of demographic change on both environment and technology.” (Boserup 1976, p. 21)


Her first point is that many technologies besides food affect population. Better transport can raise mortality by spreading epidemics, or by making it easier for “a conqueror or an indigenous ruling class to move food away from the region where it is produced.” Better military technology usually raises mortality. Walled towns reduced deaths in war but probably raised deaths from epidemics. And what she calls “administrative technology,” the organization of society, can turn a local war or harvest failure into a demographic catastrophe if it breaks down.
So Boserup doubted that pre-industrial populations sat at a food-determined ceiling. Hardship in history came from war, plague, and natural disaster, not mainly from overpopulation. In her words: “There seems to be little reason to assume that zero rates of population growth occurred more frequently in past history than other rates of growth, positive or negative.” Some unlucky peoples shrank and disappeared, while luckier ones grew slowly for long periods.


5.2.3 A typology
Table 5.1 places the models of this course in a simple grid, according to whether population and technology are explained inside the model (endogenous) or taken as given (exogenous).




Table 5.1: A typology of technology–population models (lecture).

Technology endogenous

Malthus

5  Boserup: Population Pushes Technology

title: 5  Boserup: Population Pushes Technology
text:
5.3 Two kinds of technological change
How does a larger population change technology? Boserup’s answer has two parts, and the distinction matters.

Intensification: “no new ideas, just new applications.” Methods that were already known, but not worth using at low density, become worth using as density rises. Productivity per hour of work falls, so people must work harder to get the same calories. Is a plow better than a digging stick? It depends on density. In this sense intensification is dismal, and Malthusian.
Invention: “some sticks better than others, some plows better than others.” Deeper technological change creates genuinely better tools and cumulative infrastructure, such as roads and metal industries. This can set up a virtuous circle: increasing density → better technology → bigger surplus → increasing density → …

Figure 5.2 shows the difference. Intensification is a movement along a production function. Invention shifts the production function up.








Figure 5.2: Intensification versus invention (lecture). Left: moving along a fixed production function, from hunting and gathering to multicropping, as more labor is applied per acre. Right: invention shifts the whole production function up.





The curve in the left panel is smooth because farmers can combine systems, and because returns decline within each system.
crumbs: Population and the economy: big theories
5  Boserup: Population Pushes Technology

title: 5  Boserup: Population Pushes Technology
text:
5.4 Agricultural intensification

5.4.1 The fallow sequence
The key to Boserup’s theory is fallow: leaving land uncultivated so it can recover. Table 5.2 lists the main systems of food production, from the most land-using to the most land-saving.




Table 5.2: Systems of food production, from most land-using to most land-saving (lecture; Boserup 1976, p. 25). Typical tools are from Boserup.











System
Cultivation and fallow
Typical tools




Gathering
Wild plants, roots, fruits, nuts; no cultivation
Digging sticks, fire


Forest fallow
1–2 crops, then 15–25 years of fallow
Digging sticks, fire


Bush fallow
2 or more crops, then 8–10 years of fallow
Hoes, machetes


Short fallow
1–2 crops, then 1–2 years of fallow
Plow and draft animals


Annual cropping
1 crop a year, a few months of fallow
Plow, draft animals; often irrigation


Multicropping
2–3 crops a year, little or no fallow
Plow, draft animals, irrigation








Why fallow at all? Fallow regenerates soil nutrients. It lets farmers avoid weeding, since they simply let weeds and bushes grow and then move on. And burning the regrowth puts nutrients back into the soil. In lecture, photographs show the range: extensive gardening in the Brazilian forest, with easy access to hunting and gathering; slash-and-burn plots where a farmer plants tubers among felled logs he has not bothered to clear; experimental multicropping in Brazil; and the huge labor investment of terraced rice fields in the Philippines.


Added · from readings The history in this subsection is from Boserup (1976), pp. 24–26 and 29.
Boserup used this sequence to reinterpret European history. The classical view held that primitive equipment kept most land uncultivated until better tools came along. Boserup pointed out that much of the “uncultivated” land was in fact being used, but lay fallow in most years under long-fallow systems. As early as 4500 BCE, some populations in temperate Europe seem to have practiced forest fallow. Over many centuries, fallow periods grew shorter “in step with the gradual increase of the European population,” until annual cropping spread in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Regions that stayed sparsely populated kept long fallow for centuries longer.
The environment and the tools changed along with the system. Forests thinned and disappeared, replaced by pastures and fields, and “the primitive digging sticks and stone axes used in the food-gathering and forest-fallow stages had to be replaced by other hand tools and later by ploughs.” The same gradual path appears in ancient Mesopotamia, from food gathering on mountain slopes before 8000 BCE to irrigated plow agriculture in the southern plains four to five thousand years later. “The neolithic revolution,” Boserup wrote, “is not a sweeping revolutionary change but a process of gradual evolution.”


5.4.2 Diffusion, not invention
Here is the heart of the digging-stick puzzle. Boserup argued that new systems rarely required anyone to invent anything. Tools and methods spread from denser populations to sparser ones when the sparser ones needed them.

“When we observe that even today some peoples use primitive land-using subsistence systems … we should not ask why these peoples never invented the plough and the wheel, but why the diffusion of these technologies seems to have happened fairly rapidly in some cases and not at all in other cases.” (Boserup 1976, p. 27)



5.4.3 Why stick with the digging stick?


Added · from readings Boserup (1976), pp. 27–30 (output per unit of labor, p. 27; the Kalahari studies, p. 28; labor investments, p. 30). The figure is my illustration of her argument.
Her answer is labor productivity. Land-using systems “have a higher output per unit of labor input than usually assumed.” Studies of the Kalahari Bushmen found that the women who did the food gathering needed only two to three days a week to provide the necessary food. Land-saving systems produce much more food per acre, but they demand far more work: plowing, weeding, manuring, irrigating. They also require big up-front labor investments: clearing roots and stones, building wells, dams, terraces, and irrigation channels. For a growing group that can still move, splitting up and starting long-fallow farming somewhere new is the labor-saving choice. “The yields of the labor investments — if properly maintained — may last forever, but the planning horizon of peoples who subsist by food gathering or long-fallow agriculture is a few years at most.”
Figure 5.3 puts the argument in a picture. At low density, the land-using system gives more food per hour of work. As density rises, it runs into trouble: walks get longer, fallow gets shorter, and soils give out. Past some density, the labor-intensive system becomes the better choice, even though people work harder than their ancestors did.








Figure 5.3: When is a digging stick better than a plow? An illustration of Boserup’s argument. At low population density, a land-using system (long fallow, digging stick) yields more food per hour of work. At higher densities, a land-saving system (plow, annual cropping) does better, but at a lower level of output per hour than people enjoyed at low density.







5.4.4 Does intensification mean more misery?
Not in the Malthusian sense of higher mortality. But yes, in the sense of lower utility: people must work more hours to survive. Malthus himself described this response. In the oscillation passage of Chapter 2, he wrote that “the plenty of labourers, and the necessity of an increased industry amongst them, encourage cultivators to employ more labour upon their land; to turn up fresh soil, and to manure and improve more completely what is already in tillage.”


5.4.5 A modern test: Machakos, Kenya


Added · from readings This subsection summarizes Malakoff (2011), pp. 544–546: the 1937 memo, Mortimore’s “garden,” and Siedenberg’s warning, p. 544; More People, Less Erosion and Boserup’s ideas, p. 545; the critics, the Malawi title, and Ellis, p. 546.
Is Boserup’s logic still relevant? David Malakoff’s article in Science tells the story of Machakos, a hilly, drought-prone farming district 50 kilometers south of Nairobi. In 1937, a British colonial official warned that its inhabitants were “rapidly drifting to a state of hopeless and miserable poverty and their land to a parching desert of rocks, stones and sand.” The population was then approaching 250,000. By 2011 more than 1.5 million people lived there, and Machakos had become a symbol of something else: “A landscape that was once declared good for nothing is now like a garden when the rain falls,” in the words of the geographer Michael Mortimore.
Mortimore, Mary Tiffen, and Francis Gichuki documented what happened between 1930 and 1990, as the population roughly quadrupled, in a 1994 book with a deliberately provocative title: More People, Less Erosion. Farmers built terraces to control erosion, used more animal manure, and sold food in the growing Nairobi market. Nairobi also offered seasonal jobs, which brought income for further improvements. Families had fewer children and invested more in schooling. The study, Malakoff writes, “‘controverted’ Malthus and backed Boserup.” Mortimore summarized the Boserupian idea simply: people “weren’t just mouths to feed but also brains that could think and hands and legs that could work very hard.” A farmer who could once justify weeding a field only once a season could, with more labor available, weed it three times.
The critics are worth hearing too. A coffee boom in the 1970s may have given a one-time boost. Machakos still does not grow enough food to feed its own population. The poorest families may not have shared in the “miracle.” And other studies found the opposite pattern elsewhere, with titles like “More people, more soil degradation: The Malawi experience.” “Although local successes offer hope, it is dangerous to generalize,” warns one critic, Jules Siedenberg. Boserupian responses are not “an automatic result” of population growth: farmers need markets, capital, and information. The geographer Erle Ellis, who studied land use in China, concludes that “Boserup was right,” but adds that “people are working harder than ever,” just as Boserup predicted.

5  Boserup: Population Pushes Technology

title: 5  Boserup: Population Pushes Technology
text:
5.5 Population and invention
So far, intensification only explains how people cope. It doesn’t explain progress. How might population drive genuine invention? Lecture offers three ideas.

Necessity is the mother of invention. More misery could inspire people to invent. With higher population, perhaps we move not just along the curve but upward as well. But this still doesn’t explain why.
More geniuses. More people means more inventions. This assumes that an additional person creates more solutions than problems.
Density. This is Boserup’s own emphasis.


5.5.1 Boserup on density
Higher density creates economies of scale. One kind is in human capital: an itinerant craftsman becomes a local specialist, and eventually universities become possible. Another is in physical capital: water or animal mills replace everyone grinding grain by hand at home. A third is infrastructure such as roads and canals.


Added · from readings Boserup (1976), pp. 30–32 (Adam Smith, p. 30; the trap, footpaths, and towns, p. 31; the food surplus, p. 32).
Boserup’s examples are vivid. “It is well known, since Adam Smith’s famous dictum, that the division of labor is limited by the extent of the market.” Full-time craftsmen could not exist in Amazonian villages of 50 to 150 long-fallow farmers. Such villagers must stay jacks-of-all-trades, so their high productivity in food is offset by low productivity in everything else. They are, she says, caught in a trap:






In her own words



“Such communities are caught in a trap because the maximum density consistent with their subsistence system is below the minimum density needed for development in fields other than food supply. They are not likely to escape from the trap until population density in the region becomes so high (by natural growth or by immigration) that they are forced to adopt a land-saving system of subsistence.” (Boserup 1976, p. 31)


Transport works the same way. “Even a footpath through tropical forest can exist only if used regularly by a certain number of people (or animals).” Roads and canals need a large population to build and maintain. Before that, even rulers had to keep moving:

“When population density increases, and the land-using subsistence systems are replaced by land-saving systems, both rulers and craftsmen can settle permanently in towns with the additional advantages of still more specialization, better organization, and more specialized equipment.” (Boserup 1976, p. 31)

Boserup also made a subtle point about cities. A town needs a large food surplus “in an absolute sense but not necessarily a large food surplus per agricultural producer.” Many dense, hard-working farm families each selling a little can feed a city, provided the food can be transported to it.


5.5.2 Town and country
Putting these together gives Boserup’s picture of town and country. Population growth in rural areas drives migration to cities. Cities generate economies of scale and invention, and a demand for food. That demand, and the markets and technology that come with it, raise the returns to capital investment in agriculture, driving rural intensification and invention. It is a precarious system: in bad times, food prices are high and the countryside is short of labor. The Machakos story, with Nairobi as the city, follows exactly this pattern.
crumbs: Population and the economy: big theories
5  Boserup: Population Pushes Technology

title: 5  Boserup: Population Pushes Technology
text:
5.6 The big picture
Intensification is not necessarily “progress.” Hunter-gatherers work less and eat more meat, so the “invention of agriculture” around 8000 BCE may have been more a matter of necessity. Capital investments such as draft animals, plows, and harnesses only make sense if cropping is frequent. And there is no ratchet on intensive technology: Europeans used slash-and-burn agriculture in the New World, where land was abundant.
Invention does lead to progress: better tools, more infrastructure (saved surpluses), rising standards of living, and know-how that is cumulative and not forgotten.
Is there an optimal rate of population growth? If deeper technological progress depends on density, a population that grows too slowly may never reach the densities needed. One that grows too quickly may be under constant Malthusian pressure, with small surpluses and little capital (Figure 5.4). Lecture asks whether Africa might be an example of the first, China of the second, and whether Europe simply happened to be in the sweet spot.








Figure 5.4: An optimal population growth rate? (lecture). Grow too slowly and a population never reaches the density needed for deeper technological progress; grow too fast and it stays under constant Malthusian pressure.





What determines density and growth? Lecture lists three kinds of factors:

Environment. Climate and disease set the positive check.
Culture. Marriage patterns set the preventive check, as with the European marriage pattern, but not in China.
History. War and slavery matter too.



Added · from readings The climate and disease argument is from Boserup (1976), p. 34.
Boserup herself stressed disease. Most remaining “primitive” peoples live in the wet tropics, where abundant plant growth goes together with ideal conditions for the bacteria and parasites that decimate populations. Lower disease mortality in dry and temperate climates, she suggested, “may help to explain why it was the dry and temperate climates that gave rise to most of the early civilizations.” On history, she argued that early urban civilizations captured labor from the surrounding peoples, keeping those peoples below the density needed for development:

“But if the urban civilizations skimmed off the population increase of the surrounding barbarian peoples or even decimated their numbers, the remaining barbarian population was prevented from reaching the minimum density for urbanization. The barbarians continued their land-using subsistence systems, caught in the trap of low population density described above. More recently, the American slave raids in Africa seem to have had similar effects.” (Boserup 1976, p. 34)

Boserup’s argument uses history and anthropology, not formal models. For an informal introduction to modern endogenous growth theory, which emphasizes the economics of “ideas,” lecture recommends Paul Romer’s 2018 Nobel lecture (about 30 minutes), which is structured as a rebuttal to Malthus.
crumbs: Population and the economy: big theories
5  Boserup: Population Pushes Technology

title: 5  Boserup: Population Pushes Technology
text:
5.7 Key ideas

In the technology-pull (Malthusian) view, technology changes on its own and population follows. In Boserup’s population-push view, population growth drives technological change.
Intensification (shorter fallow, more labor per acre) uses known methods, raises output per acre, but usually lowers output per hour of work. A digging stick is better than a plow at low density.
New farming systems mostly spread by diffusion, not invention, when growing density makes them worthwhile.
Density enables specialization, infrastructure, and towns. Very sparse populations can be caught in a low-density trap.

title: 5  Boserup: Population Pushes Technology
text:
5.9 Further reading

Boserup, Ester. 1976. “Environment, Population, and Technology in Primitive Societies.” Population and Development Review 2(1): 21–36. (Reprinted in D. Worster, ed., The Ends of the Earth, Cambridge University Press, 1988.) As you read: Note how agricultural technology responds to population, and the effect of population density on nonagricultural technology.
Malakoff, David. 2011. “Are More People Necessarily a Problem?” Science 333: 544–546. Applying Boserup’s logic to the contemporary world. As you read: What did Machakos have that other crowded regions might lack?

6.1.1 Doubling times
This chapter turns from the distant past (Chapter 5) to the last half century. Table 6.1 shows how long it took the world’s population to double.




Table 6.1: Doubling times of world population (lecture).






Population

Years to double from previous row

Added · new The slide gives 250 years for the 1750–1900 doubling. The dates imply 150, which is also Lam’s figure.
What comes next in the sequence 999, 750, 150, 60, 40? Take a guess before reading on.


Added · from readings Lam (2011), pp. 1232–1235.
David Lam, in his 2011 presidential address to the Population Association of America, reports that when he asks his students this question, most choose 20 or 30 years. “The correct answer is almost surely more than 100 years.” It is even plausible that the world will never reach 12 billion. World population growth peaked at just over 2 percent per year in the 1960s (about 2.2 percent by the Census Bureau’s estimates), shortly before Paul Ehrlich published The Population Bomb in 1968. Growth then fell rapidly. The UN’s 2010 medium projection, which Lam used, put the world at 9.3 billion in 2050 and 10.1 billion in 2100, with a 2050 growth rate of 0.38 percent, a doubling time of about 175 years. “It is virtually certain that world population will never again double in 40 years, making the 1960–2000 experience absolutely unique in human history.”


6.1.2 What would it mean to be “doomed”?
Before asking whether we are doomed, we should be clear about the question. Pair a condition with an outcome:



Condition
Outcome




If population grows quickly
humans go extinct


If forecasts are true
we will be worse off in the future


Even if growth stops
progress will slow


If population shrinks
progress will continue



progress will accelerate



Different combinations are very different claims. “If population keeps growing quickly, humans will go extinct” is a long way from “even if growth stops, progress will slow.”


6.1.3 Can prices save us?
The economist Julian Simon argued that “the only meaningful measure of scarcity in peacetime is the cost of the good in question.” If a resource is really running out, its price should rise.


Added · from readings Lam (2011), pp. 1241–1243.
Lam explains the economist’s reasoning: “it’s hard to develop a model in which a resource that is about to be depleted has a price that is declining, especially a resource owned by private individuals or governments.” Simon, whose 1981 book was titled The Ultimate Resource (meaning human ingenuity), was “the poster child for optimism.”
In 1980, Simon offered to bet that the price of any mineral would fall. The ecologist Paul Ehrlich and colleagues took him up on it. They chose five metals and bought $200 worth of each (on paper). If the inflation-adjusted cost of the bundle was lower in 1990, Simon won.




Table 6.2: The Simon–Ehrlich bet: value of $200 of each metal bought in 1980, in 1990 (inflation-adjusted, 1980 dollars). Source: lecture; Lam (2011).






Metal
1980
1990




Chromium
200
120


Copper
200
163


Nickel
200
193


Tin
200
56


Tungsten
200
86


Total
1000
618








Every metal fell in real price. The bundle’s cost fell 38 percent, and Ehrlich wrote Simon a check. Meanwhile, world population grew by 28 percent, or 830 million people, over the decade of the bet. Lam adds an important caveat: the longer record is more complicated. These metals’ prices rose in the 1960s and 1970s, fell in the 1980s and 1990s, and rose sharply again in the 2000s. Simon would have lost if the bet had ended in 2007, and won if it had ended in 2009. “The big picture,” Lam concludes, “is that these important nonrenewable resources cost about the same today as they did 50 years ago, despite the addition of 4 billion people.”






In the lab



In Lab 4 you replay the bet using a century of commodity prices compiled by the economic historian David Jacks. You ask how much the timing mattered, and whether different kinds of commodities behave differently.




6.1.4 Kinds of resources, and substitution
Resources come in two kinds. Some are exhaustible: copper, coal, “virgin forest.” Others are renewable: topsoil, fisheries, forests, water. For both, substitutability is an important issue.
Consider whale oil, which was burned in lamps. What people want is the service, lighting. As overfishing made whale oil more expensive, people switched to petroleum and, later, light bulbs. The outcome was not so good for whales, but fine for the service of lighting for humans. The very long-run price of lighting in the UK fell steeply from the 1800s onward, as new sources replaced old ones (a chart from Fouquet and Pearson, in lecture).
Food is a renewable resource. Figure 6.1 shows real prices of three grains since 1900, from the same data used in Lab 4.


Show the R code
op <- par(mar = c(4, 4.5, 1, 1))
grains <- c("Wheat", "Corn", "Rice"); gcols <- c("#b35806", "#e08a00", col_ag)
plot(commod$year, commod$Wheat, type = "n", log = "y", ylim = c(10, 300),
     xlab = "Year", ylab = "Real price (1900 = 100, log scale)")
abline(h = 100, lty = 3, col = col_grey)
for (i in 1:3) lines(commod$year, commod[[grains[i]]], col = gcols[i], lwd = 1.8)
legend("bottomleft", grains, col = gcols, lwd = 2, bty = "n")
par(op)








Figure 6.1: Real (inflation-adjusted) prices of wheat, corn, and rice, 1900–2015, indexed to 1900 = 100, on a log scale. Source: David Jacks’s commodity price data, as used in Lab 4.





Real grain prices were volatile, with large spikes, including in the 1970s and around 2008. But the long-run trend is down, by roughly two-thirds or more since 1900, during a century in which world population roughly quadrupled. In the 1970s, as lecture notes, fears of scarcity were not soothed by the data, because grain prices had just spiked. Since then, prices have mostly fallen.
What, then, has gotten more expensive over the last century? Any consumer goods? Any commodities? Anything at all? It’s a good question to think about.

section: 6.2 Lam’s argument: how the world survived
text:
6.2 Lam’s argument: how the world survived

6.2.1 An argument from the extreme case
Lam’s argument works by looking at an extreme case. The last fifty years saw the fastest population growth in human history. If things got better for people even then, that tells us something. He looks at three kinds of indicators: human well-being (poverty), a renewable resource (food), and exhaustible resources (metals and other commodities, discussed above).


Added · from readings Figures in this table and the next subsections are from Lam (2011), pp. 1238–1245.




Table 6.3: Lam’s scorecard for 1961–2009 (poverty: 1981–2005, at $1.25 a day). Source: Lam (2011).






Indicator
Change




World food production
× 3.1


World population
× 2.2


World food production per person
+41%


India: food per person
+37%


Sub-Saharan Africa: food production
× 3.4


Sub-Saharan Africa: population
× 3.6


Sub-Saharan Africa: food per person
about −7%


Poverty rate, low- and middle-income countries
52% → 25%


Poverty rate, China
84% → 16%


Poverty rate, sub-Saharan Africa
53% → 51%








Food. “The battle to feed humanity is already lost,” Ehrlich wrote in 1968, predicting large-scale famines within a decade. Instead, world food production grew faster than population in every decade. India, the focus of Ehrlich’s direst predictions, saw per capita food production rise 37 percent between 1961 and 2009. Sub-Saharan Africa is the exception that proves the point: its food production grew faster than the world’s, but its population grew faster still.
Poverty. The World Bank’s estimates show the share of people in poverty in low- and middle-income countries falling by half between 1981 and 2005, and the absolute number falling from 1.9 billion to 1.4 billion. China drives much of the decline. In sub-Saharan Africa the poverty rate barely moved, and the number of poor people nearly doubled.


6.2.2 How did we survive?
“Arguably the biggest mistake made by the pessimists of the 1960s,” Lam writes, “was in underestimating the impact of these adaptations.” He names six, three economic and three demographic.

Market responses. When food prices rise, farmers grow more. After Vietnam gave farmers more incentives from 1981 on, its food production soared. By 2009 it was 5.5 times its 1960 level, and Vietnam went from a major rice importer to the world’s second-largest exporter.
Innovation. “What made it possible for the world to escape from … the Malthusian trap? The answer is simple: the creation of knowledge” (D. Gale Johnson). Norman Borlaug’s high-yield wheat raised Indian wheat yields 60 percent between 1967 and 1972. Lam explicitly connects such innovations to Boserup: many were “arguably examples of population-induced technological progress.”
Globalization. Trade grew dramatically, and some of the biggest winners were the very countries people worried about in the 1960s, such as India.
Urbanization. About 65 percent of the 4 billion people added since 1960 live in towns and cities.
Fertility decline. The world’s TFR fell from 5.0 in the early 1950s to 2.5 in 2010, which is 85 percent of the way to replacement. The falling infant mortality that caused the explosion also helped end it.
Investment in children. Schooling soared even as school-age populations grew 3 to 4 percent a year. In Thailand, the share of boys completing primary school rose from 18 percent (1950) to 95 percent (1990). Families traded “quantity” of children for “quality.”



6.2.3 Have we really survived?
Lam did not claim everything had gone well. He singled out environmental problems where markets fail: “In domains with ownership of resources and well-functioning markets, as with food and most other commodities, market pressures and price signals induce increased supply, behavioral change, and innovation extremely well. In domains without markets and resource ownership, problems are much more likely.” He also pointed to successes when policy tackled such problems: U.S. sulfur dioxide emissions fell by more than half after 1970, and the 1987 Montreal Protocol cut ozone-destroying CFCs.
His closing image is worth remembering:

“Imagine someone writing in 1961 that in 50 years we would be worrying about how fast per capita consumption is growing in India and China, rather than worrying about mass starvation in those countries.” (Lam 2011)



6.2.4 The “reasonable” economist
Lam’s position is what lecture calls the “reasonable” economist’s view: with functioning markets, increasing population will not cause environmental disaster, but rather adaptation and substitution. But, as MacKellar and Horlacher put it, “When markets are structurally flawed, or when poverty inhibits the operation of market forces, population size and rate of growth usually magnify the adverse impact on natural resources and the environment.”
Sam Preston, reviewing Simon’s The Ultimate Resource, drew a careful conclusion from the historical record: “All we can conclude from a concurrence of accelerated economic growth and population growth is that population growth is not so overwhelmingly negative a factor for economic advance as to swamp the impact of all other influences.”
