title: 6  Are We Doomed? Resources, Prices, and the Commons
text:
6.3 Becker’s critique, and Lam’s reply


Added · from readings This section summarizes Becker (2013) and Lam (2013). Neither is on the slides beyond the reading list.

6.3.1 Becker: what about the rest of the world?
Stan Becker, a demographer at Johns Hopkins, did not dispute Lam’s data. His complaint was about the word “world.” “95 % of the article focuses on Homo sapiens,” he wrote. “Although Homo sapiens has done well, as Lam described, the rest of ‘the world’ has suffered from the success of our species.” He pointed to two problems.
Unsustainable use of resources. The growth in food production required fertilizer made from natural gas and phosphorus, and massive irrigation. Global groundwater overdraft is about 160 billion cubic meters a year, about twice the annual flow of the Nile. Water tables in parts of India have been falling a meter or more a year. Rivers such as the Colorado barely reach the sea.
Damage to the planetary ecosystem. Forests are being cleared at about 13 million hectares a year, an area the size of New York State. Extinction rates are estimated at 100 to 1,000 times their natural background level. Among the large primates, every species except our own is endangered. “Unfortunately, when a species is gone, it is gone forever.”
Becker proposed the framework of ecological economics: the economy is embedded in nature, development should meet “the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs,” and ecosystems can respond to stress in sudden, nonlinear ways. He ended with a question: “Will birth cohorts of 2040–2050 look back and wish our generation had done more to preserve the world that was bequeathed to us? I do believe so.”


6.3.2 Lam: externalities, not numbers
Lam’s reply opens with a nickname an online commenter had given him: “Professor Happy Talk.” He concedes that his “world” was the human world, though he notes that a 1960 forecaster who predicted the main worry of 2013 would be the effect of human success on other species would have been considered wildly optimistic. He agrees with Becker about aquifers, which suffer from the same lack of property rights as air pollution and overfishing. He is much less worried about running out of oil or other resources with clear property rights and active markets. The urgent problem, he argues, is not running out but cutting carbon emissions, which markets alone will not do.
Lam’s central point is about cause and cure:






In his own words



“Stopping population growth is unlikely to end aquifer depletion or deforestation, as long as the fundamental externality issues have not been solved.” (Lam 2013)


On deforestation, for example, he cites evidence that illegal logging in Indonesia depends on how political jurisdictions are organized. “The point is that it will take institutional change, not simply the end of population growth, to solve the problem.” Lam also pushes back on Becker’s definition of sustainable development, asking what practical guidance it really provides. Read his reply to see how he makes the case.

title: 6  Are We Doomed? Resources, Prices, and the Commons
text:
6.4 Lam’s conclusion, and ours?
Lam’s conclusion: things got better for people even during the era of peak population growth, so they should continue to get better as population growth slows.
But following Preston, we might add two cautions. The last fifty years were also a time of enormous economic growth. Perhaps economic growth will slow down faster than population growth. And even Lam’s own timing illustrates how volatile the evidence can be. As he was writing in 2011, food prices were spiking, and he asked himself what he would bet. In lecture we look at the FAO food price index: had Lam bet on falling food prices in 2011, he would have “won.”
Finally, there is risk aversion. There is a lot of uncertainty about major issues such as global warming and species extinction. If change is basically for the better, we don’t need to be afraid. If we’re not so certain, then perhaps we should be careful, even if we are not strict conservationists. Or, as lecture puts it: “How fast should we drive in the dark?”

title: 6  Are We Doomed? Resources, Prices, and the Commons
text:
6.5 When prices fail
Markets coordinate an enormous amount of behavior through prices. When something becomes scarce, its price rises, people use less of it, and producers make more. Earlier in this chapter, the resources that “survived the population bomb” were mostly ones bought and sold in markets. But some goods are badly priced, or not priced at all. Lecture lists four kinds of pricing problem:

The tragedy of the commons. Someone exploiting a shared resource gets all of the benefit but pays only a tiny fraction of the cost. Examples: ocean fisheries, tropical forests, and the library book returned to the easiest shelf rather than its proper place.
Public goods. Someone can use the good without taking it away from anyone else, as with clean air or knowledge. The problem is that individuals have little incentive to improve it or invest in it.
Externalities. Costs, such as pollution, that are not reflected in prices.
Poverty. People with no alternatives cannot respond to the price signals that tell them a resource is getting scarce.



Added · from readings Nordhaus 2018, pp. 440–442.
William Nordhaus, who shared the 2018 Nobel Prize in economics for his work on climate change, puts the problem in the language of public goods. A public good has two key features. The cost of extending it to one more person is zero (“nonrivalry”), and it is impossible to keep anyone from enjoying it (“nonexcludability”). Climate change is the mirror image, a “public bad.” Greenhouse gas emissions spread their harm around the whole planet, and no one can be shielded from it. What makes climate change “particularly thorny,” Nordhaus writes, is that the externality is global: “none of us acting individually can do anything to slow the changes.”

title: 6  Are We Doomed? Resources, Prices, and the Commons
text:
6.6 Optimal harvesting
Start with something simpler than the climate: a population of fish. Fish, timber, and fresh water are all renewable resources. A simple sustainability rule is that a renewable resource lasts forever as long as its “renewal rate” is at least as large as its “losses.”
More formally, let

\(b\) = the birth rate, the fraction of the resource newly available each year;
\(d\) = the death rate, the fraction lost each year without harvesting;
\(h\) = the harvest rate, the fraction harvested each year.

The resource is sustainable if
\[
b \ge d + h.
\]

6.6.1 A Malthusian fish population
Fish face the same constraints as Malthus’s farmers. Suppose fish have birth and death rates that depend on how much food each fish gets, and food per fish falls as the number of fish rises. This is exactly the Malthusian diagram from Chapter 3, with “food per fish” in place of wages. Without any fishing, the population settles at the equilibrium \(N^*\), where births equal deaths.
Now we harvest a fraction \(h\) of the fish every year, for a total harvest of \(H = h \times N\). To the fish, harvesting is just another source of death. The death curve shifts up by \(h\), from \(d(w)\) to \(d(w) + h\) (Figure 6.2).


Added · new The figures in this section are drawn from an illustrative model I constructed (functional forms in the setup code). They reproduce the shapes in your slides, not your app’s numbers.








Figure 6.2: A Malthusian fish population with and without harvesting. Harvesting at rate h raises the effective death rate from d(w) to d(w) + h (dashed). The new equilibrium has more food per fish and fewer fish: N*_h instead of N*.





The harvested population settles at a new, smaller equilibrium, \(N^*_h\). The surviving fish are better fed, so their birth rate rises and their natural death rate falls, just enough to make up for the fish we take. A population can be harvested forever this way.
Can we fish a population to extinction? Yes: if the harvest is so large that \(d + h > b\) at every level of food per fish, deaths always exceed births, however few fish are left and however well fed they are.


6.6.2 The maximum sustainable harvest
How much should we harvest? Think about the total sustainable harvest, \(H = h \times N^*(h)\):

If \(h = 0\), we catch nothing.
If we fish too hard, the population goes extinct, and again we catch nothing.
In between, the harvest is positive.

So there must be a harvest rate that gives the largest sustainable catch, \(H_{\max}\) (Figure 6.3).








Figure 6.3: Sustainable harvest yield, H = h × N*(h), against the harvest rate h, in the illustrative model. The yield is zero with no fishing and zero at the extinction rate; it peaks at h_optimal.





Harvesting faster than \(h_{\text{optimal}}\) is overexploitation. It leads to a smaller sustainable harvest. But a higher harvest rate can temporarily raise the catch, because it takes time for the fish population to shrink to its new, lower equilibrium. That temporary gain is the trap. Each individual fisher has an incentive to fish harder, but if everyone does, the result is a smaller, more expensive harvest for all. This is the tragedy of the commons.


6.6.3 Try it: the harvest app


Added · new The app is the course’s own harvest app (ShinyApps/harvest in the 2025 course repo), exported with Shinylive so it runs in the browser, in its own tab. The three questions are mine; they leave the harvest rate at zero, because all of the Lab 5 graded questions on this app are about the harvest rate and the yield it produces.
The app simulates a Malthusian fish population, like the one in Figure 6.2. The top-left panel shows birth and death rates against food per fish (the “wage”), the bottom-left shows the number of fish against food per fish, and the right-hand panels trace the fish population and the harvest over time. The “harvest h rate” slider sets the share of fish caught each period. It opens in a new tab, so you can make it full screen and keep this page open alongside it. (The first load can take a few seconds while R starts up in your browser.)



The harvest app at its starting values. Click to open it in a new tab.


Open the harvest app in a new tab ↗
Before you move each slider, write down what you expect to happen. Then check.

Find the resting point. With no harvest, press play. Before you do: the population starts at 7.7. Will it grow, shrink, or stay where it is? Where does it settle?
A predator arrives. Raise “d’(w) level” from 0.10 to 0.12, leaving the harvest at zero, and press play. Predict the long-run fish population and food per fish. Why are the surviving fish better fed?
Harvest versus predator. Look at how the app treats the harvest rate: it adds to the death rate, just as a predator does. What is different about a harvest from the point of view of the people doing the fishing?

Lab 5 asks you to use the app to find the harvest rate that gives the largest sustainable yield.

title: 6  Are We Doomed? Resources, Prices, and the Commons
text:
6.7 Hardin’s tragedy
The phrase “the tragedy of the commons” comes from a 1968 article in Science by the biologist Garrett Hardin. Hardin’s real target was population growth, but his argument applies to any shared resource.


Added · from readings The rest of this section draws on Hardin 1968, throughout. Your slides quote only “Mutual coercion, mutually agreed upon.”

6.7.1 Problems with no technical solution
Hardin begins with a category: problems that have “no technical solution.” A technical solution, he says, is “one that requires a change only in the techniques of the natural sciences, demanding little or nothing in the way of change in human values or ideas of morality.” His example is the game of tick-tack-toe. You cannot guarantee a win against an opponent who understands the game. You can “win” only by changing the meaning of winning: “I can hit my opponent over the head; or I can drug him; or I can falsify the records.” Hardin argued that the population problem was of this kind. People hoped that “farming the seas or developing new strains of wheat will solve the problem,” and in his view they were wrong.


6.7.2 The herdsman’s calculation
Hardin borrowed the core idea from an 1833 pamphlet by William Forster Lloyd.






In his own words



“Picture a pasture open to all. It is to be expected that each herdsman will try to keep as many cattle as possible on the commons. … As a rational being, each herdsman seeks to maximize his gain. Explicitly or implicitly, more or less consciously, he asks, ‘What is the utility to me of adding one more animal to my herd?’” (Hardin 1968)


The answer has two parts. The herdsman gets all the proceeds from selling the extra animal, so the gain to him is nearly +1. The cost is the extra overgrazing, but “since, however, the effects of overgrazing are shared by all the herdsmen, the negative utility for any particular decision-making herdsman is only a fraction of −1.” So he adds another animal, “and another; and another…. But this is the conclusion reached by each and every rational herdsman sharing a commons. Therein is the tragedy.” Hardin’s summary: “Freedom in a commons brings ruin to all.”
Why “tragedy”? Hardin uses the word in the philosopher Alfred North Whitehead’s sense: “The essence of dramatic tragedy is not unhappiness. It resides in the solemnity of the remorseless working of things.” No one in the story is wicked or stupid. Each herdsman does what is sensible for him, and that is exactly what makes the outcome inevitable.
Hardin’s examples range widely:

Fisheries. Maritime nations, “professing to believe in ‘the inexhaustible resources of the oceans,’ … bring species after species of fish and whales closer to extinction.”
National parks. The parks are open to all, “there is only one Yosemite Valley,” and crowding erodes the very thing visitors come for. Hardin lists the options: sell the parks off as private property, or keep them public and ration entry by auction, by merit, by lottery, or by first-come, first-served queues. “They are all objectionable. But we must choose.”
Parking. One Christmas season in Leominster, Massachusetts, the city covered its parking meters with bags reading “Free parking courtesy of the mayor and city council.” Facing more demand for already scarce space, Hardin noted dryly, “the city fathers reinstituted the system of the commons.”



6.7.3 Pollution: the commons in reverse
Pollution is the same tragedy run backwards. Instead of taking something out of the commons, we put something in: sewage into rivers, fumes into the air. “The rational man finds that his share of the cost of the wastes he discharges into the commons is less than the cost of purifying his wastes before releasing them.” A pasture can be fenced and turned into private property. “But the air and waters surrounding us cannot readily be fenced.” So, Hardin argued, pollution must be controlled “by coercive laws or taxing devices that make it cheaper for the polluter to treat his pollutants than to discharge them untreated.”
Hardin makes the link to population explicit. “It did not much matter how a lonely American frontiersman disposed of his waste,” because there were few people around. This leads to what he calls a principle of morality: “the morality of an act is a function of the state of the system at the time it is performed.” A plainsman of 150 years earlier could kill a bison, eat only the tongue, and leave the rest without being “in any important sense … wasteful.” With only a few thousand bison left, the same act would appall us.


6.7.4 Mutual coercion, mutually agreed upon
What can be done? Hardin rejects appeals to conscience, for two reasons. First, he argues, conscience is self-eliminating. If restraint is voluntary, those who ignore the appeal gain at the expense of those who heed it. Second, a voluntary appeal sends a contradictory message, which Hardin calls a “double bind.” Officially it says you are irresponsible if you don’t restrain yourself, while unofficially it says you are “a simpleton who can be shamed into standing aside while the rest of us exploit the commons.”
His alternative is the phrase on the lecture slide: “mutual coercion, mutually agreed upon.” Taxes are his main example. “Who enjoys taxes? We all grumble about them. But we accept compulsory taxes because we recognize that voluntary taxes would favor the conscienceless.” So are parking meters. “We need not actually forbid a citizen to park as long as he wants to; we need merely make it increasingly expensive for him to do so.” Hardin insists on calling this coercion, not persuasion: “The only kind of coercion I recommend is mutual coercion, mutually agreed upon by the majority of the people affected.”
Two more of his points are worth keeping. First, the alternative to a commons does not have to be perfect. Hardin admits that private property with inheritance is unjust, but “the alternative of the commons is too horrifying to contemplate. Injustice is preferable to total ruin.” Second, doing nothing is not neutral: “we can never do nothing. That which we have done for thousands of years is also action. It also produces evils.”


Added · new This paragraph’s assessment of Hardin is mine.
Hardin’s own conclusion was that “freedom to breed is intolerable,” and he called for abandoning “the commons in breeding.” That conclusion, along with passages in which he speculates that the “biologically more fit” should inherit more property, has made the article controversial. You can accept his analysis of the commons without accepting his prescriptions for population. Indeed, his logic applies most clearly where the costs of an action really are shared by everyone, such as emissions into the atmosphere.


6.7.5 A classroom fishing game
In lecture we play a “massively multiplayer offline game” based on the fish model. Each of you chooses a harvest rate \(h_i\): abstemious (0 percent), moderate (5 percent), or rapacious (10 percent). The class’s average harvest rate, \(h_{\text{ave}}\), determines the sustainable number of fish, \(N^*(h_{\text{ave}})\), from a table like Table 6.4. Your own catch is your own harvest rate times that number:
\[
H_i = h_i \times N^*(h_{\text{ave}}).
\]




Table 6.4: Sustainable fish population at each average harvest rate (from the lecture slides).






Average harvest rate (%)
Sustainable fish population




0
2000


1
1700


2
1400


3
1100


4
900


5
600


6
400


7
300


8
100

0

0








Notice the structure. The fish population depends on everyone’s choices, but your harvest depends mostly on your own choice. (Why “mostly”?) We play several rounds and then compare with a round in which an “enlightened ruler” regulates fishing so that the average is about 4 percent. The lesson, which the second lecture spells out, is that the “invisible hand,” everyone acting in their own interest, fails in a commons. In our example, even the greediest fisher is better off when no one is allowed to be selfish.
Why not solve the problem the way we solved the problem of the pasture, by privatization? Ask yourself why that is not practical for fish in the ocean.

title: 6  Are We Doomed? Resources, Prices, and the Commons
text:
6.8 Key ideas

World population doubled from 3 to 6 billion in just 39 years, but growth peaked in the 1960s and will almost surely never double that fast again.
Lam argues the world survived the population bomb, with more food per person, falling poverty, and stable resource prices, thanks to market responses, innovation, globalization, urbanization, fertility decline, and investment in children.
Becker counters that the environment and other species paid a heavy price. Lam replies that the root problem is externalities and missing property rights, not population numbers as such.
Some goods are badly priced: commons, public goods, externalities, and resources used by people too poor to respond to prices.
A renewable resource is sustainable if renewal is at least as large as losses, \(b \ge d + h\). In a Malthusian fish population, the sustainable harvest is zero with no fishing and zero at extinction, so there is an optimal harvest rate in between.
In Hardin’s tragedy of the commons, each user gets nearly all of the benefit of using more but pays only a fraction of the cost, so everyone overuses. Hardin’s remedy is “mutual coercion, mutually agreed upon,” such as taxes and meters.

title: 7  Population and Climate Change
text:
7.1 Global warming: a commons the size of the planet
How does global warming compare with overfishing? The similarity is that both are commons that unregulated individuals will destroy. The differences are part of what makes climate change so hard:
crumbs: Resources and the environment
7  Population and Climate Change

title: 7  Population and Climate Change
text:
It is global, not local.
The feedback is delayed. Emissions today warm the climate for decades and centuries.
We must rely even more on models, of both the climate and the economy.
The downside could be unimaginably bad.


7.1.1 The science, briefly


Added · from readings This subsection and the next three draw on Nordhaus 2018, pp. 444–459.
Nordhaus summarizes the science in a paragraph. The main source of warming is burning fossil fuels. The carbon dioxide this releases accumulates in the atmosphere and stays there for a long time, and feedbacks in the atmosphere, oceans, and ice sheets amplify the initial warming. Atmospheric CO2 was 280 parts per million in 1750 and more than 413 in 2018. Without forceful steps, it will reach 700–900 parts per million by 2100, leading to global warming of 3–5°C by 2100 and more after that.
Nordhaus’s favorite metaphor is a “climate casino”:






In his own words



“Economic growth is producing unintended but dangerous changes in the climate and earth systems. These changes will lead to unforeseeable consequences. We are rolling the climatic dice, the outcome will produce surprises, and some of them are likely to be perilous. The message is that we need not roll the climatic dice — that there is time to turn around and walk back out of the casino.” (Nordhaus 2018, pp. 444–445)




7.1.2 An economist’s approach
The economist’s approach to global warming has four steps: recognize the tragedy of the commons; agree, within and between nations, to reduce emissions; choose among methods such as carbon taxes and subsidies; and model the costs and benefits of different approaches to find the path that is best for human welfare. In lecture we watch parts of Nordhaus’s Nobel lecture: the introduction and overview, strategies and costs, his DICE model, and the carbon tax.
Three strategies. Nordhaus considers three ways to slow climate change. Plan C, “geoengineering,” would make the earth more reflective, for example with particles in the stratosphere. He compares it to “salvage therapy,” a dangerous treatment for when all else has failed: “no responsible country should undertake geoengineering as the first line of defense against global warming.” Plan B, removing carbon from the air, is “running combustion in reverse,” but no technology can yet do it at scale at a reasonable cost. That leaves Plan A, abatement, which means burning less carbon. Estimates put its cost at a bit above 1 percent of world output for a 50 percent cut in emissions, and about 3.5 percent for eliminating emissions entirely.
Damages. Estimating the damage from warming is harder than estimating the cost of preventing it. Highly managed sectors of rich economies can adapt for a while. Unmanaged systems cannot: rain-fed agriculture, snow packs, coastal communities, natural ecosystems, and especially low-income and tropical regions. Scientists also worry about “tipping points,” such as the melting of the Greenland and West Antarctic ice sheets or changes in the Gulf Stream, which are hard to reverse once triggered. In Nordhaus’s DICE model, damages are about 2 percent of output at 3°C of warming and 8 percent at 6°C. Other estimates, he notes, “are all over the map.”
The optimal path. Too much warming would be terrible. So would too much limitation on economic growth. The optimum has some warming and some limitation on growth, and finding it means putting costs and benefits in a common metric. Nordhaus defends this against the alternative of fixed temperature targets. If meeting a 1.5°C target “would require deep reductions in living standards in poor nations, then the policy would be the equivalent of burning down the village to save it.” His most controversial result is that the cost-benefit optimum allows warming of more than 3°C by 2100, well above international targets.
The social cost of carbon. One by-product of the model is an estimate of the damage done by one more ton of CO2, called the social cost of carbon. In an optimal policy, that is what a carbon tax should be: about $36 per ton in Nordhaus’s standard model, and much more for strict temperature targets. The estimate depends heavily on the discount rate, meaning how much weight we put on the welfare of future generations compared with our own. Nordhaus calls discounting “perhaps the most important conceptual issue facing current climate policy.”


7.1.3 The big challenge: coordination
Lecture sums up the economist’s view in two points. The “price” of slowing climate change is not terribly high, but doing it is a problem because of coordination. The challenge is the one Hardin laid out: how do we mutually agree to mutually coerce ourselves?
Nordhaus’s name for the obstacle is free-riding. The actual global carbon price, he reports, is at most a tenth of even his modest $36 estimate. Why?






In his own words



“No single country has an incentive to cut its emissions sharply. Suppose that when country A spends $100 on abatement, global damages decline by $200. However, country A might get only $20 of the benefits, so it would tend to decline the responsibility.” (Nordhaus 2018, p. 457)


This is Hardin’s herdsman again. Country A captures nearly all the benefit of burning carbon but only a small fraction of the damage. Nordhaus adds a second layer, generational free-riding: the current generation can push the costs onto future generations, because “most of the benefits of costly emissions reductions today would accrue many decades in the future.”
The record of international agreements bears this out. Under the Kyoto Protocol of 1997, high-income countries agreed to limit their emissions. The United States withdrew early, and no middle-income or developing countries joined. The protocol “died a quiet death, mourned by few, on December 31, 2012.” The Paris Accord of 2015 asks each country for voluntary “nationally determined contributions,” with no penalty for missing them. Nordhaus’s verdict: “The world is therefore just where it stood in 1994, recognizing the dangers of climate change without effective policies to stop it.” He finds no break in the long-run decline of the world’s carbon intensity (emissions per dollar of output, outside China) after any of the landmark agreements.
Climate clubs. Nordhaus’s proposed solution is a “climate club.” Member countries would agree on a minimum carbon price, and, crucially, they would penalize non-members, for example with a uniform tariff on their exports to club members. The penalty is what turns a voluntary agreement into mutual coercion. It changes each country’s self-interested calculation, so that joining becomes the better choice.


7.1.4 Dismal conclusions?
If there are no “mutual agreements for mutual coercion,” what can save us? Lecture suggests three possibilities:

Self-interest. Technological change may make low-emission energy cheaper on its own.
The prospect of future agreements may encourage investment now. (Why would a government want access to lithium if it didn’t expect more electric cars?)
Going beyond abatement, to carbon removal and climate engineering.



Added · from readings Nordhaus 2018, pp. 464–465.
Nordhaus ends his lecture with four steps: understanding the gravity of the problem, raising the price of carbon, coordinating action globally (through a club), and developing low-carbon technologies. “Knowledge, proper pricing, coordinated action, and new technologies — these are the steps that are necessary if we are to tame this Colossus that threatens our world.”

title: 7  Population and Climate Change
section: 7.2 How much does population matter for emissions?
text:
7.2 How much does population matter for emissions?
So far, population has been in the background. Now we ask directly: how much does population growth contribute to climate change? Consider a claim to discuss: A proportional increase in population will cause a proportional increase in global warming. For example, if warming along some population trajectory would be 2.0 degrees, a 10 percent larger population would lead to 2.2 degrees. True or false?

7.2.1 Decomposition versus model
The economist David Lam approaches this question with a decomposition, an approach for which lecture tips its hat to Paul Ehrlich and others.


Added · new The name “IPAT” for Ehrlich’s version is from general knowledge, not your slides.
Start with an example that has nothing to do with climate. Total output is output per person times the number of people: \(Y = y \times N\). Is this just an identity, an algebraic way of factoring a number? Or is it a model of how the world works? As an identity, it is always true. But if we use it to predict what happens when one factor changes, we are assuming that the other factors stay the same, ceteris paribus. If population itself depends on income, as in Malthus, then changing income also changes \(N\). To use the decomposition as a model, we need to know whether the factors depend on each other. (Ehrlich’s version of this idea, “IPAT,” writes environmental Impact as Population × Affluence × Technology.)
For carbon emissions, the decomposition is
\[
\text{CO}_2 = N \times \frac{\text{dollars of output}}{\text{person}} \times
\frac{\text{CO}_2}{\text{dollar of output}}, \qquad\text{or}\qquad C = N \times y \times c.
\]
Nordhaus’s DICE model includes feedbacks among these factors, such as how the economy is hurt by climate damage. If we ignore those feedbacks and hold everything else constant, the decomposition tells us what would happen if we changed one factor, such as population.


7.2.2 Lam’s approach
Lam divides the world into four groups of countries by income: low-income (LIC), lower-middle-income (LMIC), upper-middle-income (UMIC), and high-income (HIC). For each group \(i\),
\[
C_i = N_i \times y_i \times c_i,
\]
and world emissions are the sum over the groups. To project to 2084, 60 years ahead, Lam assumes each factor changes at a constant exponential rate: population at rate \(R\), income per person at rate \(g\), and carbon per dollar at rate \(s\). Because the factors multiply, their growth rates add. Emissions in each group grow at the rate \(R + g + s\).

Three things stand out. Population growth is concentrated in the poorest countries, and population actually falls in the upper-middle-income group. Income grows fastest in poorer countries. And carbon intensity falls everywhere, fastest in low-income countries, which may “leapfrog” directly to cleaner technologies.


Added · from readings The UN figures and the per-capita comparison are from Lam 2025.
Just as important is where the extra people will be. The UN projects that world population will peak at 10.3 billion in 2084, 2.1 billion more than in 2024. In Lam’s words, “coming decades will see a large shift in population from countries with high consumption and emissions to countries with low consumption and emissions.” Per capita CO2 emissions in high-income countries are about 35 times those in low-income countries.


7.2.3 Lam’s results
Figure 7.1 reproduces Lam’s calculation with the numbers from Lab 5. It compares emissions in 2024 with two projections for 2084: one with the UN’s projected population change, and a counterfactual with each group’s population frozen at its 2024 level.


Show the R code
mat <- rbind(`2024` = lam$C_2024,
             `2084, no population change` = lam$C_2084_nopop,
             `2084, with population change` = lam$C_2084) / 1e9
colnames(mat) <- c("Low income", "Lower middle", "Upper middle", "High income")
op <- par(mar = c(4, 4.5, 1, 1))
bp <- barplot(mat, beside = TRUE, col = c("grey70", "#4a7fc1", "#c0392b"),
              border = NA, ylim = c(0, 17),
              ylab = "Billions of tons of CO2 per year")
text(bp, mat + 0.5, sprintf("%.1f", mat), cex = 0.75)
legend("topleft", rownames(mat), fill = c("grey70", "#4a7fc1", "#c0392b"),
       border = NA, bty = "n", cex = 0.9)
par(op)








Figure 7.1: CO2 emissions by income group in 2024 and projected for 2084, with and without population change (billions of tons per year). Reproduced from Lam’s (2025) decomposition using the Lab 5 parameters.





World emissions fall by about 52 percent between 2024 and 2084 with population change, and by about 52 percent without it. The two projections are almost identical.
How can two billion more people make almost no difference? Look at the groups. Population growth raises 2084 emissions in the low-income group by about 0.4 billion tons and in the lower-middle-income group by about 1.4 billion tons. But population decline in the upper-middle-income group lowers its emissions by about 1.6 billion tons. The effects cancel. And the big declines from 2024 happen in the two richer groups, whether or not population changes, because their emissions per dollar fall fast and their populations are not growing.


Added · from readings Lam 2025.
Lam’s own summary: “The surprising bottom line is that the net effect of projected population changes over the next 60 years is an almost neutral impact on CO2 emissions, despite the addition of over 2 billion people.” He adds two qualifications. First, population growth does raise emissions in the poorest countries. In low-income countries it turns a 1.1 percent annual decline in emissions into a 0.4 percent annual increase. If population in low- and lower-middle-income countries did not grow at all, global emissions in 2084 would be 15 percent lower than projected. Second, carbon is not the whole story. Population growth matters much more for food and water. With population growth, world food consumption rises by 45 percent by 2084, compared with 15 percent from income growth alone, and water use by 21 percent compared with almost no increase. Lam also draws a broader lesson. Food and non-renewable resources respond well to market signals, while water and greenhouse gases are “sectors in which market signals are less effective”: exactly the commons problems of this chapter and Chapter 6.


7.2.4 What the answer depends on
So what is the effect of population growth on climate change? The answer depends on:

how much population changes;
who grows: high emitters or low emitters. Population growth in a high emitter such as Russia would have a big effect, and growth in a low emitter such as Ghana a small one;
how emissions per person change over time.

Lam’s analysis shows that projected population growth has little effect on emissions, because of where that growth is expected to happen and because of his assumptions about decarbonization and economic growth. All of this is “all else equal.” The lab gives you a chance to see how robust the finding is when the assumptions change. The lesson, perhaps, is to worry more about how to reduce emissions from economic activity, and less about how to slow population growth.






In the lab



In Lab 5 you reproduce Lam’s calculation, including the counterfactual with no population change, and then change his assumptions to see whether the conclusion holds. You also use the harvest “app” to explore the relationship between the harvest rate and the sustainable yield.

7.3 Key ideas

Climate change is a global commons. Nordhaus estimates that slowing it is not very expensive, but free-riding, by countries and by generations, has defeated voluntary agreements. He proposes a climate club that penalizes non-members.
Emissions can be decomposed as \(C = N \times y \times c\), so their growth rate is \(R + g + s\). A decomposition is only a model if we can hold the other factors constant.
Lam finds that 2 billion more people will barely change global CO2 emissions, because population grows where emissions per person are low and falls where they are high.

title: 8  Aging and Social Security: A Ponzi Scheme?
text:
8.1 A “Ponzi scheme”?
In February 2025, Elon Musk told the podcaster Joe Rogan that “Social Security is the biggest Ponzi scheme of all time.” People pay in, he said, “and the money goes out of Social Security immediately,” while “people are living way longer than expected and there are fewer babies being born.”
Is he right? A Ponzi scheme pays early investors with money from later ones, and collapses when new recruits run out. Social Security does pay today’s retirees with today’s workers’ taxes. So the comparison is not crazy. But whether such a system is a swindle, a sensible arrangement, or something in between depends on demography: on how fast each generation grows relative to the one before. This chapter works out why. Chapter 9 then asks the bigger question behind it: if low fertility makes pensions harder to pay for, should we want more children?

8  Aging and Social Security: A Ponzi Scheme?

title: 8  Aging and Social Security: A Ponzi Scheme?
text:
8.2 The life-cycle savings dilemma

8.2.1 Consumption and production by age
People are dependent in childhood, and often again in old age. Yet in general we want to consume at a fairly steady level throughout our lives. The result is a life-cycle dilemma: we produce most of what we will ever produce in a few decades of working life, but we need to consume in every year of life.
The pattern shows up everywhere it has been measured. In lecture we look at age profiles of earnings and consumption for the United States, for urban and rural Côte d’Ivoire, and for the Aché, hunter-gatherers of the Amazon. Aché children run a food “deficit,” consuming more calories than they produce, until their late teens. Adults run a “surplus” that peaks in their thirties.
Figure 8.1 shows the same thing for Japan, using the data from the lab: the value of what people produce (labor income) and consume at each age, in U.S. dollars per person per year.


Show the R code
op <- par(mar = c(4, 4.5, 1, 1))
plot(x, yx / 1000, type = "l", lwd = 2.5, col = col_y, ylim = c(0, 34),
     xlab = "Age", ylab = "Thousands of dollars per year")
lines(x, cx / 1000, lwd = 2.5, col = col_c)
text(47, 33, "Production (labor income)", col = col_y, pos = 4, cex = 0.9)
text(88, 25, "Consumption", col = col_c, cex = 0.9)
par(op)








Figure 8.1: Per capita labor income (production) and consumption by age, Japan, in U.S. dollars per year. Consumption includes publicly provided education and health care. The profiles are held constant above about age 90 in the data. Source: National Transfer Accounts (lab data).





Children produce nothing, and their consumption jumps in the school years (education is counted as consumption). Labor income rises steeply in the twenties, peaks in the late forties, and falls away in the sixties. Consumption rises again in old age, largely because of health care.


Added · from readings The National Transfer Accounts and the U.S.–Thailand comparison are from Lee et al. 2014 (text and Fig. 1).
Profiles like these come from the National Transfer Accounts (NTA), a project in which research teams in 40 countries used “existing surveys, administrative data, and the United Nations System of National Accounts” to estimate what people produce and consume at each age. The profiles differ in revealing ways. In the United States, Lee and coauthors write, “elderly consume far more than young adults and labor income falls off rapidly at older ages,” and public transfers to the elderly are generous. In Thailand, “elderly and young adults consume at similar levels,” the elderly earn somewhat more than in the United States, the public system for the elderly is “very modest,” and “familial support is very important.”


8.2.2 Three ways to solve the dilemma
How can the young and the old consume more than they produce?

Private transfers. Children “borrow” from their parents, who feed and raise them, and pay them back when the parents grow old. (What could go wrong?)
Public transfers. The government taxes people in the surplus ages and redistributes to the deficit ages. (What could go wrong?)
Private savings. People save their own surplus during their working years and live on it in old age. This requires goods that last, or else you still have to rely on a younger generation to sell you what you need. (What could go wrong?) And it doesn’t help you as a child.



Added · from readings Lee et al. 2014.
Lee and coauthors put the first two together under the heading of intergenerational transfers, which “shift resources from some generations to others with no expectation of direct repayment.” Private transfers occur “when parents rear their children and when older people assist their adult children or alternatively receive assistance from them.” Public transfers include “public education, publicly funded health care, public pensions, and the taxes to pay for these programs.” In rich countries the two flow in opposite directions: “public transfers are predominantly to the elderly, while private transfers go mostly to children.”

section: 8.3 A worked example: walnuts and chocolate
text:
8.3 A worked example: walnuts and chocolate
To see how population growth affects these solutions, consider a stylized economy. Make some simplifying (but not essential) assumptions:

Life has two stages, “middle age” and “old age,” one generation apart.
No one dies until the end of old age.
Everyone wants perfectly smooth consumption.
Each person produces 18 units in middle age and 6 in old age.

A. A “nut” economy with durable goods. Suppose output is walnuts, which keep. Each person can simply save. Lifetime production is 18 + 6 = 24, so smoothed consumption is 12 per period, 24 per lifetime.
B. A “chocolate” economy with no durable goods, and zero population growth. Chocolate melts, so it can’t be saved. To smooth consumption, the middle-aged must transfer to the old. With 100 middle-aged and 100 old people, total output is 100 × 18 + 100 × 6 = 2,400, shared among 200 people: 12 per person per period, 24 per lifetime. Transfers do exactly as well as saving.
C. A chocolate economy where each generation is twice the size of the last. Now there are 200 middle-aged and 100 old people. Total output is 200 × 18 + 100 × 6 = 4,200, shared among 300 people: 14 per person per period, 28 per lifetime.

In the growing chocolate economy, everyone, in every generation, consumes more over their life than they produce. Where does the extra come from? Each generation receives more in old age than it gave in middle age, because there are more workers behind it. A growing population creates what we call transfer wealth.
So, for transfers from young to old like Social Security, population growth is good:

it increases lifetime consumption,
by creating “transfer” wealth,
and, in our example, it does better than private saving of durable goods.



Added · new Samuelson is credited from Lee et al.’s reference list (Samuelson 1958); the description of his result is mine.
When are transfers and saving equally good? When the interest rate on savings equals the population growth rate plus the growth rate of wages. Then each dollar paid into a transfer system earns the same “return” as a dollar invested. This insight goes back to a famous 1958 paper by the economist Paul Samuelson. When population and wages grow faster than the interest rate, transfers beat saving. When they grow more slowly, saving wins.

title: 8  Aging and Social Security: A Ponzi Scheme?
text:
8.4 The PAYGO identity
A pay-as-you-go (PAYGO) pension system is one in which each year’s benefits are paid out of the same year’s taxes:
\[
\text{annual benefits paid} = \text{annual taxes collected}.
\]
Break each side into an amount per person times a number of people. Let \(b\) be the benefit per old person, \(N_O\) the number of old people, \(t\) the tax rate, \(y\) the earnings per worker, and \(N_W\) the number of workers. Then
\[
b \, N_O = t \, y \, N_W.
\]
Rearranging gives the PAYGO identity:
\[
t = \frac{b}{y} \times \frac{N_O}{N_W},
\]
or, in words,
\[
\text{tax rate} = \text{replacement rate} \times \text{old-age dependency ratio}.
\]
The replacement rate \(b/y\) is how large the average benefit is compared with the average wage. The old-age dependency ratio \(N_O/N_W\) is the number of beneficiaries per worker. The identity is just accounting, but it is powerful. It tells us exactly how the tax rate, the generosity of benefits, and demography have to fit together.
A worked example. In 2023 the United States had about 180 million workers paying Social Security taxes and about 60 million beneficiaries. Suppose we want a replacement rate of 40 percent. Then the tax rate must be
\[
t = 0.40 \times \frac{60}{180} = 0.40 \times \frac{1}{3} \approx 13.3\%.
\]


Added · from readings Payroll tax rates, the earnings cap, and the 2017 beneficiary counts are from the 2018 Trustees Report, pp. 2 and 7–8.
That is close to the real thing. In 2017, employees and employers each paid 6.2 percent of covered earnings, for a combined OASDI (Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance) payroll tax of 12.4 percent, on earnings up to $127,200. Payroll taxes made up 88 percent of the trust funds’ income.
Actual Social Security has many details that our identity ignores. It is progressive, giving higher replacement rates to the poor than to the rich. It pays benefits to the disabled and to children whose parents die, as well as to retirees. Benefits are indexed to inflation, and the retirement age and working years are indexed too. And the tax is based on taxable wages, not on the entire economy. The Trustees Report shows how much the “details” matter. At the end of 2017, Social Security was paying benefits to about 62 million people: “45 million retired workers and dependents of retired workers, 6 million survivors of deceased workers, and 10 million disabled workers and dependents of disabled workers.”

title: 8  Aging and Social Security: A Ponzi Scheme?
section: 8.5 Demographic change and Social Security’s future
text:
8.5 Demographic change and Social Security’s future

8.5.1 Fewer workers per beneficiary


Added · from readings Numbers and quotations in this subsection are from the 2018 Trustees Report, pp. 2–6, 12–14, and 23. The slides show the corresponding figures from the 2024 report, which has somewhat different numbers (for example, payable benefits of 83 percent in 2035).
The Trustees Report explains why Social Security’s costs are rising faster than its income:






In their own words



“Projected OASDI cost increases more rapidly than projected non-interest income through 2039 primarily because the retirement of the baby-boom generation will increase the number of beneficiaries much faster than the number of covered workers increases, as subsequent lower-birth-rate generations replace the baby-boom generation at working ages.” (2018 Trustees Report, p. 4)


The number of covered workers per beneficiary “had been stable, remaining between 3.2 and 3.4 from 1974 through 2008.” It was about 2.8 in 2017, and the Trustees project it will fall to 2.2 by 2035, “when the baby-boom generation will have largely retired,” and then decline “very gradually thereafter due to increasing longevity.”
The PAYGO identity turns these numbers directly into tax rates. Figure 8.2 shows the tax rate needed to pay a 40 percent replacement rate at each ratio of workers to beneficiaries.








Figure 8.2: The PAYGO identity: the payroll tax rate needed to fund a 40 percent replacement rate, by the number of workers per beneficiary. Marked points use the Trustees’ figures for 1974–2008, 2017, and 2035.





At about 3.3 workers per beneficiary, a 40 percent replacement rate costs a 12 percent tax. At 2.2, it costs 18 percent. Nothing about the generosity of the system has changed. The difference is entirely demographic.


8.5.2 Running out the trust fund
Social Security is not purely PAYGO. For decades it collected more than it paid out and built up a reserve, the trust funds, which held $2.9 trillion at the end of 2017. But the Trustees projected that in 2018 total cost would exceed total income “for the first time since 1982,” so reserves would begin to fall. The cost of the program, measured as a share of taxable payroll (the “cost rate”), rises from 13.81 percent in 2018 to 16.83 percent in 2039, while the income rate stays “stable at about 13 percent.” The combined reserves would be depleted in 2034.


Added · new The explanation of why Social Security has a trust fund at all (it ran surpluses for decades) is my framing. The report states the reserve amounts.
What happens then? Not a total collapse. Under current law, benefits can only be paid out of current income once the reserves are gone. “At the time of depletion of these combined reserves, continuing income to the combined trust funds would be sufficient to pay 79 percent of scheduled benefits,” falling to 74 percent by 2092. In other words, after 2034 the system becomes PAYGO again, and the PAYGO identity decides what can be paid.


8.5.3 How can we adapt?
With the PAYGO identity, there are only three options:

raise taxes,
cut benefits,
or a partial combination of the two.

The Trustees put numbers on these choices. To keep the system solvent for the next 75 years, “revenues would have to increase by an amount equivalent to an immediate and permanent payroll tax rate increase of 2.78 percentage points” (to 15.18 percent), or “scheduled benefits would have to be reduced by an amount equivalent to an immediate and permanent reduction of about 17 percent applied to all current and future beneficiaries, or about 21 percent if the reductions were applied only to those who become initially eligible for benefits in 2018 or later.” Waiting makes it worse. If nothing is done until 2034, the tax increase becomes 3.87 percentage points or the benefit cut 23 percent, because “the changes necessary to maintain Social Security solvency would be concentrated on fewer years and fewer generations.”
One popular proposal, as a reader asked the newsletter Tangle in 2025, is to lift the cap on taxable earnings, then about $176,000 a year. In terms of the PAYGO identity, that is a special case of the first option: higher taxes, falling on higher earners. Combined with slower benefit growth for the best-off, it amounts to a combination of raising taxes and reducing benefits.

8.6 Winners and losers in PAYGO

8.6.1 Transitions
Who gains from starting a PAYGO system? Suppose a system starts in period 0. In every period from then on, the young (age I) pay 6 and the old (age II) receive 6. Follow each birth cohort diagonally through Table 8.2.

The cohort that is old in period 0 receives 6 without ever having paid anything. That is a windfall gain. Every cohort in between pays 6 when young and gets 6 back when old. And if the system is ended in period 4, the cohort that paid 6 in period 3 gets nothing back. Those are the transition costs. This is why it is almost impossible to leave a PAYGO system. Someone, the generation caught at the end, would have to pay twice: once for their parents’ pensions and again for their own.


8.6.2 The implicit rate of return
To compare Social Security with an investment, imagine that all taxes are paid at age 40 and all benefits received at age 70. Then the implicit annual return on a PAYGO “contribution” is
\[
P = \frac{\log(\text{benefit} \times \text{chance of still being alive} / \text{tax})}{\text{time}}.
\]
Martin Feldstein reports estimates (from a study by Dean Leimer) based on the actual history of taxes, benefits, and survival in U.S. Social Security (Table 8.3).




Table 8.3: Internal rate of return on Social Security (OASI) by birth cohort. Source: Leimer (1994), as reported by Feldstein (lecture slide). Assumes PAYGO balance in the future and adjusts for inflation; mixes rich and poor.

The earliest cohorts got a fabulous deal. These were the windfall generations, who paid in for only part of their working lives and then collected full benefits. Later cohorts get about 2 percent. Is that a good deal? It is about what you would earn on a risk-free investment like Treasury bills, and less than the stock market’s average return. But Social Security insures against many risks that an investment account doesn’t. It is an annuity, protecting against outliving your money (or dying early). It protects against mistiming the market, such as retiring in 2008. And it protects against the variation in investment returns from person to person.


8.6.3 Other countries
For many other industrial countries the story is less favorable: their demography is older, and their benefits are higher. Using the PAYGO identity with old-age dependency ratios projected to 2050 gives very high implied tax rates (Table 8.4).

title: 8  Aging and Social Security: A Ponzi Scheme?
text:
8.7 Key ideas

Every society faces a life-cycle dilemma: people produce in mid-life but consume throughout life. Private transfers, public transfers, and saving are the three solutions.
In a PAYGO system, population growth creates transfer wealth. Transfers beat saving when population growth plus wage growth exceeds the interest rate.
The PAYGO identity: tax rate = replacement rate × old-age dependency ratio.
As the ratio of workers to beneficiaries falls from about 3.3 to 2.2, Social Security must raise taxes, cut benefits, or both. Without action, the trust funds run out in the 2030s, and benefits fall to what current taxes can pay.
Starting a PAYGO system gives a windfall to the first old generation. Ending one imposes transition costs, which makes it almost impossible to leave.

text: 9.1 The population pyramid as history
crumbs: Age structure
9  Are Too Few Children a Problem? Age Structure and Optimal Fertility

title: 9  Are Too Few Children a Problem? Age Structure and Optimal Fertility
text:
9.1.1 Reading a pyramid
The size of each age group today depends on how many babies were born in each past year and how many of them survived. A population pyramid is therefore a record of history. A pyramid of France on January 1, 1999 shows the marks of the twentieth century: the deficit of births during the 1914–1918 war, the echo when those small “hollow classes” reached childbearing age, the deficit of births during the 1939–1945 war, the baby boom, and fertility’s fall below two children per woman. (How can you tell the men from the women, besides reading French?)
How to “read” an age pyramid:

First, look at the shape to get the growth rate.
Then look for variations in rates. These can come from wars, famines, or changes in fertility, such as China’s one-child policy, the U.S. baby boom, or the fertility transition.
Lastly, look for immigration. The telltale signs are one-sided dents and bulges, where one sex is much more numerous than the other at certain ages.



9.1.2 Stable populations
What determines the shape? Assume a closed population and focus on one sex. Let \(B(t)\) be the number of births in year \(t\) and \(\ell(x)\) the proportion of a birth cohort surviving to age \(x\). People aged \(x\) today are the surviving babies of \(x\) years ago:
\[
P(x, t) = B(t - x)\, \ell(x).
\]
A stable population is one in which age-specific birth and death rates have been fixed long enough that there are no more echoes or “instability.” A mathematical result is that a stable population grows exponentially in every age group, at a rate \(r\) called the intrinsic growth rate. Then there were \(B(t)e^{-rx}\) births \(x\) years ago, so \(P(x,t) = B(t)\,e^{-rx}\,\ell(x)\). In proportions,
\[
p(x) = b \, e^{-rx} \, \ell(x),
\]
where \(b\) is the birth rate. The age structure is the product of two things: survival, \(\ell(x)\), and the history of growth, \(e^{-rx}\). When the population is growing (\(r > 0\)), each older cohort was born into a smaller population, so the pyramid narrows quickly with age. When \(r < 0\), older cohorts are larger at birth than younger ones, and the pyramid bulges at older ages.
Figure 9.1 shows the stable age structures implied by Japan’s 2009 survival with growth rates of −1, 0, and +1 percent per year.


Show the R code
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 3.5, 2.5, 0.5), mgp = c(2.2, 0.6, 0))
rs <- c(-0.01, 0, 0.01)
cols <- c(col_shrink, col_zero, col_grow)
titles <- c("r = −1% (shrinking)", "r = 0 (stationary)", "r = +1% (growing)")
for (i in 1:3) {
  n <- 100 * stable_nx(rs[i])
  plot(n, x, type = "n", xlim = c(0, 2), ylim = c(0, 105),
       xlab = "Percent at each age", ylab = if (i == 1) "Age" else "",
       main = titles[i], font.main = 1, cex.main = 1)
  segments(0, x, n, x, col = cols[i], lwd = 1.2)
}
par(op)








Figure 9.1: Stable age structures with Japan’s 2009 survival schedule and three growth rates. Bars show the percentage of the population at each age. Source: Human Mortality Database; computation as in the lab.





There are only three stable cases. A growing population has a classic pyramid. A stationary population has a beehive, nearly straight-sided until old age. A shrinking population has an inverted shape, narrowest at the bottom.


9.1.3 Try it: the stable age pyramid app


Added · new This app comes from earlier years of the course (the 2016 transition lecture, the 2021 and 2023 age-pyramid lectures, and the 2018–2021 population-projection labs); it isn’t in the 2025 course repo. I copied it into course_apps_extra/stable and exported it with Shinylive. It uses Swedish life tables rather than Japan’s. The questions are mine; they use only the fertility slider, to stay clear of the Lab 6 graded questions on survival and optimal fertility.
The app draws the stable age structure, \(p(x) = b\,e^{-rx}\,\ell(x)\), for any total fertility rate and life expectancy. It turns the life expectancy into a Swedish historical life table with about that life expectancy, computes the long-run growth rate \(r\) implied by the TFR, and shows the resulting proportion of the population in each five-year age group. It opens in a new tab, so you can make it full screen and keep this page open alongside it. (The first load can take a few seconds while R starts up in your browser.)



The stable age pyramid app at its starting values. Click to open it in a new tab.


Open the stable age pyramid app in a new tab ↗
Before you move each slider, write down what you expect to happen. Then check.

Two children is not always replacement. At the starting values (TFR = 2, life expectancy = 60), the app reports a negative growth rate. Before you look, can you say why? Then find, roughly, the TFR that gives zero growth with this life expectancy.
High fertility. Raise the TFR to 6, a pre-transition level. Predict the shape of the pyramid and the share of the population under age 15 before you move the slider.
Very low fertility. Lower the TFR to 1.3, about where Japan and much of Southern Europe have been. Which age group is now the largest? Roughly what share of the population is 65 or older, compared with the TFR = 2 case?

title: 9  Are Too Few Children a Problem? Age Structure and Optimal Fertility
text:
9.2 Optimal fertility

9.2.1 Three sides of the story
Now the big question. What rate of population growth, and so what fertility, is best for the standard of living? Three forces pull in different directions:

Population growth is good because it means more workers per elderly person. This is the PAYGO lesson.
Population growth is bad because it means more children per worker.
Population growth is bad because of capital dilution: every new worker has to be equipped with capital. This is the Solow lesson.



9.2.2 The question, and its limits


Added · from readings This subsection and the next three draw on Lee et al. 2014 (text and Box 1).
Ronald Lee and his coauthors begin by noting a “remarkable reversal.” For decades, people worried about high fertility. Now 48 percent of the world’s people live in countries with below-replacement fertility. In 2013, “governments in 102 countries reported that population aging was a ‘major concern’ and 54 countries had enacted policies intended to raise fertility.”
They are candid that the full question can’t be answered:






In their own words



“Identifying an optimal population policy is likely to be impossible for several reasons. First, children yield direct satisfaction and impose costs on parents that are difficult or impossible to measure. Second, the environmental consequences of continuing population growth are exceedingly complex and difficult to value or weigh against other costs and benefits of low fertility. Third, assessing the welfare consequences of differences in fertility requires comparing the welfare of those not yet born to those who will never be born.” (Lee et al. 2014)


So their goal is “more modest”: to ask how fertility and population aging affect the material standard of living.


9.2.3 Two support ratios
Lee and coauthors use the NTA age profiles to build two measures of how age structure affects the economy:

The fiscal support ratio is “the ratio of tax payers to beneficiaries.” Each age group is weighted by the taxes it pays and the public benefits it receives. It measures the effect of age structure on government budgets.
The support ratio is “the ratio of earners to consumers.” Each age group is weighted by its labor income and its consumption, public and private combined:

\[
\text{support ratio} = \frac{\sum_x n(x)\, y(x)}{\sum_x n(x)\, c(x)},
\]
where \(n(x)\) is the share of the population at age \(x\), \(y(x)\) is labor income, and \(c(x)\) is consumption at age \(x\). A higher support ratio means more resources per person.
The two ratios give different answers because public and private transfers go to different ages. Since public transfers in rich countries go mostly to the elderly and private transfers mostly to children, “the age structure that favors public finances is much younger than the age structure that favors the combined finances of the public and private sectors.”
There is an elegant way to see which way a change in growth pushes the support ratio. Compare the average age at which people consume in the population with the average age at which people earn. If consumption happens later in life, on average, than earning, then a younger population, one that is growing faster, adds more earners than consumers, and the support ratio rises. If consumption happens earlier, a younger population lowers it. At the growth rate that maximizes the support ratio, the two average ages are equal.
Figure 9.2 computes the support ratio for Japan at each fertility level, using the stable age structures from Figure 9.1 and the NTA profiles from Figure 8.1.


Show the R code
tfr <- seq(1, 4, 0.01)
sr <- sapply(tfr, function(f) { n <- stable_nx(r_of_tfr(f)); sum(n * yx) / sum(n * cx) })
op <- par(mar = c(4, 4.5, 1, 1))
plot(tfr, sr, type = "l", lwd = 2.5, ylim = c(0.52, 0.70),
     xlab = "Total fertility rate", ylab = "Support ratio")
f_opt <- tfr[which.max(sr)]
abline(v = f_opt, lty = 3)
text(f_opt, 0.535, paste("Maximum at TFR =", f_opt), pos = 4, cex = 0.9)
par(op)








Figure 9.2: The support ratio for Japan’s stable population at each total fertility rate, using Japan’s NTA age profiles and 2009 survival (age-structure effects only; no capital). Computation as in the lab.





Taking only age structure into account, the support ratio for Japan peaks at a TFR of about 2.37, above replacement. But notice how flat the curve is. Over a wide range of fertility, from about 1.5 to 3.5 children per woman, the support ratio is never more than about 6 percent below its maximum. Higher fertility means more children and fewer elderly. Lower fertility means fewer children and more elderly. The two kinds of dependency largely cancel out.


9.2.4 Adding capital
The support ratio leaves out the third force. Faster population growth requires more saving and investment just to equip each new generation of workers with capital, and that saving can’t be consumed. Lee and coauthors call this the “capital cost” of higher fertility. Because it depends on how households, firms, and governments respond, they consider two cases:

a low capital cost case, in which the ratio of capital to output stays constant at about 3, the value observed in many rich countries between 1980 and 2004, and
a high capital cost case based on the neoclassical (Solow) growth model, with saving at the “golden rule” rate that maximizes consumption per person. Here “capital per worker rises when fertility falls as has been true in Japan.”



9.2.5 The results
Table 9.1 shows the fertility rates that maximize each objective, averaged over the countries in each income group.




Table 9.1: Total fertility rates that maximize each objective, by income group. Source: Lee et al. (2014), Table 1 (the lecture slide shows the first four columns).














Income group
Fiscal support ratio
Support ratio
Consumption, low capital cost
Consumption, high capital cost
Actual TFR, 2005–10




Lower income
1.08
1.75
1.21
0.91
4.03


Upper-middle income
2.96
2.01

1.20

2.94
2.27
1.78

1.65








Read the high-income row from left to right. Government budgets alone would be best served by about 2.9 children per woman, well above replacement, because children grow up to be taxpayers who pay for the elderly. Counting private family support for children as well, the best fertility falls to about 2.3, because children are expensive for families. Counting the cost of capital, it falls to 1.8 or even 1.5. The striking result is that below-replacement fertility can be “optimal” for the material standard of living.
Lee and coauthors draw the conclusion carefully:






In their own words



“Fiscal pressures on public programs due to population aging are real and important. … In a number of countries, particularly those with very low fertility, standards of living would be moderately higher if fertility increased. Fertility as low as 1.6 births per woman and possibly even lower should not in itself be a matter of concern. Fertility below replacement and modest population decline favor higher material standards of living.” (Lee et al. 2014)




Added · from readings The −2% and Japan figures are from Lee et al. 2014. The quotation on immigration is one Lee et al. take from a 2009 handbook chapter by Goldstein.
Very low fertility is another matter. With the age profiles of high-income countries, a population shrinking at 2 percent a year (a TFR of about 1.1) would have consumption per person about 4 percent lower than at replacement, and 7.6 percent lower with Japan’s very low mortality. Japan, the world’s oldest population, shows both sides. Its support ratio fell 0.6 percent a year in the 2000s and its fiscal support ratio 0.9 percent, and public debt is very high. Yet because slower labor force growth reduced the cost of equipping new workers, consumption per person “also rose at more than 2% annually.” Could immigration help? Only for a while: as the authors quote, “a steady stream of migrants almost always makes a population younger in the short-term but older in the long-term.”


9.2.6 Conclusions and caveats
So low fertility might be something to aim for, not be scared of. Why?

Both kids and the elderly are expensive. In a stable population, an increase in one is largely cancelled out by a decrease in the other.
Capital deepening, the Solow effect, makes slow population growth attractive.

But there are important caveats:

The age schedules of production and consumption are treated as exogenous and fixed.
There is no endogenous technological growth of the kind Romer or Boserup emphasize, in which more people means more ideas or more innovation.







In the lab



In Lab 6 you reproduce Lee and coauthors’ calculations for Japan: from fertility to growth rates, from growth rates to stable age structures, and from age structures to support ratios, first without and then with capital. Then you ask how the answer changes with a different survival schedule.

title: 10  How Do Economists Think We Decide How Many Children to Have?
text: 10.1 The big questions
crumbs: Fertility and the family
10  How Do Economists Think We Decide How Many Children to Have?

title: 10  How Do Economists Think We Decide How Many Children to Have?
text:
10.1.1 A puzzle for economics, and for biology
Economists usually assume that when people get richer, they buy more of most things. Goods like that are called normal goods. If children were a normal good, richer people and richer societies would have more children. Over the last century and a half, the opposite has happened. In the United States, the total fertility rate fell from about 7 in 1800 to around 2 today, with one big interruption, the baby boom after World War II, even as incomes rose enormously.
The same puzzle troubles biology. Natural selection rewards whatever leaves more descendants. So why doesn’t social and economic success translate into more offspring?


Added · from readings Darwin, Malthus, and the Italian village example are from Becker 1991, pp. 136–137.
Becker opens his chapter with exactly this tension. Malthus assumed that populations grow rapidly unless held back by limited food. Darwin, who wrote that reading Malthus gave him “a theory by which to work,” extended the logic: the children of fertile parents make up a larger share of the next generation, so “populations tend to become dominated by the highly fertile.” But, Becker points out, “most families have controlled their fertility and have had fewer children than their capacities permit.” Seventeenth-century Italian village women who married at twenty-five averaged only six children, when their biological capacity “probably exceeded eight.” Neither Malthus nor Darwin can explain why Western fertility fell so far in the last century as family incomes “rose dramatically.”


10.1.2 Two kinds of evidence
There are two kinds of questions here.

Over time. Why did fertility fall during the demographic transition, and why does it keep falling?
Across people and places. Within a society, who has more children and who has fewer? Between societies, why is fertility high in some and low in others?

On differences across people: in Zimbabwe in 1999, the TFR was 4.0 for women as a whole, but more than 5 for women with no education and under 2 for women with higher education. (The TFR is a “period” measure, with some caveats.) Across the states of India in 2010–13, the TFR ranged from below 1.65 in some states to above 3 in others. And we would like to know what will happen in the future.
This chapter covers two economic models. The first, the opportunity cost of childbearing, gives children a price that includes the parents’ time. The second, Becker’s quantity–quality tradeoff, lets parents choose how much to invest in each child as well as how many children to have.

title: 10  How Do Economists Think We Decide How Many Children to Have?
text:
10.2 Consumer choice: a quick review
We all make choices between goods all the time: rent or food, books or movies, more leisure or more income. The economist’s model of these choices has three ingredients:

We choose a bundle of goods together, \((X_1, X_2)\), not one at a time.
Our total spending is limited by a budget constraint: \(p_1 X_1 + p_2 X_2 \le\) the available budget.
Among all the bundles we can afford, we choose the one that maximizes our utility, \(U(X_1, X_2)\).



Added · from readings The definitions in the next two paragraphs follow the Wikipedia entry “Consumer choice,” recommended in the course calendar.
We picture preferences with indifference curves. Each curve connects bundles that make the person equally happy, and curves farther from the origin are better. They are usually bowed toward the origin, because people are willing to give up less and less of one good to get more of another as they have more of it. The best affordable bundle is where the highest reachable indifference curve just touches the budget line.
When a price changes, the effect on what people buy can be split into two parts. The substitution effect is the change in demand “resulting from a price change that alters the slope of the budget constraint but leaves the consumer on the same indifference curve”: people switch toward whatever has become relatively cheaper. The income effect is the change in demand from the change in purchasing power. The Wikipedia entry ends with the case that matters most for us, the trade-off between labor and leisure. A person has a fixed endowment of time, and every hour not spent working is an hour of earnings given up. Time has a price, and that price is the wage.

title: 10  How Do Economists Think We Decide How Many Children to Have?
text:
10.3 The cost-of-time model

10.3.1 Setting up the model
Our first model of fertility puts these pieces together.

Utility depends on goods and children: \(U(X, N)\), where \(X\) is consumer goods and \(N\) is the number of children.
The budget constraint: a family can spend only what it earns.
Earnings depend on the wage, the hours worked, and “other income.”
Time is spent either working or taking care of children. For simplicity, we leave out leisure.

The key idea is that the model counts the opportunity cost of time. For convenience, we measure goods in dollars, so the price of \(X\) is 1.
The time constraint. If \(T\) is the total hours available, \(L\) is hours in the labor force, and each child takes \(c\) hours of care, then
\[
T = L + cN.
\]
The money budget. Spending on goods \(X\) plus spending on children, at \(p\) dollars per child (food, clothes, and so on), must equal earnings plus other income \(I\):
\[
X + pN = wL + I = w(T - cN) + I.
\]
Moving the time cost of children to the left side gives
\[
X + (p + wc)N = wT + I.
\]
This reframes the problem. The right side, \(wT + I\), is full income: what the family would have if every available hour were spent working. The left side counts all expenses, including opportunity costs. The full price of a child is \(p + wc\): the money cost plus the earnings given up to care for the child.


10.3.2 A worked example
Take the example from lecture: a wage of \(w = \$20\) an hour, \(T = 40\) hours a week, other income \(I = \$1{,}000\) a week, money costs of \(p = \$200\) per child per week, and time costs of \(c = 5\) hours per child per week. Full income is \(20 \times 40 + 1000 = \$1{,}800\) a week, and the full price of a child is \(200 + 20 \times 5 = \$300\). So the family can afford $1,800 of goods and no children, or 6 children and no goods, or anything on the line between: \(X = 1800 - 300N\).
To find the best bundle, we need preferences. Lecture uses the Cobb–Douglas utility function \(U(X, N) = X^{0.7} N^{0.3}\). Figure 10.1 shows the budget line, a few indifference curves, and utility along the budget line.


Show the R code
w <- 20; T <- 40; I <- 1000; p <- 200; c <- 5; a <- 0.7
Ns <- N_star(w, T, I, p, c, a); Xs <- X_star(w, T, I, p, c, a)
Us <- util(Xs, Ns, a)
N <- seq(0.01, 6, 0.01)
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4.5, 1, 1))
plot(N, 1800 - 300 * N, type = "n", ylim = c(0, 2000), xlim = c(0, 6.2),
     xlab = "Number of children (N)", ylab = "Goods (X, $ per week)")
for (Ui in Us * c(0.75, 1, 1.25))
  lines(N, X_on_U(Ui, N, a), lty = 3, col = col_grey)
segments(0, 1800, 6, 0, col = col_goods, lwd = 2.5)
points(Ns, Xs, pch = 19)
arrows(1.75, 520, Ns, Xs - 50, length = 0.07)
text(1.75, 520, sprintf("best bundle:\nN = %.1f, X = $%.0f", Ns, Xs), pos = 1, cex = 0.8)
text(4.1, 600, "budget line", col = col_goods, pos = 4, cex = 0.85)
Ub <- util(1800 - 300 * N, N, a)
plot(N, Ub, type = "l", lwd = 2.5, ylim = c(0, max(Ub) * 1.1),
     xlab = "Number of children (N)", ylab = "Utility along the budget line")
abline(v = Ns, lty = 3)
par(op)








Figure 10.1: The cost-of-time model with the lecture example (w = $20, T = 40, I = $1,000, p = $200, c = 5, U = X^0.7 N^0.3). Left: the budget line and indifference curves; the best bundle is where an indifference curve just touches the line. Right: utility along the budget line, a slice through the ‘utility mountain.’





The family’s best choice here is about 1.8 children, and $1,260 a week of goods. (Children come in whole numbers, of course. Think of \(N\) as an average across many families.) In one sentence: given the budget constraint, we pick the combination of goods and children that maximizes utility.






For those who like formulas





With Cobb–Douglas utility \(U = X^a N^{1-a}\), the best choice can be found exactly (the lab shows the derivation):
\[
N^* = (1 - a)\,\frac{I + wT}{p + cw}, \qquad X^* = a\,(I + wT).
\]
The family spends a fixed share \(1 - a\) of full income on children. In the example, \(N^* = 0.3 \times 1800 / 300 = 1.8\). You don’t need to memorize this.
