section: 10.4 Effects of income and wage changes
text:
10.4 Effects of income and wage changes

10.4.1 More non-wage income
Suppose non-wage income \(I\) rises, perhaps because of an inheritance or, in a family where only the mother cares for children, a raise for the father. The budget line shifts out parallel to itself: its slope, \(-(p + wc)\), doesn’t change. The family can afford more of both goods and children, and if both are normal goods, it buys more of both. More non-wage income raises fertility.


10.4.2 Higher wages: two effects pulling in opposite directions
A higher wage is different, because the wage appears on both sides of the budget. It raises full income, \(wT + I\), and it raises the price of a child, \(p + wc\). So the budget line becomes steeper as well as shifting out.

The income effect of a higher wage could raise fertility: more income to spend, including on the fixed money costs of childbearing.
The substitution effect could lower fertility: each hour spent with a child now costs more in lost earnings, so the family substitutes toward goods.

The effect on the number of children is ambiguous. It depends on which effect is bigger. Figure 10.2 shows both possibilities. Following lecture, we split the move from the old choice A to the new choice C into two steps. A → B is the income effect: we hold prices (the slope) fixed and move to the new level of utility. B → C is the substitution effect: we change the price and move along the new indifference curve.


Added · new The parameter values in this figure are my choices, picked to show each case clearly.


Show the R code
decomp_plot <- function(T, I, p, c, a, w0, w1, main) {
  P0 <- full_price(p, c, w0); P1 <- full_price(p, c, w1)
  F0 <- full_income(w0, T, I); F1 <- full_income(w1, T, I)
  A <- c(N = N_star(w0, T, I, p, c, a), X = X_star(w0, T, I, p, c, a))
  C <- c(N = N_star(w1, T, I, p, c, a), X = X_star(w1, T, I, p, c, a))
  UA <- unname(util(A["X"], A["N"], a)); UC <- unname(util(C["X"], C["N"], a))
  B <- tangent_on_U(UC, P0, a)                      # new utility, old prices
  nmax <- max(F0 / P0, F1 / P1, B["N"] * 1.6)
  N <- seq(0.02, nmax, length.out = 400)
  plot(N, N, type = "n", xlim = c(0, nmax), ylim = c(0, F1 * 1.05),
       xlab = "Number of children (N)", ylab = "Goods (X)", main = main,
       font.main = 1, cex.main = 0.95)
  lines(N, X_on_U(UA, N, a), lty = 3, col = col_grey)
  lines(N, X_on_U(UC, N, a), lty = 3, col = col_grey)
  segments(0, F0, F0 / P0, 0, col = col_old, lwd = 2.5)
  segments(0, F1, F1 / P1, 0, col = col_new, lwd = 2.5)
  FB <- B["X"] + P0 * B["N"]                        # income needed at old prices
  segments(0, FB, FB / P0, 0, col = col_old, lwd = 1.5, lty = 2)
  pts <- rbind(A = A, B = B, C = C)
  points(pts[, "N"], pts[, "X"], pch = 19)
  text(pts[, "N"], pts[, "X"], rownames(pts), pos = c(1, 4, 2), font = 2)
  invisible(pts)
}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4.5, 2.5, 1))
p1 <- decomp_plot(T = 40, I = 2000, p = 50, c = 10, a = 0.7, w0 = 20, w1 = 40,
                  main = "Substitution effect dominates")
p2 <- decomp_plot(T = 40, I = 200, p = 400, c = 5, a = 0.7, w0 = 20, w1 = 40,
                  main = "Income effect dominates")
par(op)








Figure 10.2: A doubling of the wage (from $20 to $40) under two sets of circumstances. Green: old budget line; red: new budget line; dashed green: a line with the old slope tangent to the new indifference curve. A → B is the income effect and B → C the substitution effect. Left: the substitution effect dominates and the family has fewer children. Right: the income effect dominates and it has more.





In the left panel, the wage rise moves the family from 3.4 to 2.4 children. In the right panel, the same doubling of the wage moves it from 0.6 to 0.9. In both cases the income effect (A → B) is toward more children and the substitution effect (B → C) is toward fewer. What differs is their relative size. Roughly, the substitution effect wins when the time cost of children is large compared with their money cost, and when much of the family’s income does not depend on the wage.


10.4.3 Try it: the cost-of-time app


Added · new The app is the course’s own cost-of-time app (ShinyApps/cost-of-time in the 2025 course repo), exported with Shinylive so it runs in the browser, in its own tab. The three questions are mine; they use only the “Defaults” sliders, to stay clear of the Lab 7 graded questions.
The app is the one used in Lab 7. It opens in a new tab, so you can make it full screen and keep this page open alongside it. (The first load can take a few seconds while R starts up in your browser.) The black choice uses the “initial” values on the left; the grey choice uses the “perturbed” values in the middle column, so you can compare two situations side by side.



The cost-of-time app at its starting values. Click to open it in a new tab.


Open the cost-of-time app in a new tab ↗
A few things to try, using only the “Defaults” column on the right:

Read the formula off the graph. With the starting values (\(w = 15\), \(p = 100\), \(c = 10\), \(I = 1000\), \(T = 40\), \(a = 0.6\)), use \(N^* = (1-a)(I + wT)/(p + cw)\) to compute the number of children by hand. Does it match the black point?
Change tastes. Move \(a\), the weight on goods, from 0.6 down to 0.4. What happens to the number of children? Why does the share of full income spent on children depend only on \(a\)?
Change the time available. Move \(T\) from 40 to 50 hours. Which part of the budget line moves, and why does more time raise the number of children even though the wage and the prices of children are unchanged?

The lab asks you to use the app to explore changes in wages, income, and the money and time costs of children.


10.4.4 Is the model great, or terrible?
The effect of a wage increase can go either way. That is bad for prediction, though good for explaining things after the fact. But the model makes much stronger predictions about other changes:

A higher money price of children, \(p\), lowers fertility. (Would cheaper schools raise fertility?)
More non-wage income, \(I\), raises fertility. (What if “male” income rises?)
A higher time cost per child, \(c\), lowers fertility. (What about labor-saving devices for child care, like washing machines for children’s clothes?)
A higher wage, \(w\), is ambiguous.

So the idea that rising wages reduce fertility is based on empirical research, not theoretical necessity.
What does the evidence say about income and fertility? A recent study of the United States (Hauer and Schmertmann 2020) estimated the TFR by household income from 2010–2018. Fertility falls as household income rises, up to a point, and then turns back up among the highest-income households, for both white and nonwhite women: a U-turn. Ask yourself: in what income range does the substitution effect seem to dominate, and in what range the income effect?


10.4.5 Who bears the cost of time?
The cost of children’s time falls disproportionately on women. That gives the model a sharper prediction. Higher wages for men work mostly through the income effect and should raise fertility. Higher wages for women bring a substitution effect as well, and should lower fertility, or at least raise it less than men’s wages do. A number of older studies have found this pattern. One study of Sweden (Schultz 1985) compared the price of butter, whose production was largely women’s work, with the price of grain, largely men’s. Another, by Butz and Ward (1979), was titled “The emergence of countercyclical U.S. fertility.” When women’s wages are an important part of family income, a recession, which lowers the opportunity cost of time, could actually raise fertility.


Added · from readings The two-thirds figure, the household survey evidence, and Becker’s caution about causation are from Becker 1991, p. 140.
Becker makes the same argument. “The cost of the mother’s time is a major part of the total cost of producing and rearing children,” he writes. In the United States it contributes “about two-thirds of the total cost.” “I believe that the growth in the earning power of women during the last hundred years in developed countries is a major cause of both the large increase in labor force participation of married women and the large decline in fertility.” Because fathers have spent relatively little time on children, their rising earnings have not much affected the cost of children. Household surveys bear this out. The number of children is “strongly negatively related to the wage rate or other measures of the value of time of wives, and is more often positively rather than negatively related to the wage rate or earnings of husbands.” Becker adds a caution about causation. Part of the relationship runs from children to wages, “because women invest less in market skills and more in household skills and men do the reverse when families have more children.”
More recent evidence complicates the story. Across 15 industrialized countries, fertility used to rise when unemployment rose, in the late 1950s and 1960s. Since the mid-1970s, it has fallen when unemployment rises (Örsal and Goldstein 2018). Fertility has become “pro-cyclical” again.


10.4.6 What the cost-of-time model helps explain

Kuwait versus Switzerland. Both are rich, but one has high fertility and the other low.
Women’s share of income. Why, as an increasing share of family income comes from women, fertility might decline.
Female education. Why increasing female education might decrease fertility.



Added · new The interpretation of Kuwait and Switzerland in terms of the model is my addition. Your slide lists the comparison without explanation.
In the language of the model, the difference between Kuwait and Switzerland is about where income comes from. Much of Kuwait’s wealth comes from oil, which, from a family’s point of view, behaves like non-wage income \(I\): it raises income without raising the price of anyone’s time. Switzerland’s wealth comes largely from the earnings of skilled workers, women included, so getting richer there also means a higher opportunity cost of time spent with children.

title: 10  How Do Economists Think We Decide How Many Children to Have?
text:
10.5 The quantity–quality model

10.5.1 Two puzzles
The cost-of-time model leaves two problems.

An empirical problem. Very large fertility declines have happened with fairly small economic changes (Table 10.1). Children have no close substitutes, so we would not expect demand for them to swing so much.
A theoretical problem. In the cost-of-time model, the cost per child is fixed. But we know the cost of raising a child has risen enormously.





Table 10.1: Some rapid fertility declines. Source: Becker (1991), Table 5.1 (shown in lecture).






Country and period
Change in birth rate (%)

-24

-38

-45

-51


England and Wales, 1871–1901
-26










Added · from readings Becker 1991, pp. 135, 148, and 149 (footnote 12).
Becker himself had been stuck on the first problem. In his first paper on fertility, in 1960, he wrote that economic theory had “little to say about the quantitative relationship between price and quantity. There are no good substitutes for children, but there may be many poor ones.” By 1991 he saw the way out: the “interaction between quantity and quality of children,” which he called “probably the major contribution of the economic analysis of fertility.”


10.5.2 Adding quality
Becker’s idea is that parents get utility not only from the number of children, \(n\), but also from their quality, \(q\): how much is spent on each child’s schooling, health, and so on. Utility becomes \(U(X, n, q)\). (Following lecture, we use Becker’s notation \(n\) for the number of children and \(p_c\) for the cost of one unit of quality for one child, but keep \(X\) for goods, which Becker calls \(Z\).)
Assume that every child in a family gets the same quality, and every unit of quality costs the same \(p_c\). Then spending on children is \(p_c q n\), and the budget constraint goes from
\[
X + p n = \text{income} \quad\text{to}\quad X + p_c q n = \text{income}.
\]
There are now three choices instead of two. Holding total income \(I\) and spending on goods \(X\) fixed, quality and quantity must satisfy
\[
q = \frac{I - X}{p_c\, n}.
\]
The budget constraint is no longer a straight line. It is a curved hyperbola, like \(y = c/x\). Doubling the number of children halves the quality you can afford for each.


Added · from readings The car comparison is from Becker 1991, p. 148.
Why should children be different from other goods in this way? Becker’s answer: “a rich person might well plan to own both expensive and inexpensive cars, but is unlikely to plan on having both expensive and inexpensive children.” Every child in a family gets roughly the same treatment. So the quality chosen for one child applies to all of them, and multiplies with their number.


10.5.3 The interaction between quantity and quality
Becker’s fuller version of the budget includes three kinds of cost (p. 149):
\[
\text{total child costs} = p_n n + p_q q + p_c q n.
\]

\(p_n\) is a price per child, of any quality: pregnancy, other fixed costs, and also the cost of contraception.
\(p_q\) is a price per unit of quality, regardless of the number of children: a set of encyclopedias, faster internet, things shared by all the children in a household.
\(p_c\) is a price that depends on both \(q\) and \(n\): school fees, visits to the doctor, new shoes.

How much does it cost to add one more child? About \(p_n + p_c q\): the fixed cost plus the quality that child will receive. How much does it cost to add one unit of quality? About \(p_q + p_c n\), because the extra quality goes to every child. So the “shadow” or “full” price of quality depends on the number of children, and the price of quantity depends on quality.






In his own words



“Since an increase in q raises the amount spent on each child, it raises the relevant cost of each child. Similarly, an increase in n raises the cost of adding to the quality of each child because a larger number of children would be affected.” (Becker 1991, p. 145)


This creates a feedback loop. Suppose something makes children a little more costly. Families have somewhat fewer children. With fewer children, quality is cheaper, so they invest more in each child. With more invested in each child, another child is more expensive, so they have still fewer. And so on, until a new equilibrium is reached.


Added · from readings Becker 1991, pp. 146–147. Your slide 16-09 shows the shape of the budget curve. The specific utility function in the figure is my choice.
A surprising implication: this feedback does not require that quantity and quality be close substitutes. On the contrary, Becker shows that “equilibrium would not be possible if they were close substitutes!” The budget curve bows in toward the origin, so a family will choose some of both only if its indifference curves bow in even more sharply. That is, if it doesn’t consider quality and quantity easy to trade off. Otherwise it would pile everything into one or the other. In Figure 10.3 the indifference curves are more curved than the budget curve, and the family settles at \(e_0\).


Show the R code
S0 <- 100; pn0 <- 10; pn1 <- 20
e0 <- opt_nq(S0, pn0)
S1 <- unname(pn1 * e0["n"] + e0["n"] * e0["q"])  # compensated: passes through e0
e1 <- opt_nq(S1, pn1)
n <- seq(1.5, 8.5, 0.01)
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4.5, 1, 1))
for (panel in 1:2) {
  plot(n, n, type = "n", xlim = c(1.5, 8.5), ylim = c(0, 32),
       xlab = "Number of children (n)", ylab = "Quality per child (q)")
  lines(n, q_on_U(e0["U"], n), lty = 3, col = col_grey)
  qb <- q_budget(n, S0, pn0); qb[qb < 0] <- NA
  lines(n, qb, col = "#2c5fb8", lwd = 2.5)
  points(e0["n"], e0["q"], pch = 19)
  text(e0["n"], e0["q"], expression(e[0]), pos = 4)
  if (panel == 1) {
    legend("topright", c("budget curve", "indifference curve"),
           col = c("#2c5fb8", col_grey), lty = c(1, 3), lwd = c(2.5, 1),
           bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
  } else {
    qb1 <- q_budget(n, S1, pn1); qb1[qb1 < 0] <- NA
    lines(n, qb1, col = "#2c5fb8", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
    lines(n, q_on_U(e1["U"], n), lty = 3, col = col_grey)
    points(e1["n"], e1["q"], pch = 19)
    text(e1["n"], e1["q"], expression(e[1]), pos = 2)
    legend("bottomleft", c("old budget", "new budget\n(compensated)"),
           col = "#2c5fb8", lty = c(1, 2), lwd = c(2.5, 2), bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
    arrows(e0["n"] - 0.1, e0["q"] + 0.6, e1["n"] + 0.15, e1["q"] - 0.6,
           length = 0.07, col = col_kids)
  }
}
par(op)








Figure 10.3: Becker’s quantity–quality model. The budget curve (blue) is bowed toward the origin because spending on children is quality × quantity. Left: the family’s best choice e0 is where an indifference curve just touches the budget curve. Right: a compensated increase in the fixed cost per child rotates the budget curve through e0 (dashed). The family moves to e1, with fewer children and more quality per child. Illustrative CES preferences.





In the figure, a compensated doubling of the fixed cost per child moves the family from 4.3 to 3.8 children, a drop of 11 percent, while quality per child rises 32 percent. Becker argues that “a moderate increase in the fixed cost of children … that raised the initial shadow price of quantity relative to quality by only 10 to 20 percent would reduce the demand for quantity and increase the demand for quality by significantly larger percentages.”


10.5.4 A close reading: why cheaper contraception raises the cost of a child






In his own words



“Therefore, an increase in, say, the fixed cost of n, perhaps because of reduced child allowances or reduced costs of contraception, would induce a substitution away from n and toward q as well as Z … The interaction between n and q implies that the increase in q raises πn further, while the decrease in n lowers πq further, which encourages still more substitution away from n and toward q. The decrease in n and increase in q could be sizable even if the increase in the fixed cost of n were modest …” (Becker 1991, pp. 149–150)


Reduced child allowances obviously raise the cost of a child. But how can cheaper contraception do so? Think of the cost of a child as including what the family does not spend on avoiding that child. If contraceptives are expensive, avoiding a child is expensive, and having one “saves” on contraception. If contraceptives become cheap, having a child saves less, so the net cost of a child goes up.
To see how the feedback in Becker’s passage can turn a small shock into a big change, it helps to work through a numerical example.


Added · new The worked example is my construction (Cobb-Douglas preferences; closed-form solution), approved by Josh; the mechanism and quote are Becker’s (1991, pp. 149–150).






Worked example: how a small shock becomes a big change





Two families have the same preferences, \(U = a\ln n + b\ln q + g\ln z\), with \(a = 0.3\) and \(g = 0.45\). They differ only in the budget:

With interaction: \(c\,n + p\,n\,q + z = I\). Quality is bought for each child.
Without interaction: \(c\,n + p\,q + z = I\). Quality is bought once for the family (think of a set of encyclopedias).

The shock: \(b\) rises from 0.25 to 0.27, an 8% rise in how much the family values quality.
1. Without interaction (the benchmark). With a linear budget, the first-order conditions are \(a/n = \lambda c\), \(b/q = \lambda p\), \(g/z = \lambda\). Multiply each by its quantity and add: \(a + b + g = \lambda I\). So each good gets a fixed share of income:
\[
n = \frac{a}{a+b+g}\cdot\frac{I}{c}, \qquad q = \frac{b}{a+b+g}\cdot\frac{I}{p}.
\]
With \(I = 100\), \(c = 10\), \(p = 1\):

Raising \(b\) affects \(n\) only by slightly shrinking the share of the budget going to children. The prices of children and quality don’t change at all.
2. With interaction. Now the budget has the term \(p\,n\,q\), so the first-order conditions are
\[
\frac{a}{n} = \lambda\,(c + p q), \qquad \frac{b}{q} = \lambda\,p n, \qquad \frac{g}{z} = \lambda .
\]
The terms in parentheses are the shadow prices: an extra child costs \(c + pq\), and an extra unit of quality costs \(pn\). Solving step by step:

Multiply the quality condition by \(q\): \(b = \lambda\,p\,n\,q\).
Multiply the quantity condition by \(n\): \(a = \lambda c n + \lambda p n q = \lambda c n + b\), so \(\lambda c n = a - b\).
Add up all spending: \(\lambda(cn + pnq + z) = (a - b) + b + g = a + g\), so \(\lambda = (a+g)/I\).
Therefore

\[
n = \frac{a-b}{a+g}\cdot\frac{I}{c}, \qquad q = \frac{b}{a-b}\cdot\frac{c}{p}.
\]
Now \(b\) sits inside the formula for \(n\), as \(a - b\). With \(I = 100\), \(c = 2\), \(p = 1\) (units chosen so that \(n\) is about 3):

An 8% rise in \(b\) is a 40% fall in \(a - b\), and \(n\) is proportional to \(a - b\). Meanwhile \(q\) is proportional to \(b/(a-b)\), which goes from 5 to 9.
3. The “20×” and where it comes from. The fall in \(n\) is 40% with interaction and 2.0% without, a ratio of about 20. The no-interaction response is exactly what the interaction family would do if its shadow prices were frozen. Facing its starting prices (\(\pi_n = 12\), \(\pi_q = 3.33\)) as fixed market prices, it would cut \(n\) by only 2.0%. So the decline splits into a first-round response of about 2% and a feedback effect of about 38% more. The feedback shows up in the shadow prices:




\(\pi_n = c + pq\)
\(\pi_q = pn\)
\(\pi_n / \pi_q\)

The relative price of a child almost triples, although no market price changed: \(c\) and \(p\) are constant. Valuing quality more raises \(q\). Higher \(q\) raises the cost of a child, so \(n\) falls. Lower \(n\) lowers the cost of quality, so \(q\) rises further, and so on.
4. Caveat: the multiplier depends on \(a - b\). The multiplier is large here because \(a - b\) is small: the family values numbers only a little more than quality, so it is near the edge of wanting all quality and no quantity. For the same 0.02 rise in \(b\), the fall in \(n\) with interaction is 40% if \(a - b\) starts at 0.05, 20% if it starts at 0.10, and 10% if it starts at 0.20. The no-interaction response stays near 2% in each case. The requirement \(a > b\) for an interior solution is a version of Becker’s point that quantity and quality cannot be close substitutes.



This example uses a shift in \(b\) rather than a change in the fixed cost \(c\), as in Figure 10.3. With Cobb-Douglas preferences, a change in \(c\) does not magnify the response of \(n\) (only of \(q\)); the CES preferences behind Figure 10.3 have more curvature, which is why a compensated rise in the fixed cost there produces a larger drop in the number of children.


10.5.5 “Induced demand”: a small family planning program, a big decline in fertility
Becker uses the interaction to reconcile two sides of a long debate. One side held that family planning programs were needed before fertility would fall. The other held that the value of children had to fall first.






In his own words



“Suppose that an effective family planning program could be expected to reduce births by 10 percent because that many births are ‘unwanted.’ However, births would actually fall by a much larger percent; the interaction between quantity and quality implies that a 10-percent fall in births raises the demand for quality of children, which raises the cost of (lowers the value of) quantity and further lowers the demand for births. Although family planning might take credit for the whole decline in births because it is the initiating force, the induced increase in the demand for higher-quality children and the induced decrease in the demand for quantity of children are responsible for more than half of the decline in births.” (Becker 1991, p. 151)


To recapitulate:

The cost of contraception falls, so \(n\) goes down, because there are fewer unintended births.
The total price of a unit of quality falls too, since there are fewer children to provide it to, and parents buy more \(q\).
But as they do, the price per child rises. This induces a further fall in \(n\).
That can lead to further increases in \(q\) and declines in \(n\), until a new equilibrium is reached.



10.5.6 Is contraception the cause, or the response?


Added · from readings This subsection summarizes Becker 1991, pp. 141–144. Your slides raise contraception’s role in the model but don’t cover this evidence.
If cheaper contraception sets off the feedback loop, is the contraceptive revolution the real cause of falling fertility? Becker says no. He once thought so, but by 1991 he believed “that these improvements in birth control methods are mainly an induced response to other decreases in the demand for children rather than an important cause of the decreased demand.”
He gives two kinds of evidence. First, simple methods have always been enough to cut births substantially. Without birth control, women who married at twenty averaged about eleven live births (the Hutterites are his example), one every 26 months or so. Delaying marriage by three years, reducing the frequency of intercourse by 10 percent, and breastfeeding three months longer would cut that to about 8.7 births. Using withdrawal half the time would cut it to about 6.6. Second, societies with access to birth control did not always use it, and societies without modern methods sometimes had small families anyway. The ruling families of Europe averaged more than 5.5 births from the sixteenth to the eighteenth century, though they could have had fewer with known methods. The Greeks and Romans had small families through delayed marriage, infanticide, abortion, and other means. The Jews of Florence and Leghorn halved their birth rates between 1670 and 1840, while forced to live in ghettos. And fertility began falling in the United States and Japan in the 1950s, before the pill was widely used in the United States and while it was illegal in Japan.
Becker also notes why Malthus might have put so much weight on the age at marriage. When women are having eleven births, a 10 percent rise in the age at marriage reduces births by almost three times as much as a 10 percent fall in the frequency of intercourse. Delaying marriage was simply the most effective method available.


10.5.7 Bringing the evidence together


Added · from readings The figure uses Becker 1991, Tables 5.1 and 5.2. Your slides show Table 5.1 only.
If the quantity–quality interaction is important, rapid falls in the number of children should come together with rapid rises in investment per child. Figure 10.4 puts Becker’s two tables side by side.


Show the R code
ep <- c("US\n1920–30", "US\n1960–72", "Japan\n1950–60", "Taiwan\n1960–75",
        "England &\nWales\n1871–1901")
births <- c(-24, -38, -45, -51, -26)
school <- c(81, 33, 37, 100, 21)
op <- par(mar = c(2, 4.5, 1, 1))
bp <- barplot(rbind(births, school), beside = TRUE, names.arg = rep("", 5),
              col = c(col_kids, col_goods), border = NA, ylim = c(-85, 125),
              ylab = "Percent change", las = 1)
abline(h = 0)
text(colMeans(bp), -75, ep, cex = 0.8, xpd = NA)
text(bp, rbind(births, school) + ifelse(rbind(births, school) > 0, 5, -5),
     rbind(births, school), cex = 0.75)
legend("top", c("Birth rate", "Schooling"), fill = c(col_kids, col_goods),
       border = NA, bty = "n", horiz = TRUE, inset = -0.02)
par(op)








Figure 10.4: Rapid fertility declines (red) and the accompanying increases in schooling (green) in Becker’s five episodes. Schooling measures differ by country: secondary enrollment ages 14–17 (US 1920–30), high-school completion ages 25–34 (US 1960–72, Japan, Taiwan), and male literacy (Great Britain). Source: Becker (1991), Tables 5.1 and 5.2.





While the fertility rate in Taiwan fell by 51 percent, the fraction of people aged 25–34 with a high-school education doubled.


Added · from readings The rural–urban evidence is from Becker 1991, pp. 138–139 and 152–153, including the Adam Smith quotation (p. 139, note 2).
The model also helps explain why farm families have been larger than city families. The evidence covers centuries. In 1427, the average household in the city of Florence was about 20 percent smaller than in the surrounding countryside. In 1800, the rural reproduction rate in the United States was about one and a half times the urban rate. Part of the reason is that food and housing are cheaper on farms. But Becker believes “farm families have had more children mainly because children have been considerably more productive on farms than in cities.” In rural India and Brazil, children begin contributing to farm work by age five or six. Adam Smith wrote of colonial America: “Labour is there so well rewarded that a numerous family of children, instead of being a burthen is a source of opulence and prosperity to the parents.” As agriculture mechanized, farm children spent more time in school, and rural schooling was costly. So the cost advantage of farm children narrowed, and rural fertility in some advanced countries has fallen slightly below urban fertility.


10.5.8 Why don’t recessions bring fertility back?
We have seen fertility generally fall over time as wages rise. Why doesn’t it rise again in an economic crisis, when the opportunity cost of time falls? The quantity–quality model offers one possible answer. Faced with a loss of income, parents could spend less by investing less in each child, or by having fewer children. But social norms about child quality may be irreversible. Once a family, or a society, expects a certain level of schooling, health care, and so on for every child, the way to save is to have fewer children.

10  How Do Economists Think We Decide How Many Children to Have?

title: 10  How Do Economists Think We Decide How Many Children to Have?
text:
10.6 Putting the models together

The quantity–quality interaction is good for explaining the demographic transition: rapid, large fertility declines.
The cost-of-time model is good for explaining more recent trends, especially as women’s wages rise.
It is not either/or. A full treatment combines both models.

So how could fertility fall with economic growth? There are three possible answers:

It doesn’t, because the income effect dominates.
It does, because the substitution effect, the cost of time, dominates.
Parents get utility from quality too. So once fertility starts falling, there is a big shift toward quality.



Added · from readings Becker 1991, p. 154.
Becker draws a broader lesson. “Economic development can have significant negative effects on fertility even when the ‘true’ income elasticity of demand for fertility is positive and sizable.” Richer families can have fewer children than poorer families, because development also raises the returns to investing in children.
Some mysteries remain. Why don’t we just have one child and invest a lot in her? Why has fertility become more pro-cyclical in recent years? And why hasn’t U.S. fertility recovered from the recession?






In the lab



In Lab 7 you experiment with a “cost of time” app to see how changes in wages, income, and the costs of children move the best choice. Then you turn to data on 47 French-speaking provinces of Switzerland around 1888, during the historical fertility decline. Before you look at the data, you’ll write down what the models predict, and then compare and summarize what you found.

title: 10  How Do Economists Think We Decide How Many Children to Have?
text:
10.7 Key ideas

Fertility has fallen as incomes have risen, a puzzle if children are a normal good, and for biology too.
The cost-of-time model gives children a full price of \(p + wc\): money costs plus the earnings given up to care for them. Full income is \(wT + I\).
More non-wage income raises fertility. Higher money or time costs lower it. A higher wage has opposing income and substitution effects, so its effect is ambiguous in theory.
Because child care falls mostly on women, higher women’s wages tend to lower fertility more than men’s wages do.
In Becker’s quantity–quality model, spending on children is quality × quantity, so the price of each depends on the other. This interaction magnifies small changes in costs into large swings in the number of children and investment per child.
The interaction explains “induced demand”: an initial fall in births, from family planning for example, sets off a further fall.

title: 10  How Do Economists Think We Decide How Many Children to Have?
text:
10.8 Check your understanding


Added · new These questions are new. Q5 draws on the slide “Still many mysteries.” They avoid the lab’s graded questions.

Full price. In the lecture example (\(w = \$20\), \(c = 5\) hours, \(p = \$200\)), what is the full price of a child per week? What does it become if the wage rises to $30? Which part of the price changed, and why?
Butter and grain. Schultz studied fertility in Sweden in relation to the price of butter, largely produced by women, and grain, largely produced by men. Using the cost-of-time model, predict how a rise in each price would affect fertility, and explain why the predictions differ.
Marriage age. Becker writes the number of births as \(n = E/(C + S)\), the months of “exposure” divided by the average interval between births. With 288 months of exposure and 26-month intervals, \(n \approx 11\). How many births would there be if marriage were delayed by five years (60 fewer months of exposure), with intervals unchanged?
Cars and children. Explain Becker’s remark that a rich person “might well plan to own both expensive and inexpensive cars, but is unlikely to plan on having both expensive and inexpensive children.” Why is this assumption essential for the quantity–quality interaction?
Why not one child? Becker shows that a family will choose some of both quantity and quality only if they are not close substitutes. Use this idea to discuss the slide’s question: why don’t parents just have one child and invest a lot in her?
Cause or response? Summarize Becker’s evidence that improvements in contraception were mainly a response to falling demand for children, not a cause. Which piece of evidence do you find most convincing, and what evidence would persuade you otherwise?
Kuwait and Switzerland. Suppose a country’s income doubles. Use the model to explain why it matters whether the extra income comes from oil revenues or from higher wages for women.

10.9 Further reading

Becker, Gary S. 1991. “The Demand for Children.” Chapter 5 of A Treatise on the Family, enlarged edition. Harvard University Press. Pages 135–154. A difficult reading. As you read: skip the equations and focus on the arguments. Why does Becker think the quantity–quality interaction explains rapid fertility declines? Why doesn’t he think contraception is the main cause? Look at Tables 5.1 and 5.2 together.
“Consumer choice.” Wikipedia. A refresher on budget constraints, indifference curves, and income and substitution effects. As you read: pay particular attention to the section on the labor–leisure trade-off at the end, which is the closest relative of the cost-of-time model.

title: 11  Fertility Policy I: China’s One-Child Policy
text:
11.1 Policy and fertility: did it matter, and how would we know?
In earlier chapters we studied theories of fertility decline. Now we look at two cases (this chapter and Chapter 12) where governments or courts deliberately changed the rules, and ask what happened to births. Both cases are controversial, and both are useful for the same reason: they force us to think carefully about causation.
The problem is simple to state. Fertility was falling in China before the one-child policy, and it was falling in the United States before Roe v. Wade. If births fell after a policy, did the policy cause the fall, or would it have happened anyway? To answer, we need a counterfactual: what would have happened without the policy. We can never observe it directly. The art is in finding a comparison that stands in for it.
Speed of decline is one place to start. Across the world, the time it took fertility to fall from more than 6 children per woman to fewer than 3 has shrunk dramatically. In the United Kingdom it took 95 years (1815–1910). In the United States it took 82 years. In China it took 11 years (1967–1978), and in Iran only 10 (1986–1996). Notice China’s dates: its fall from 6 to 3 children per woman was finished before the one-child policy began in 1979. And Iran achieved an even faster decline with no one-child policy at all.

title: 11  Fertility Policy I: China’s One-Child Policy
section: 11.2 The one-child policy: beginnings and end
text:
11.2 The one-child policy: beginnings and end

11.2.1 Before the one-child policy: “Later, Longer, Fewer”


Added · from readings Mao’s views, Ma Yinchu, the 1971 slogan, and the “menstrual monitors” quotation are from Zhang 2017, pp. 142–143.
China’s population policy did not begin in 1979. Mao Zedong, China’s leader from 1949 to 1976, “believed in the principle: ‘More people, more power,’” as Junsen Zhang puts it. In the mid-1950s the economist Ma Yinchu, president of Peking University, recommended family planning. Mao was briefly supportive, but during the Great Leap Forward (1958) he reverted to the belief that a larger population was better, and Ma was denounced as a “rightist.” After the famine of the Great Leap Forward, fertility rebounded to more than six births per woman in the early 1960s.
By the end of the 1960s, China’s population passed 800 million and the economy was stagnating. A serious family planning campaign began in 1971 with the slogan “One child isn’t too few, two are just fine, and three are too many.” In 1973 it was formalized as the Later–Longer–Fewer campaign (wan–xi–shao):

Later marriage. People were encouraged to marry three years after the legal minimum ages: at least 25 (rural) or 27–28 (urban) for men, and at least 23 (rural) or 25 (urban) for women. Couples who married late got 7 to 30 days of “late marriage leave.”
Longer spacing. At least four years between births.
Fewer children. No more than two per couple.

The campaign worked. China’s fertility fell by half during the 1970s. Hesketh and colleagues put the total fertility rate (TFR) at 5.9 in 1970 and 2.9 in 1979; Zhang gives 5.8 in 1970 and 2.7 in 1978. By 1978, Zhang reports, urban fertility was already down to 1.55 children per woman, and rural fertility to 2.97.
The campaign was officially voluntary, but it had coercive elements. Zhang quotes the sociologists Martin Whyte, Wang Feng, and Yong Cai:

“These birth planning enforcers kept detailed records on each woman of child-bearing age under their responsibility, including past births, contraceptive usage and even menstrual cycles, in many reported instances becoming ‘menstrual monitors’ who tried to detect out-of-quota pregnancies at an early stage.”

Still, Zhang concludes, the 1970s campaign was “significantly less coercive than the one-child policy that followed.”


11.2.2 From Later–Longer–Fewer to just one child
When Deng Xiaoping came to power in 1978, the new leadership’s priority was the economy. A group of control theorists argued that China would achieve the highest level of well-being around 2050 if its population could be reduced to 650–700 million. Local governments began moving toward a one-child rule in late 1979. The policy was formally announced in September 1980, in “An open letter to all party members and all youth league members” published in the People’s Daily. The letter said that the State Council “advocates that each couple should have only one child,” and promised that after 30 years the policy might be changed.


Added · from readings Hesketh et al. 2005, p. 1171; Zhang 2017, p. 144.
Hesketh and colleagues summarize the government’s reasoning:






In their own words



“At the time, China was home to a quarter of the world’s people, who were occupying just 7 percent of world’s arable land. Two thirds of the population were under the age of 30 years, and the baby boomers of the 1950s and 1960s were entering their reproductive years. The government saw strict population containment as essential to economic reform and to an improvement in living standards.” (Hesketh, Lu, and Xing 2005)


Zhang adds that Deng had set a goal of quadrupling GDP per capita by the end of the century. Fewer people was one way to raise income per person. The policy was launched, Zhang writes, “in the context of both a neo-Malthusian concern over population and ambitious economic development goals.”


11.2.3 How the policy actually worked


Added · from readings Details of enforcement are from Hesketh et al. 2005, pp. 1171–1172, and Zhang 2017, pp. 144–145, including footnote 2.
The name “one-child policy” is misleading. “Despite its name,” Hesketh and colleagues write, “the one-child rule applies to a minority of the population.” In practice there was a two-tier system:

Urban residents and government employees were held strictly to one child. Many worked for state-owned enterprises and could lose their jobs and benefits if they had a second.
Rural residents, about 70 percent of the population, were generally allowed a second child after five years, often only if the first was a girl, “a clear acknowledgment of the traditional preference for boys.” Ethnic minorities and remote areas could have a third.

Enforcement was in the hands of local officials, who used rewards and penalties: economic incentives for compliance, and fines, confiscation of belongings, and dismissal from work for violations. The policy relied on near-universal contraception and abortion. By the early 2000s, 87 percent of married women used contraception, and IUDs and sterilization made up more than 90 percent of methods. Eighty percent of women in one large study said they had no choice of method and simply accepted what the family-planning worker recommended. Zhang notes that the heavy-handedness peaked in 1983, with “a nationwide campaign of mandatory sterilization, abortion, and IUD insertion.”
The policy also changed over time:

Flexibility and decentralization (1984–1989). Because of “practical difficulties,” especially resistance from rural families whose only child was a girl, the Party allowed more exceptions. The guiding phrase was “open a small hole to close up a big one.” Fertility rebounded somewhat in 1984–1986.
Restrengthening (from 1989). The policy was tightened again and tied to the careers of local officials: “No achievements, no promotion.” Family planning was listed among the three basic state policies in the 8th Five-Year Plan in March




The fines varied enormously from province to province and over time, as you can see in the data economists have collected on them. That variation will turn out to be useful for research.


11.2.4 The end of the one-child policy
The policy was relaxed in steps:

1984–2011: local governments allowed two children for couples in which both parents were themselves only children.
2014: two children allowed if either parent was an only child.
2016: a universal two-child policy. The abolition of the one-child policy was announced on October 29, 2015.
2021: a three-child policy, which lifted limits on third births.

Official motivations for the switch included a lower population growth rate, the recent decline in the size of the labor force, the challenges of an aging society, a lasting imbalance in the sex ratio, and the promise made in the 1979 open letter. Official propaganda has turned around completely. Banners that once read “Strictly limit second births, totally eradicate third births” and “One child is best, the government aids in elder care” now read “Three children are better than two” and “Three children are best, no need for state-supported elder care.”

section: 11.3 Did the one-child policy reduce fertility?
text:
11.3 Did the one-child policy reduce fertility?

11.3.1 The mystery: where is the policy hiding?
Figure 11.1 plots the total fertility rates reported in our two readings. The shaded bands show the Later–Longer–Fewer campaign and the one-child policy.


Show the R code
op <- par(mar = c(4, 4.2, 1, 1))
plot(NA, xlim = c(1965, 2015), ylim = c(0, 6.5), xlab = "Year",
     ylab = "Total fertility rate (children per woman)")
rect(1971, -1, 1979, 7, col = adjustcolor("#e08a00", 0.15), border = NA)
rect(1979, -1, 2015.5, 7, col = adjustcolor(col_grey, 0.12), border = NA)
text(1975, 6.3, "Later–Longer–\nFewer", cex = 0.8, col = "#a05a00")
text(1997, 6.3, "One-child policy (1979–2015)", cex = 0.8, col = col_grey)
abline(h = 2.1, lty = 3, col = col_grey)
text(2013.5, 2.1, "replacement", pos = 3, cex = 0.75, col = col_grey)
yr <- c(1970, 1978, 1979, 1995, 2004, 2010)
tfr <- c(5.8, 2.7, 2.8, 1.8, 1.7, 1.5)
lines(yr, tfr, lty = 2, col = col_all)
points(yr, tfr, pch = 19, col = col_all)
text(yr, tfr, c("5.8", "2.7", "2.8", "1.8", "1.7", "~1.5"),
     pos = c(4, 1, 4, 3, 3, 1), cex = 0.8)
points(c(1978, 1978), c(1.55, 2.97), pch = c(17, 15), col = c(col_urban, col_rural))
text(1978, 1.55, "urban 1.55", pos = 2, cex = 0.8, col = col_urban)
text(1978, 2.97, "rural 2.97", pos = 2, cex = 0.8, col = col_rural)
par(op)








Figure 11.1: China’s total fertility rate at dates reported in the readings. Black: national; blue and red: urban and rural in 1978. The steepest decline came during the ‘Later–Longer–Fewer’ campaign of the 1970s, before the one-child policy. Sources: Zhang (2017) for 1970, 1978, 1979, 1995 and the 1978 urban/rural rates; Hesketh et al. (2005) for 2004; Wang, Cai, and Gu (2013), as quoted by Zhang, for ‘around 1.5’ in 2010.





If you were shown only the curve and asked to find the year the one-child policy began, it would be hard to pick it out. The big drop came in the 1970s. Afterward, fertility fell much more gradually, to around 1.8 by the mid-1990s, and then roughly stabilized. Zhang puts the numbers side by side: the TFR fell from 5.8 to 2.7 between 1970 and 1978, but from 2.8 to 1.8 between 1979 and 1995 under the one-child policy. Whyte, Wang, and Cai calculate that roughly three-quarters of the decline in fertility from 1970 to the present occurred before the one-child policy began.


11.3.2 Comparison countries
Of course, fertility might have risen after 1979 without the policy. So we need a comparison. Zhang compares rural and urban China with four other developing countries that also had high fertility in the 1960s: South Korea, Thailand, Mexico, and India. None had a one-child policy. All saw rapid declines after 1970.


Added · from readings Zhang 2017, pp. 146–148.
South Korea and Thailand, which had fast economic growth and voluntary family planning programs, fell more slowly than urban China in the 1960s and 1970s, but by 2010 their fertility was as low as China’s. Thailand, Zhang notes, “is especially worth noting because it had fertility and GDP per capita similar to China’s by 2010.” Even India, with a weaker family planning program and much slower growth, saw a marked decline. Zhang’s conclusion: “Given that the economic growth rate of China was higher than those of the four other countries from 1979, I believe that even without the one-child policy, China’s fertility rate would have declined substantially after 1978.”
Another comparison, shown in lecture, is Taiwan, which never had a one-child policy. Taiwan’s fertility followed a path quite similar to mainland China’s and has since fallen even lower.
A related observation: China was “ahead of the curve.” When we plot fertility against GDP per capita, China’s fertility fell to low levels at an exceptionally low income. Zhang points out that in China, India, South Korea, and Thailand fertility fell sharply before GDP per capita reached $3,000. China’s economy was nearly stagnant in the 1970s, so economic development cannot explain the fertility decline of that decade. The family planning campaign was “widely believed to be the main contributor.” Some demographers called it an “induced fertility transition.”


11.3.3 How economists try to identify the effect


Added · from readings The four approaches and their assumptions are from Zhang 2017, pp. 148–150.
Zhang describes four strategies that researchers have used, each with its own assumption:

Before and after 1979. Compare births before and after the policy, controlling for a time trend. This assumes that any break from the trend after 1979 is due to the policy, not to the economic reforms that began at the same time.
Variation in fines. Compare places with higher and lower penalties. The problem is that local governments may set fines according to local conditions and local demand for children. Fines are not randomly assigned.
Han versus minorities. Han Chinese women were held strictly to the policy, while minority women were often allowed two children. Comparing the change in Han fertility to the change in minority fertility is a difference-in-differences design. It assumes the two groups would otherwise have followed the same trend, which economic reforms may have violated.
Variation in enforcement intensity. Compare prefectures that enforced the policy more and less strictly (measured by “excess” births above the one-child rule), and cohorts with more and less exposure.

The ideal, Zhang observes wryly, “would have been useful for research purposes if China had randomly selected a cross-section of prefectures to implement the one-child policy and then forbidden interprefecture migration.” That never happened, so every estimate rests on assumptions.


11.3.4 What the evidence says
The studies agree that the policy did reduce fertility, especially at first. Ahn (1994), for example, found that the probability of a second child in urban areas fell by 50 percent in Hebei and Shaanxi and by 86 percent in Shanghai after the policy. But most studies find the effect was “rather small, especially in the longer-term.” Zhang offers a reconciliation:






In their own words



“A plausible reconciliation of these views is that the one-child policy accelerated the already-occurring drop in fertility for a few years, but in the longer term, economic development played a more fundamental role in leading to and maintaining China’s low fertility level.” (Zhang 2017)


Hesketh and colleagues reach the same view. China’s neighbors, without such policies, had some of the lowest fertility rates in the world: 1.04 in Singapore, 1.38 in Japan, 0.91 in Hong Kong. “It is reasonable to speculate,” they write, “that there would have been a further decline in China’s total fertility rate had the voluntary policy of the 1970s continued.” A Bayesian projection by Wang, Cai, and Gu, quoted by Zhang, concluded that without the policy, “By 2010, fertility would have fallen to its currently observed level of around 1.5 children per woman.”
That raises an awkward point about official claims. Chinese authorities claimed the policy prevented 250 to 300 million births. But that claim depends on assuming fertility would have stayed high without the policy. Wang and colleagues concluded, in Zhang’s summary, that “China’s government exaggerated the effect of the one-child policy.”


11.3.5 Fewer children, better educated children?


Added · from readings Zhang 2017, pp. 152–153.
If families can have only one child, they might invest more in that child. This is the quantity–quality trade-off from Gary Becker’s theory of fertility. Did the one-child policy produce better-educated children?
An ingenious test uses twins. In urban Kunming, where the policy was strictly enforced, about 95 percent of households without twins had one child, while households whose first birth was twins necessarily had two. Twins are a matter of chance, so comparing these families isolates the effect of an extra child. Mark Rosenzweig and Zhang found that the policy-induced fall in fertility had “a moderately positive effect on children’s human capital at most”: it raised schooling by at most 4 percent and the probability of attending college by less than 9 percent. Other studies, using variation in enforcement, find similarly small effects on education.


11.3.6 What lessons for other countries?
Zhang’s verdict on the policy as a whole is blunt. It “may have mildly accelerated the fertility transition,” but “it also brought substantial costs, including political costs, human rights concerns, a more rapidly aging population, and an imbalanced sex ratio resulting from a preference for sons. In retrospect, one may question the need for introducing the one-child policy in China.” For other countries:

“If the country is already experiencing a decline in fertility rates, then a one-child policy doesn’t seem useful. … Rather than focusing on a one-child policy, a developing country may want to consider an aggressive but less-coercive family planning program such as the policy implemented in China in the 1970s.” (Zhang 2017)

11  Fertility Policy I: China's One-Child Policy

title: 11  Fertility Policy I: China’s One-Child Policy
text:
11.4 Fewer daughters: an unintended consequence?

11.4.1 The sex ratio at birth
In every population, slightly more boys are born than girls. Hesketh and colleagues report that the sex ratio at birth ranges from 1.03 to 1.07 boys per girl in industrialized countries. In China, the reported ratio rose from 1.06 in 1979 to 1.11 in 1988 and 1.17 in 2001, and reached 1.3 in some rural provinces. Figure 11.2 shows how the ratio varied by birth order.


Show the R code
sr <- rbind(Urban = c(1.13, 1.30, 1.19, 1.19), Rural = c(1.05, 1.23, 1.29, 1.32))
colnames(sr) <- c("1st", "2nd", "3rd", "4th+")
op <- par(mar = c(4, 4.2, 1, 1))
bp <- barplot(sr, beside = TRUE, col = c(col_urban, col_rural), ylim = c(0.9, 1.4),
              xpd = FALSE, xlab = "Birth order", ylab = "Boys per girl",
              legend.text = TRUE, args.legend = list(x = "topleft", bty = "n"))
abline(h = 1.05, lty = 3, col = col_grey)
box()
text(bp, sr + 0.012, format(sr, nsmall = 2), cex = 0.75)
par(op)








Figure 11.2: Sex ratio at birth (boys per girl) by birth order in China, 1980–2001, for urban and rural areas. The dotted line marks a typical biological ratio of 1.05. Source: Hesketh et al. (2005), Table 2 (data from Kang and Wang).





The pattern fits the policy’s rules closely. In rural areas, where a second child was usually allowed (especially after a girl), the first-birth ratio was normal, 1.05, but it rose steeply for later births. In urban areas, where only one child was allowed, the ratio was already high, 1.13, for first births. Hesketh and colleagues explain:

“The picture that emerges is that some urban Chinese make the choice to perform sex selection with the first pregnancy, since they are allowed only one child. In rural areas, most couples are permitted to have a second child, especially if the first is female. So if the second (or subsequent) child is female, the pregnancy often ‘disappears,’ allowing the couple to have another child in an attempt to have a son.”



11.4.2 Stopping rules can’t change the sex ratio. Behavior can.
Could parents raise the share of boys simply by deciding when to stop having children? For example, “keep having children until you get a boy.” In class we test this with coins. The lesson: stopping rules alone can’t change the sex ratio. Each birth is still about as likely to be a boy as a girl, whatever the parents plan to do next. Stopping rules can, however, amplify gender inequality in other ways. (Think about how many brothers and sisters a typical boy or girl has under such a rule.)
So if we see the sex ratio change, it must be due to behavior that affects which births are born or counted:

sex-selective abortion, made possible by ultrasound;
differential reporting, or “hiding girls” from census takers and officials;
differential mortality, if girls receive less care;
and possibly other channels.



Added · from readings Hesketh et al. 2005, pp. 1172–1173; Zhang 2017, pp. 153–154.
The readings suggest that all three behaviors played a role. Sex-selective abortion “undoubtedly accounts for a large proportion of the decline in female births,” Hesketh and colleagues write, although it is illegal and hard to measure. Underreporting was large too. A 1995 household survey in three provinces found a normal sex ratio among children under 14, with the actual number of girls exceeding the number registered by 22 percent. Daniel Goodkind estimated that 19 percent of all children aged 0–4 in 2000 were unreported to the authorities. Infanticide of girls is “probably very rare now,” but “less aggressive treatment of sick female infants is known to occur.”
Was the policy itself to blame? Only partly, say Hesketh and colleagues. China had a high sex ratio in the 1930s and 1940s, and other Asian countries with son preference and falling fertility, but no one-child policy, also saw imbalances: Taiwan (1.19), Singapore (1.18), South Korea (1.12), and parts of northern India (1.20). Most tellingly, “the marked increase in the sex ratio between the 1980s and 1990s coincided with much easier access to cheap ultrasonography and not with any substantial change in enforcement of the one-child policy.” The policy amplified son preference, but technology made acting on it easy.


11.4.3 Other consequences
Hesketh and colleagues list several more consequences:

A marriage squeeze. The shortage of women has left some men unable to marry. The authors link it to the kidnapping and trafficking of women for marriage.
The “4:2:1” problem. With few children and longer lives, a growing number of couples will be solely responsible for one child and four parents. About 70 percent of elderly people still depended financially on their children.
Health risks. Women with unapproved pregnancies often avoided prenatal care and gave birth at home. One study found that maternal deaths doubled for unapproved pregnancies.







In the lab



In Lab 8 you use a sample of the 1990 Chinese census, about 200,000 households, to look for traces of the one-child policy in the sexes of children. You compare the proportion female by birth order and year of birth, and you ask whether parents’ decisions to have another child depended on the sexes of the children they already had. Keep in mind that the 1990 census is known to undercount young children, and that we see only surviving children.

title: 11  Fertility Policy I: China’s One-Child Policy
text:
11.5 Key ideas

To know what a policy caused, we need a counterfactual. Comparison countries, comparison groups, and natural experiments stand in for it.
China’s fertility fell by half during the voluntary but coercive Later–Longer–Fewer campaign of the 1970s, before the one-child policy. The policy itself seems to have had a modest, mostly short-term effect.
China’s sex ratio at birth rose sharply, especially for later births in rural areas and first births in cities. Stopping rules cannot change the sex ratio; sex-selective abortion, underreporting, and differential care can.

text: 12.1 Abortion policy and fertility in the United States
crumbs: Fertility and the family
12  Fertility Policy II: Abortion and the Pill in the United States

title: 12  Fertility Policy II: Abortion and the Pill in the United States
text:
12.1.1 Why the U.S. is special


Added · from readings The amicus brief (pp. 16–19, 23–24) gives similar figures for 2017 and on the women who seek abortions.
Among rich countries, the United States has relatively high fertility. One reason is unwanted births. In a decomposition of fertility shown in lecture (Morgan 2003), the multiplier for unwanted fertility was 1.12 in the United States, compared with 1.04 in Italy. That is, unwanted births raised U.S. fertility by about 12 percent, three times as much as in Italy.
Before Dobbs, abortion was not rare. There were about a million abortions a year, about 20 percent of pregnancies, and an estimated one in four American women had an abortion by age 45. The economists’ amicus brief reports 862,320 abortions in 2017, and that “nearly half of all pregnancies are unintended, and nearly half of these unintended pregnancies end in abortion.” Contraception fails too: the pill fails for about 7 percent of women in their first year of use, mostly through user error.
Who seeks an abortion? We often hear about teenagers. But the typical woman seeking an abortion is an adult (97 percent are over 18), already has a child (59 percent), has low income (75 percent), and has recently experienced a disruptive life event, such as a job loss, a death in the family, or the end of a relationship.
The legal history in brief:

Roe v. Wade (1973) legalized abortion in all states. In recent years there was mounting pressure and reduced access in some states.
Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health (2022) overturned Roe and allows states to ban abortion. About 23 states were expected to end up banning it.

Dobbs raises many questions: How will it affect women’s lives? Sexual and contraceptive behavior? The children born from unintended pregnancies? Here we focus on the first and most measurable: how much do abortion bans increase births?


Added · from readings Levine et al. 1999, p. 199.
As Phillip Levine and his coauthors put it a quarter century before Dobbs: “Although positions are largely developed on philosophical and moral grounds, the empirical magnitude of the effect of legal access to abortion is both important and rarely studied.” Economics cannot settle the moral question. It can try to measure the consequences.


12.1.2 Causal inference: difference-in-differences
This is a causal question, so a simple correlation won’t do. The tool that most of the research uses is difference-in-differences: compare the change in births in places where the policy changed with the change in places where it did not.


Added · from readings Amicus brief, pp. 4–6.
The 154 economists who signed the amicus brief explain the idea:






In their own words



“While many know the familiar mantra that ‘correlation does not necessarily equal causation,’ the field of causal inference focuses precisely on figuring out when correlation does equal causation. … By comparing changes for the treatment group to those for the control group, the difference-in-differences methodology inherently controls for any differences that were present between the two groups, even without the policy change, while simultaneously controlling for other events occurring around the time of the policy change that potentially impacted outcomes for both groups.” (Brief of Amici Curiae Economists, 2021)




12.1.3 Study design 1: early legalization
Roe was not the beginning. Five states (California, New York, Washington, Alaska, and Hawaii) legalized abortion early, in 1969 or 1970. That gives a natural experiment. From 1970 to 1973, abortion was legal in these “repeal states” but not elsewhere. After 1973, it was legal everywhere.
Figure 12.1 shows crude birth rates in New York, an early repeal state, and Ohio, which waited for Roe.


Show the R code
yrs <- 1970:1975
ny <- c(17.4, 15.5, 13.8, 13.1, 13.2, 13.0)
oh <- c(18.7, 17.7, 15.8, 15.0, 15.0, 14.8)
op <- par(mar = c(4, 4.2, 1, 1))
plot(yrs, ny, type = "o", pch = 19, col = col_ny, lwd = 2, ylim = c(12, 19.5),
     xlab = "Year", ylab = "Crude birth rate (per 1,000)")
lines(yrs, oh, type = "o", pch = 15, col = col_oh, lwd = 2)
abline(v = 1972.5, lty = 2, col = col_grey)
text(1972.5, 19.3, "Roe v. Wade (Jan. 1973)", pos = 4, cex = 0.8, col = col_grey)
text(1971.3, 14.9, "New York", col = col_ny, pos = 1, cex = 0.9)
text(1970.2, 18.9, "Ohio", col = col_oh, pos = 4, cex = 0.9)
par(op)








Figure 12.1: Crude birth rates (births per 1,000) in New York, which legalized abortion in 1970, and Ohio, where it became legal with Roe v. Wade in 1973. Data: lecture slides.





Both states’ birth rates fell in the early 1970s, so a simple before-and-after comparison in Ohio would wrongly credit Roe with the whole national decline. The difference-in-differences logic asks a sharper question. Did the gap between New York and Ohio shrink after 1973, when Ohio, too, got legal abortion? (Try computing the first and second differences yourself. It’s the fourth “Check your understanding” question.)


Added · from readings Results in this subsection are from Levine et al. 1999, pp. 199–202, Tables 1–3.
Levine and colleagues did this systematically, for all states, controlling for state and year effects, state-specific trends, and economic conditions. They found that birth rates in the repeal states fell by about 4 percent relative to other states in 1971–1973, exactly the years when abortion was legal only there. After Roe, the gap closed. The effects were much larger for some groups: births fell by 12 percent for teenagers, 8 percent for women 35 and older, and 12 percent for non-white women (more than three times the effect for white women).
But 4 percent may be an underestimate, because women could travel. Before Roe, women in Ohio could, and did, go to New York for an abortion, so Ohio is not a clean “untreated” comparison. Levine and colleagues tested this by comparing the repeal states with non-repeal states at different distances. Figure 12.2 shows the result.


Show the R code
lab <- c("Repeal\nstates", "< 250\nmiles", "250–750\nmiles", "> 750\nmiles")
abr <- c(37.3, 25.5, 19.1, 17.8)
eff <- c(4.45, 4.52, 10.77)
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(3.2, 4.2, 2, 1), mgp = c(2.6, 0.6, 0))
b1 <- barplot(abr, names.arg = lab, col = c(col_ny, rep(col_grey, 3)),
              ylim = c(0, 45), ylab = "Abortions per 1,000 women",
              main = "Abortion rate, 1976", font.main = 1, cex.names = 0.75)
text(b1, abr + 2.5, abr, cex = 0.8)
b2 <- barplot(eff, names.arg = lab[-1], col = col_grey, ylim = c(0, 13),
              ylab = "Relative decline in births (%)",
              main = "Effect on births, 1971–73", font.main = 1,
              cex.names = 0.75)
text(b2, eff + 0.8, sprintf("%.1f", eff), cex = 0.8)
par(op)








Figure 12.2: Distance to legal abortion and its effects. Left: abortion rate in 1976 (per 1,000 women aged 15–44), by distance from the five early ‘repeal’ states. Right: estimated decline in births in repeal states, 1971–73, relative to non-repeal states at each distance (percent). Source: Levine et al. (1999), Tables 2 and 3.





Compared with states more than 750 miles away, where few women would have traveled, births in the repeal states fell by almost 11 percent. That is the better estimate of the full effect of legal access. Even after Roe, access was not uniform. In 1976, 96.8 percent of women in repeal states lived in a county with an abortion provider, compared with only 52–56 percent of women in the distant states.
Writing in 1999, Levine and colleagues even made a forecast. If Roe were replaced by a nationwide ban, births might rise by 11 percent, “perhaps as many as 440 000 additional births per year.” If instead the decision returned the question to the states and the five repeal states kept abortion legal, births in the banning states might rise by about 4.5 percent. “If more states were to keep abortion legal,” they added, “the effect on births probably would be smaller since interstate travel to obtain abortions would increase.”


12.1.4 Study design 2: recent clinic closures
A second natural experiment came from Texas. In 2013, Texas passed HB-2, a law that shut down many of the state’s abortion clinics. Overnight, some women found the nearest clinic much farther away, while others were barely affected. Justice Elena Kagan, during oral arguments in Whole Woman’s Health v. Hellerstedt (2016), called it “almost like the perfect controlled experiment.” Researchers compared counties whose travel distance jumped with counties where it did not:

Fischer, Royer, and White (2018), Texas: an increase in travel distance from 0 to more than 100 miles reduced abortions by about 38 percent and increased births by about 1.9 percent.
Lindo, Myers, Schlosser, and Cunningham (2020), Texas: an increase from 5 to 105 miles reduced abortions by about 30 percent. They argue they lacked the statistical power to identify effects on births.
Venator and Fletcher (2020), Wisconsin: an increase from 0 to 100 miles reduced abortions by about 31 percent and increased births by about 3 percent.



Added · from readings Amicus brief, pp. 26–34. The national figures in the brief differ from the slide’s “8% nationally.” Both come from versions of the Myers et al. model; see the report.
The amicus brief adds that even modest distances matter. An increase of 25 miles reduced abortion rates by 10 percent, and an increase of 50 miles by 18 percent.
Using estimates like these, Caitlin Myers and coauthors forecast what would happen if 23 states banned abortion. In the affected regions, they predicted a 25.5 percent decrease in abortions (about 8 percent nationally). The brief, filed before the decision, reported that bans in those states would increase the travel distance to the nearest provider for 26 million women of childbearing age. In the counties affected, the average distance would rise from 35 miles to 279 miles.


12.1.5 What actually happened (so far)
Forecasts are only as good as their assumptions, and here events surprised the forecasters. Several things were left out of the natural experiments:

travel funds that help women reach distant clinics;
self-managed abortions with pills, including by mail;
congestion at clinics in states where abortion remained legal;
the possibility of a ban on mifepristone, one of the abortion pills.

The result: abortions increased nationally after Dobbs. The forecast that abortions would fall by about 25 percent in banning states (a bit less than 10 percent nationally) appears so far to have been wrong.
But births did rise. A difference-in-differences study by Daniel Dench, Mayra Pineda-Torres, and Caitlin Myers (2023) compares states with total bans to states that protected abortion. It finds fertility in the banning states rising above trend in 2023. The effects show a dose–response pattern: they were larger in states farther from a state where abortion was legal, such as Texas, Mississippi, and Louisiana. The forecast that births would rise by about 2 percent in banning states appears so far to have been right.


12.1.6 Long-term effects
What about the long run? If abortion bans increase births in the short run, there could be compensating effects:

more early unintended births might mean fewer later, intended births;
couples might change their contraceptive use;
people might lower their target family size, to avoid going over it.

One simulation suggests what this could look like. If the rate of unintended births rises, the TFR first spikes, then declines to a new equilibrium that is still higher than before. The decline comes from compensation: fewer intended births.


Added · from readings Amicus brief, pp. 10–15 and 24–25. These are the brief’s characterizations of the studies it cites.
The longer-term effects on women’s lives are harder to measure. In their brief, written to persuade the Court to uphold Roe, the 154 economists summarized studies of the legalization era that found:

legalization, together with laws letting young women obtain abortions without parental consent, reduced teen motherhood by 34 percent and teen marriage by 20 percent;
for young women with an unintended pregnancy, access to abortion raised the probability of finishing college by nearly 20 percentage points and of entering a professional occupation by nearly 40 percentage points;
delaying an unplanned start to motherhood by one year raised hourly wages later in women’s careers by 11 percent.

They also cited the Turnaway Study. It compared women who arrived at a clinic just before its gestational limit and obtained an abortion with women who arrived just after and were turned away. Over the following five years, the women turned away saw a 78 percent increase in past-due debt and an 81 percent increase in negative public financial records such as bankruptcies and evictions.
Not everyone agrees on how much these studies show. The state of Mississippi and other amici, including a group of “240 Women Scholars and Professionals,” argued that it is “so very difficult to untangle” the effects of abortion legalization from everything else changing for women in the 1970s, and criticized individual studies, for example the Turnaway Study’s small sample. The economists’ brief responds to these criticisms point by point. An amicus brief is an argument, not a neutral survey. Read it, and its opponents, as you would any advocate’s case.

12  Fertility Policy II: Abortion and the Pill in the United States

title: 12  Fertility Policy II: Abortion and the Pill in the United States
text:
12.2 The power of the pill


Added · from readings This section summarizes Goldin and Katz 2002, the replication-project reading. The slides mention it only in announcing the replication project.
The lecture opens with a reminder that Claudia Goldin won the 2023 Nobel Prize in Economics “for having advanced our understanding of women’s labour market outcomes.” This year’s replication project is her paper with Lawrence Katz, “The Power of the Pill.” It is a model of how to make a causal argument about fertility technology with imperfect data.

12.2.1 The puzzle
Two things changed abruptly for American college-educated women born around 1950. First, careers: women were 10 percent of first-year law students in 1970 but 36 percent in 1980. Their share of first-year medical students rose from about 10 to 30 percent over the same decade. Second, marriage: among college graduate women born in 1950, almost half married before age 23, but fewer than 30 percent of those born in 1957 did. Goldin and Katz ask whether the birth control pill, and the legal changes that let young unmarried women get it, caused both.


12.2.2 Two effects of the pill
The pill was approved in 1960 and spread rapidly among married women. But until the late 1960s, young single women generally could not get it without parental consent. (Some got around the law by claiming to be engaged, or to have irregular periods.) Goldin and Katz argue the pill mattered in two ways:

A direct effect. A woman embarking on years of professional education had to choose between abstinence and “considerable uncertainty regarding pregnancy.” The pill, with a failure rate in typical use of 3 percent per year compared with 20 percent for the diaphragm, made career investment far less risky.
An indirect effect through the marriage market. If many people delay marriage, then a woman who postpones marriage to finish law school no longer finds that the best partners have all been taken. The pill created a “thicker” marriage market for career women.







In their own words



“The pill enabled young men and women to put off marriage while not having to put off sex. Sex no longer had to be packaged with commitment devices, many of which encouraged early marriage. Before the pill was widely available, young people devised means to secure commitments that enabled sexual relations. They ‘went steady,’ fraternity men ‘pinned’ coeds, and couples got ‘engaged.’” (Goldin and Katz 2002)


Their simple model has a cost of delaying marriage, an “impatience factor,” that the pill lowers. Women whose career payoff exceeds that cost delay marriage and invest in careers. When the pill lowers the cost, more women do so. The model also shows that not everyone gains: women with poorer labor market prospects may lose out in the marriage market.


12.2.3 The natural experiment
How can one separate the pill from feminism, antidiscrimination laws, and everything else happening around 1970? Goldin and Katz exploit an accident of history. Between 1969 and 1974, almost every state lowered its age of majority to 18 or extended “mature minor” rights. That let young single women obtain the pill without parental consent. These legal changes, they argue, “were not generally motivated by demands for teenage contraception.” Rather, the Vietnam War, and the Twenty-sixth Amendment giving 18-year-olds the vote, drove them. And states changed their laws at different times. So women born in the same year had different access to the pill depending on their state.
Using this variation, Goldin and Katz find that a state law giving minors access to the pill reduced the share of college women married before age 23 by about 2 to 3 percentage points. That is 24–37 percent of the total decline across cohorts. Pill access can also explain much of the increase in college women working as lawyers and doctors: 1.2 to 1.6 percentage points of a 1.7-point increase from 1970 to 1990. Abortion legalization had similar, though less robust, effects.
Goldin and Katz are careful not to overclaim. “No great social movement is caused by a single factor,” they write. And “the pill is not necessary for demographic change”: Japanese women also married later and had fewer children from the 1970s, yet saw little change in economic status, and the pill was not legal in Japan until 1999. But a “virtually foolproof, easy-to-use, and female-controlled contraceptive” seems to have been important for real change in women’s economic position.

12  Fertility Policy II: Abortion and the Pill in the United States

title: 12  Fertility Policy II: Abortion and the Pill in the United States
text:
12.3 Lessons
Substantive conclusions.

China’s one-child policy probably accelerated an already rapid fertility decline for a few years. Most of China’s decline happened before it, and economic development probably explains China’s low fertility today. Its costs, including coercion, a distorted sex ratio, and rapid aging, were large.
In the United States, legal abortion reduced births by at least 4 percent, and perhaps 11 percent, when it was introduced in the early 1970s. Dobbs has a big effect on women (and men), especially poor women. In banning states, births were forecast to rise by about 2 percent, and so far this appears right. We are unlikely to see a big national rise in fertility, but the long-term consequences for many women could be large.

Methodological conclusions.

Causal inference tries to identify the effect of a single change, such as the closing of abortion clinics or a lower age of majority.
But natural experiments can miss changes that weren’t part of the “experiment,” such as internet prescriptions of abortion pills. That is why the post-Dobbs abortion forecasts went wrong.
We need statistical methods, but also awareness of what we might be leaving out: feedback, reactions, and the difference between the short term and the long term. This is Malthus-like thinking applied to new issues.

12  Fertility Policy II: Abortion and the Pill in the United States

title: 12  Fertility Policy II: Abortion and the Pill in the United States
text:
12.4 Key ideas

To know what a policy caused, we need a counterfactual. Comparison countries, comparison groups, and natural experiments stand in for it.
Difference-in-differences compares changes in treated and untreated places. Early legalization of abortion in five states reduced births there by about 4 percent, or about 11 percent when travel to legal states is accounted for.
After Dobbs, births rose in banning states as forecast, but abortions did not fall nationally as forecast. Natural experiments can miss new responses, such as pills by mail.
Goldin and Katz use state differences in the age of majority to show that access to the pill delayed marriage and moved women into professional careers.
