text:
17.4 Momentum: why young populations keep growing
The projection matrix explains one of the most important facts about population forecasts. Suppose that, starting today, every woman had just enough children to replace herself and her partner. Would population growth stop?


Added · from readings UN, WPP 2022, Key messages, p. i, and pp. 8–9; UN, WPP 2024, p. 12 and pp. 20, 23.
No. A population that has been growing has a young age structure: lots of people in or about to enter their childbearing years, compared with the number of old people who will die. Even at replacement fertility, those large young cohorts have more babies than the small old cohorts leave behind in deaths, for decades. This is population momentum. The UN estimated in 2022 that “two-thirds of the projected increase in global population through 2050 will be driven by the momentum of past growth that is embedded in the youthful age structure of the current population. Such growth would occur even if childbearing in today’s high-fertility countries were to fall immediately to around two births per woman.” The 2024 revision raised the share to 79 percent, about 1.4 billion people.
Momentum works in reverse, too. After decades of low fertility, the number of women of childbearing age shrinks, and births keep falling even if fertility recovers. The UN calls this negative momentum, and in 2024 found it was “likely to be the main driver of population decline in 18 countries and areas between now and 2054.” For the countries whose populations have already peaked, “even if fertility were to return instantly to the replacement level and stay there for several decades, the population of the group would start to decline after 2040.”

17.4.1 Try it: the momentum app


Added · new This app (momentum) is from Goldstein’s Shiny sandbox (research_to_file/sandbox_from_oldlaptop/shiny/momentum, 2024); it is not in any C175 lab or slide. I copied ui.R and server.R into course_apps_extra/momentum (leaving out an unrelated test file in the same folder) and exported it with Shinylive. Headless Chrome hung on the live app, so the image is the app’s own plot drawn with its own code at the default settings with the time slider at its end (T = 20), not a screenshot. The questions are mine.
The app projects a five-age-group population with a Leslie matrix you control. It starts the population in the stable state for your matrix, then, at time 0, cuts fertility instantly to exactly replacement (it rescales the first row so the net reproduction rate is 1) and projects 20 steps. Press play on the time slider, or drag it, to watch births, total population and the age distribution respond. It opens in a new tab. (The first load can take a few seconds while R starts up in your browser.)



The momentum app’s plot at its default settings after 20 projection steps. Click to open the app in a new tab.


Open the momentum app in a new tab ↗
Before you move each slider, write down what you expect to happen. Then check.

How much more growth? At the default settings the net reproduction rate falls from about 1.56 to exactly 1 at time 0. Before pressing play, guess the ratio of the final population to the population at time 0. Is it bigger or smaller than you expected, and which age groups account for the growth?
Faster growth, more momentum? Raise firstrow[1] and firstrow[2] from 0.8 to 1.2, so the population was growing faster before time 0. Predict whether the final “Pop ratio” will be larger or smaller than before. Why?
Births versus population. In the default run, the number of births barely changes after time 0, but the total population keeps rising for several steps. Explain how both can be true at once.

text:
17.5 When will population peak?

17.5.1 The puzzle of the long lag


Added · new The framing and the Japan example follow Goldstein and Cassidy (2024), Demography, pp. 419–423, which is not on the reading list. The lecture topic is from the calendar (“time paths of world fertility and the timing of peak population”).
Japan’s fertility fell below replacement in the early 1970s. Its population did not start to shrink until about 2009, some 35 years later. Italy, South Korea and China show similar lags (Table 17.2). Why does it take so long for low fertility to show up as decline? And can we use the answer to predict when the world as a whole will peak?




Table 17.2: Years from replacement fertility (NRR = 1) to peak population, selected countries and the world. Peak population for the world is the UN’s 2024 projection. Source: UN World Population Prospects 2024 (medium variant), my calculation.












Country
NRR falls below 1
Population peaks
Lag, NRR = 1 to peak (years)




Japan
1973
2009
36


Italy
1975
2014
39


South Korea
1983
2020
37


China
1990
2021
31


India
2017
2061 (projected)
44


World
2036 (projected)
2084 (projected)
48










Added · new The net reproduction rate (NRR) is the number of daughters a woman would have, counting the chance she dies before or during her childbearing years. NRR = 1 is exact replacement. It is used here instead of the TFR because replacement TFR differs across countries (it is near 2.1 only where mortality is low).

Added · new The Coale results and the extensions are from Goldstein and Cassidy (2024), pp. 421–425. The numbers are theirs (typical \(\mu \approx 30\), \(A \approx 40\)). Josh’s peak-population app (below) lets you check them.



17.5.2 Coale’s answer
The demographer Ansley Coale worked out what happens in a simple case: a closed population with constant mortality whose fertility falls steadily, by the same percentage every year. Two results come out of the projection arithmetic.
Births peak before fertility reaches replacement. This is surprising. You might think the momentum of past growth would keep births rising even after fertility hits replacement. But think about what replacement means: each generation exactly replaces the one before it. So at the moment fertility reaches replacement, this year’s births are about equal to births one generation (about 30 years) earlier. If births a generation apart are equal, and births rose and then fell in between, the peak must lie between them. In Coale’s scenario births peak about half a generation, roughly 15 years, before fertility reaches replacement.
Population peaks when the biggest birth cohort reaches the average age of the population. Total population is the sum of all past birth cohorts that are still alive. Roughly speaking, it keeps growing until the largest cohort has aged to the middle of the population, about 40 years. So population peaks about 40 years after births do, or about \(40 - 15 = 25\) years after fertility reaches replacement.
In symbols, with \(t_0\) the date the NRR reaches 1, \(\mu\) the average age of childbearing and \(A\) the average age of the population,
\[
t_{\text{births peak}} \approx t_0 - \frac{\mu}{2}, \qquad
t_{\text{population peaks}} \approx t_0 - \frac{\mu}{2} + A.
\]


17.5.3 Why real populations take even longer
Twenty-five years is too short. In Table 17.2, the lags are 30 to 40 years and more. Joshua Goldstein and Thomas Cassidy (2024) show that the extra years come from three features of real demographic change that Coale left out:

Rising longevity. If people keep living longer, the population keeps getting a bit bigger even after births start to fall. With life expectancy rising about 1.6 years per decade, the peak comes several years later.
Fertility decline slows down below replacement. Real fertility doesn’t fall at a steady rate forever; it levels off. A leveling-off makes the population take longer to turn down.
Immigration adds to the population and to births.

With these extensions, their models “predict a typical lag between replacement-level fertility and population decline of about 35 to 40 years, consistent with projections by the United Nations and about 15 years longer than the lag predicted by Coale.”
Figure 17.2 applies this to the world as a whole, using the UN’s 2024 projection.


Show the R code
w <- wpp_get("World")
t0w <- t0_of(w)
tB <- w$Time[which.max(w$Births)]
tN <- w$Time[which.max(w$Pop)]
op <- par(mfrow = c(3, 1), mar = c(2.5, 4.8, 1.6, 1), las = 1, oma = c(1.5, 0, 0, 0))
shade <- function() rect(2024, -1e9, 2101, 1e9, col = "grey94", border = NA)

plot(w$Time, w$NRR, type = "n", ylim = c(0.8, 2.4), xlab = "", ylab = "NRR")
shade(); abline(h = 1, col = col_grey); abline(v = t0w, lty = 2)
lines(w$Time, w$NRR, lwd = 2.5, col = col_nrr)
text(2101, 2.25, "UN projection", pos = 2, cex = 0.9, col = col_grey)
text(t0w, 2.1, paste0("NRR = 1 in ", round(t0w)), pos = 4, cex = 0.9)
mtext("Net reproduction rate", side = 3, line = 0.2, adj = 0, cex = 0.8)

plot(w$Time, w$Births / 1000, type = "n", ylim = c(80, 160),
     xlab = "", ylab = "Millions per year")
shade(); abline(v = t0w, lty = 2)
lines(w$Time, w$Births / 1000, lwd = 2.5, col = col_c)
points(tB, max(w$Births) / 1000, pch = 19, col = col_c)
text(tB, max(w$Births) / 1000, paste("Highest year,", tB), pos = 3, cex = 0.9)
mtext("Births", side = 3, line = 0.2, adj = 0, cex = 0.8)

plot(w$Time, w$Pop / 1e6, type = "n", ylim = c(2, 11),
     xlab = "", ylab = "Billions")
shade(); abline(v = t0w, lty = 2)
lines(w$Time, w$Pop / 1e6, lwd = 2.5, col = col_y)
points(tN, max(w$Pop) / 1e6, pch = 19, col = col_y)
text(tN, max(w$Pop) / 1e6, paste("Peak,", tN), pos = 1, cex = 0.9)
mtext("Population", side = 3, line = 0.2, adj = 0, cex = 0.8)
mtext("Year", side = 1, outer = TRUE, line = 0.3, cex = 0.8)
par(op)








Figure 17.2: The world’s net reproduction rate (top), annual births (middle) and population (bottom), estimates 1950–2023 and UN medium projection 2024–2100. The dashed vertical line marks the year the NRR reaches 1. Source: UN World Population Prospects 2024.







Added · new My reading of the UN data. World births are fairly flat from the late 1980s on (the UN notes they “remained stable at around 140 million since the late 1980s,” WPP 2022, p. 13), so the exact year of the birth peak is not well defined.
The world fits the pattern, with a twist. In the UN’s projection, the world NRR reaches replacement in the mid-2030s and population peaks in the mid-2080s, a lag of almost 50 years. Births have stayed between about 130 and 145 million a year since the late 1980s, so in the data the birth “peak” is less a peak than the top of a long, flat hill. Part of the extra lag reflects the features above: the UN assumes life expectancy keeps rising and fertility levels off just below replacement. Part reflects the fact that the world is a mix of countries at very different stages, so it is not one smooth Coale-style decline.


17.5.4 Try it: the peak-population app


Added · new This is the app Josh built for Goldstein and Cassidy (2024) (research/peak-population-shiny, June 2026 version). It needs functions and data from his peakpop package, so I added a global.R that copies the package’s projection, rescaling, analytic and plotting functions and the bundled WPP 2024 world schedules (world_wpp2024_Fx_Lx.csv). Exported with Shinylive to apps/peak_pop. The image is the app’s own plot, drawn with its code at the default settings with the time slider moved to 50 (it starts at −50, with almost nothing drawn); headless Chrome hung on the live app. The app’s sidebar lists its own six exercises; my questions overlap with its first, third and fourth.
The app projects a population, using the world’s 2024 age schedules, in which the NRR falls by a fixed percentage \(k\) each year (the Coale scenario), crossing replacement at time 0. You can also make life expectancy rise at rate \(\rho\), add “extra curvature” so that fertility decline slows down, and show the formulas’ predicted peaks next to the exact projection. A second tab lets you draw your own NRR path. Press play on the time slider to run the projection. It opens in a new tab.



The peak-population app’s plot at its default settings (k = −1.5%, constant life expectancy) with the time slider at 50. Click to open the app in a new tab.


Open the peak-population app in a new tab ↗
Before you change each setting, write down what you expect to happen. Then check.

Does the speed of decline matter? At \(k = -1.5\%\), births peak about 14 years before replacement and population about 26 years after. Predict what happens to each peak if fertility falls faster (\(k = -2\%\)) or more slowly (\(k = -1\%\)). Then try it.
Longer lives. Set \(\rho\) to 0.2% (life expectancy rising about 1.5 years per decade). Which peak moves, births or population, and by roughly how much? Does the answer depend on \(k\)?
A stall. On the “Custom NRR” tab, make fertility level off before it reaches replacement (raise the anchors at \(t = -30\) and \(t = -15\) to about 1.1). Before you look, predict whether the population peak comes earlier or later than Coale’s formula says.

title: 17  Population Projection, Age Pyramids, and “Our Shrinking Future?”
text:
17.6 The ingredients of a forecast
Every projection needs three sets of assumptions: future fertility, future mortality and future migration. The “Our Shrinking Future?” lectures planned one topic for each.

17.6.1 Fertility: the postponement transition and period fertility


Added · from readings SSA 2023, Fertility, pp. 2–5 and Table 1.1; CBO 2023, p. 3.
The total fertility rate in a given year is a period measure: it adds up that year’s birth rates at every age, as if one woman lived through all of them. The Social Security actuaries explain the distinction with another measure, completed cohort fertility:






In their own words



“The period TFR speaks to the birth rates of women at various ages in a given calendar year and is strongly influenced by economic and other factors affecting birth rates during that year. The completed cohort TFR answers the question: ‘how many children will women born in a given year have over their lifetime?’” (SSA, Long-Range Demographic Assumptions for the 2023 Trustees Report, Fertility, p. 2)


The two can tell different stories when the timing of births changes. If women in their twenties start postponing births to their thirties, then for a while fewer births happen each year, and the period TFR falls, even if each woman eventually has just as many children. Demographers call this a tempo effect: “a temporary drop in the TFR due to a delay in childbearing to older ages.” When the postponement stops, the period TFR bounces back. The long shift toward later childbearing in rich countries is sometimes called the postponement transition.


Added · new The 2023 and 2024 values are from the World Bank (the file is data/us_tfr_worldbank_1960_2024.csv, used in ch. 7). The assumptions are from SSA 2023 (Table 1.1; the 2.0 ultimate is reached in 2056), CBO 2023 (p. 3) and, for the Census Bureau’s 2017 projections, as reported by SSA 2023 (Fertility, p. 4).
Tempo matters a great deal for U.S. forecasts. The U.S. period TFR fell from 2.12 in 2007 to 1.64 in 2020, a record low. Is that a temporary postponement, or a lasting drop in family size? The forecasters disagree (Figure 17.3):

Social Security’s actuaries assume the TFR will climb back to 2.0 by 2056, “consistent with an ultimate completed cohort fertility rate of 2.0.” Their reasons: women’s reported birth expectations remain “well above 2.00,” which “strongly suggests that the current reduction in the TFR will not be permanent,” and “the cultural and economic climate in the U.S. makes it highly unlikely that our TFR will remain below a level of 1.7 for any sustained period.”
The CBO assumes the TFR rises from 1.66 to 1.75 by 2030 and stays there, as birth rates for women 30 to 49 rise while those for younger women fall, “consistent with the trends of delayed childbearing and rising average age of mothers.”
The Census Bureau’s 2017 projections held the TFR almost constant, at 1.83 in 2060.



Show the R code
ssa <- data.frame(year = c(2021:2032, 2035, 2040, 2045, 2050, 2055, 2060),
                  tfr = c(1.663, 1.686, 1.704, 1.723, 1.742, 1.763, 1.785, 1.808,
                          1.833, 1.857, 1.869, 1.881, 1.920, 1.974, 1.996, 2.000,
                          2.000, 2.000))
cbo <- data.frame(year = c(2021, 2023, 2030, 2053), tfr = c(1.66, 1.66, 1.75, 1.75))
op <- par(mar = c(4, 4.5, 1, 1), las = 1)
plot(us_tfr$year, us_tfr$tfr, type = "n", xlim = c(1960, 2078), ylim = c(1.4, 3.8),
     xlab = "Year", ylab = "Total fertility rate")
abline(h = 2.1, col = "grey80")
text(1990, 2.1, "about replacement (2.1)", pos = 3, cex = 0.8, col = col_grey)
lines(us_tfr$year, us_tfr$tfr, lwd = 2.5)
lines(ssa$year, ssa$tfr, lwd = 2.5, lty = 2, col = col_y)
lines(cbo$year, cbo$tfr, lwd = 2.5, lty = 2, col = col_c)
points(2060, 1.83, pch = 17, col = col_grow, cex = 1.3)
text(2061, 2.0, "SSA", col = col_y, pos = 4, cex = 0.85)
text(2045, 1.75, "CBO", col = col_c, pos = 1, cex = 0.85)
text(2061, 1.80, "Census (2017)", col = col_grow, pos = 4, cex = 0.8)
text(1985, 1.62, "Period TFR (data)", cex = 0.85)
par(op)








Figure 17.3: U.S. period total fertility rate, 1960–2024, and the long-run assumptions of three federal forecasters. Sources: World Bank (TFR); SSA 2023 intermediate assumption (Table 1.1); CBO 2023; Census Bureau 2017 projections as reported by SSA 2023.





The most recent data have not been kind to the rebound story: the World Bank series puts the U.S. TFR at about 1.62 in 2023 and 1.63 in 2024, below the SSA path.


Added · from readings Vollset et al. 2020, pp. 1286–1288 and 1301; UN, WPP 2022, Box III.1, p. 33; UN, WPP 2024, Box 2.1, p. 19.
The same question, multiplied across the world, is the biggest source of disagreement among global forecasters. The UN assumes that in low-fertility countries fertility will rebound somewhat, an assumption “informed by trends from 39 countries that have experienced declines in total fertility below 2 children per woman, followed by a subsequent rebound,” and “consistent with an expectation of continued progress towards gender equality and women’s empowerment.” The IHME team led by Stein Emil Vollset, writing in The Lancet in 2020, criticized this. They modeled completed cohort fertility instead of the period TFR, precisely because cohort fertility is “much less affected by the delay of childbearing that occurs as females become more educated, which leads the period measure of the TFR to initially decline to low levels and then increase.” Between 1965 and 2017, in countries with below-replacement fertility, the period TFR rose in 29.4 percent of country-years, but completed cohort fertility in only 13.9 percent. Their conclusion is blunt:






In their own words



“Perhaps the most important determinant of world population in our 2100 forecasts was the rate of fertility that countries moved towards once they reached a rate lower than the replacement level of 2·1. Even differences in the post-transition TFR as small as 0·1 births per female for populations with a rate already lower than replacement level translated into 528 million (95% UI 421–573) more people on the planet in 2100.” (Vollset et al. 2020, p. 1301)




17.6.2 Mortality: the future of longevity


Added · from readings SSA 2023, Mortality, pp. 3–7 and 11–13; CBO 2023, p. 4; UN, WPP 2024, Key messages, p. VIII.
How long will people live? The Social Security actuaries call mortality the assumption “subject to uncertainty that is possibly greater than any other variable used in the Trustees’ assumptions.” They describe the debate this way: “Some demographers argue that life expectancy is potentially limitless and that rates of mortality reduction will match or exceed historical trends indefinitely into the future. Others believe that biological limitations make mortality improvement more difficult to achieve in the future.”
On one side, the actuaries cite the argument by Jim Oeppen and James Vaupel (2002) that life expectancy in the “best nation” has risen in a straight line and will keep doing so. On the other, they note that the oldest verified human lived to 122, a record that “shows no signs of extending significantly,” and that the big sources of past progress (antibiotics, clean water, access to primary care, the spread of Medicare and Medicaid) will contribute less in the future. U.S. history shows how uneven progress has been. Death rates at ages 65 and over fell 1.79 percent a year from 1999 to 2009 but only 0.63 percent a year from 2009 to 2019. In its intermediate scenario, Social Security assumes death rates at ages 65 and over will fall about 0.67 percent a year from 2019 to 2097, a bit slower than the 0.78 percent average for 1900–2019.
The CBO projects U.S. life expectancy at birth to rise from 77.8 years in 2023 to 82.3 in 2053. It also notes that for Americans aged 15 to 44, death rates have recently risen, “driven primarily by deaths from suicide and drug overdoses (particularly opioids).” Globally, the UN projects life expectancy rising from 73.3 years in 2024 to about 77.4 in 2054, and by the late 2050s more than half of all deaths will occur at age 80 or older.
For the timing of the peak, longevity is a brake on decline. In the countries whose populations have already peaked, the UN notes that falling mortality is “the only demographic component projected to contribute positively to population change,” but it “will compensate for only one third of the negative effect of fertility.”


17.6.3 Migration and the future population of the United States


Added · from readings Census Bureau press release CB23-189 (2023); CBO 2023, p. 1; UN, WPP 2024, pp. 23, 43; Vollset et al. 2020, pp. 1302–1303.

Added · new The 333 million figure for 2022 is my inference from the release (226 million in 2100 is “roughly 107 million lower than the 2022 estimate”). The release does not give the share 65+ for the low-immigration scenario.
Different levels of immigration, the Census Bureau notes, “could change the projection of the population in that year by as much as 209 million people.” In every scenario, the country gets older: in the main series, people 65 and over outnumber children under 18 from 2029 on.
The CBO tells the same story over a shorter horizon. It projects the population (measured as the “Social Security area population”) growing from 336 million in 2023 to 373 million in 2053, just 0.3 percent a year, “about one-third the pace experienced from 1983 to 2022.” Immigration accounts for about three-quarters of growth in the first decade, and, as deaths come to exceed births, “accounts for all population growth beginning in 2042.” The UN reaches a similar verdict: without immigration, “the population of the United States of America would likely peak already in the mid-2030s instead of continuing to grow until the end of the century.”


Added · new Josh’s calendar note for this lecture asks about “demographic drivers (Mexico?),” i.e., falling fertility in sending countries. None of the readings discusses it, so I have not written it up.
Could immigration rescue the countries that are shrinking? The UN thinks not, in the long run: “International migration alone, however, cannot offset population decline or population ageing in the long term and should not be seen as a ‘solution’ to what is ultimately a universal and irreversible process: the demographic transition.” Vollset and coauthors are more enthusiastic, calling “liberal immigration with effective assimilation” the “optimal strategy for economic growth, fiscal stability, and geopolitical security” for rich, low-fertility countries, while noting that the supply of migrants may shrink as sending countries develop.

title: 17  Population Projection, Age Pyramids, and “Our Shrinking Future?”
text:
17.7 Comparing the forecasters


Added · from readings UN, WPP 2022, Key messages and pp. 27–31; UN, WPP 2024, Key messages, pp. 3, 34; Vollset et al. 2020, pp. 1285 and 1297.
The world forecasts agree closely until about 2050. After that they diverge, mainly because of what they assume about fertility (Figure 17.4).

UN, 2022: 9.7 billion in 2050 and 10.4 billion in 2100, with a peak “during the 2080s” and about a 50 percent chance the peak comes before 2100.
UN, 2024: a peak of about 10.3 billion in the mid-2080s and 10.2 billion in 2100, with an 80 percent chance of a peak this century. The revision is “due to several factors including lower-than-expected levels of fertility in recent years in some of the world’s largest countries, particularly China.”
IHME (Vollset et al. 2020): a peak of 9.73 billion in 2064, falling to 8.79 billion in 2100, with global TFR at 1.66 in 2100. India, Nigeria, China, the USA and Pakistan would be the five largest countries, and 23 countries, including Japan, Thailand and Spain, would shrink by more than half.
Wittgenstein Centre (2023): 9.9 billion in 2100, now close to the UN.



Show the R code
w22 <- wpp_get("World", 2022); w24 <- wpp_get("World", 2024)
op <- par(mar = c(4, 4.5, 1, 1), las = 1)
plot(w24$Time, w24$Pop / 1e6, type = "n", xlim = c(1950, 2105), ylim = c(2, 11),
     xlab = "Year", ylab = "World population (billions)")
rect(2024, 0, 2110, 12, col = "grey94", border = NA)
lines(w22$Time[w22$Time >= 2022], w22$Pop[w22$Time >= 2022] / 1e6,
      lwd = 2.5, lty = 2, col = col_grow)
lines(w24$Time, w24$Pop / 1e6, lwd = 2.5, col = col_y)
ihme <- data.frame(year = c(2017, 2064, 2100), pop = c(7.64, 9.73, 8.79))
lines(ihme$year, ihme$pop, lty = 3, col = col_c)
points(ihme$year, ihme$pop, pch = 19, col = col_c)
text(2100, 10.75, "UN 2022", col = col_grow, pos = 2, cex = 0.85)
text(2100, 9.75, "UN 2024", col = col_y, pos = 2, cex = 0.85)
text(2100, 8.79, "IHME 2020", col = col_c, pos = 1, cex = 0.85)
text(1955, 10.5, "Estimates to 2023;\nprojections shaded", pos = 4, cex = 0.8,
     col = col_grey)
par(op)








Figure 17.4: World population, estimates and three forecasts: the UN’s 2022 and 2024 medium projections (lines) and the IHME reference forecast published in 2020 (points: 2017 start, 2064 peak, 2100). Sources: UN World Population Prospects 2022 and 2024; Vollset et al. (2020).







Added · from readings UN, WPP 2022, pp. 3, 31; Vollset et al. 2020, p. 1287.
The disagreement is partly about methods. The UN projects each country’s fertility from its own history and the experience of other countries, with time as the only driver; the IHME models fertility as a function of women’s education and access to contraception, so its forecasts build in the expectation that faster schooling means faster fertility decline. Each side has criticized the other. Vollset and coauthors call the UN’s models “sophisticated curve-fitting exercises,” while the UN notes that “independent reviews have suggested that the IHME projections may overstate the likely pace of fertility decline.”
Two lessons follow. First, the near future is fairly certain. As the UN puts it, “the size of the world population in the near future is relatively certain because the size and age structure of the population over the next few decades are largely the result of demographic processes that have already taken place in the recent past. In particular, most of the women whose offspring will contribute to the population growth through 2050 are already alive.” That is the projection matrix at work. Second, the long-run future depends on a few numbers we do not know, above all the level at which fertility settles once it falls below replacement.

title: 17  Population Projection, Age Pyramids, and “Our Shrinking Future?”
text:
17.8 Key ideas

A projection matrix (Leslie matrix) moves a population forward one step: the first row adds up babies born to each age group, and the subdiagonal moves survivors up one group. Projection is matrix multiplication, \(P(t+1) = A\,P(t)\).
With constant rates, any starting population converges to a stable age structure and grows exponentially. The growth rate largely determines the shape of the pyramid; survival matters less.
Momentum: a young population keeps growing for decades after fertility falls to replacement, and an old one keeps shrinking after fertility recovers.
In a steady fertility decline (the Coale scenario), births peak about half a generation before replacement and population peaks about 25 years after. Rising longevity and leveling fertility stretch the lag to 35–40 years.
The period TFR can fall temporarily when births are postponed (a tempo effect). Whether recent low fertility is postponement or lasting decline is the key unknown in U.S. and world forecasts.
Official forecasts use the same cohort-component arithmetic; they differ in their assumptions about fertility, longevity and migration. For the United States, immigration decides whether and when the population peaks.

title: 17  Population Projection, Age Pyramids, and “Our Shrinking Future?”
text:
17.9 Check your understanding


Added · new All questions are new. None reuses the slides’ in-class matrix examples, the Peru practice problem, or the 2021 lab’s self-study exercise.

One step by hand. A population has 40 young, 40 middle-aged and 20 old, with \(F = (0.2, 0.8, 0.1)\), \(S_1 = 0.95\) and \(S_2 = 0.9\). Compute the population one step later. Did it get younger or older? Did it grow?
Structural zeros. Suppose we use 10-year age groups but still project 20 years at a time. Why would the simple projection matrix no longer work? (Hint: think about who becomes whom.)
Predict, then check. Before computing anything, predict whether the stable age structure of the worked example would be older or younger if \(F_2\) fell from 0.9 to 0.6. Explain using the conclusion that “the growth rate largely determines the age pyramid.”
Momentum in words. The UN says two-thirds of the world’s population growth to 2050 would happen even if fertility fell immediately to replacement. Explain to a friend, without using matrices, why.
Births before replacement. Explain why, if fertility falls steadily, births must peak before the NRR reaches 1. Use the idea that at replacement, births equal births one generation earlier.
Reading Table 17.2. Japan’s population peaked about 35 years after its NRR fell below 1. What is Coale’s prediction for the lag? Name two reasons the actual lag was longer.
Tempo. Suppose every American woman decided to have her children two years later than women do now, but the same number of them. What would happen to the period TFR during the years of the shift, and afterward? What would happen to completed cohort fertility?
Whose assumption? Social Security assumes an ultimate U.S. TFR of 2.0 and the CBO 1.75. Which assumption makes Social Security’s finances look better in the long run, and why? (Use the old-age dependency ratio from Chapter 8.)

text:
18.1 Why migrate?
The simple answer is that life is better there than here. Economists and demographers sort the reasons into:
But a wage gap alone explains surprisingly little about who actually moves. Several other factors matter a great deal:
The models in this chapter were built to explain migration from the countryside to the cities of poor countries. But they apply more widely. The same logic of incentives and decisions might help us think about today’s flows of asylum seekers, or about domestic migration and homelessness. The common feature is people making decisions in response to incentives.

title: 18  Why People Move: Cities, Borders, and Development
text:
Pull effects: higher wages, a better life.
Push effects: persecution, famine, war.



Proximity, both physical and cultural.
Social networks: friends and family who have already moved.
Frictions and transaction costs: the money, information, and risk involved in moving.
Policy: who is allowed to move, and on what terms.

title: 18  Why People Move: Cities, Borders, and Development
text:
18.2 A world of cities

18.2.1 From 2 megacities to 28
In 1950 the world had 2 cities of more than 10 million people. By 2014 it had 28. In your lifetimes, the world flipped: before the late 2000s, most people lived in rural areas, and today most live in cities.
How fast do cities grow? Urban growth is the sum of the urban population’s natural increase (births minus deaths) and net migration into cities. Net migration typically adds about 1 percent per year. Table 18.1 shows how much faster urban populations have grown than populations as a whole.




Table 18.1: Annual growth rates (%) of total and urban populations. MDCs = more developed countries; LDCs = less developed countries. Source: lecture slides (2024), based on UN estimates and projections.













Region

At 3.7 percent per year, the urban population of the developing world was doubling about every 19 years.


18.2.2 Governments push back
Many governments are unhappy with where their people live. According to the UN’s World Population Policies 2013, 60 percent of all governments wanted a major change in the spatial distribution of their population. That included 80 percent of governments in the least developed countries and 29 percent in the more developed regions. A growing share have active policies to slow migration from rural to urban areas: 38 percent of all countries in 1996, 70 percent in 2005, and 80 percent in 2013. In the least developed countries the figure reached 88 percent.
Megacities in poor countries raise real concerns: pollution, unemployment, and enormous demands for infrastructure. But keep in mind that governments may have interests of their own.


18.2.3 A brief history of theories
Economists’ views of urban migration have swung back and forth:

1950s and early 1960s. Cities are the manufacturing base and the engines of economic growth. Migration is a natural accompaniment of economic development, and a good thing.
Late 1960s to early 1980s (Todaro). Urban growth harms welfare. Rural areas deserve more policy attention, as an antidote to the “urban bias” in subsidies and programs.
Since the 1980s (Todaro–Harris). A “balanced perspective”: urban growth can be positive for both city and countryside.

title: 18  Why People Move: Cities, Borders, and Development
section: 18.3 Todaro’s first model: why move to a city with no jobs?
text:
18.3 Todaro’s first model: why move to a city with no jobs?

18.3.1 The Nairobi paradox
Michael Todaro set out to explain a puzzle he saw in Kenya in the 1960s: lots of unemployment in the cities, but still strong migration from the countryside to the cities. If cities have no jobs, why keep coming?
Kenya’s government tried a direct solution. It set up a “tripartite agreement” among itself, private employers, and trade unions, with the avowed intention of wiping out unemployment in the greater Nairobi area. Employers agreed to increase their employment immediately by 15 percent. In return, the unions agreed to forgo demands for general wage increases. What do you think happened?






In their own words



“The effort was a colossal failure. The private employers did take on additional workers and this acted like a magnet attracting new workers into the urban labor markets; in a few months the working forces in most of the private establishments had dropped to their former levels through attrition not offset by new hires. In the end, the volume of unemployment, as a consequence of the expansion of the modern labor force in response to the prospect of more jobs was probably increased rather than decreased.” (Frederick Harbison, as quoted by Todaro 1969, who added the italics; shown in lecture)




18.3.2 Migrating for expected earnings
Todaro’s key idea is that migration responds to expected earnings, not to the wage alone. His assumptions:

Urban wages are fixed at \(w_U\), above the market level. Why? Minimum-wage legislation, the political influence of trade unions, and government employment.
Rural wages are fixed at \(w_R\). (Todaro–Harris will relax this.)
The chance of getting a job in the city is \(e\): the number employed, \(E\), divided by the urban labor force, which is the employed plus the unemployed: \[
e = \frac{E}{E + UE}.
\]
People move to the city if the expected urban wage beats the rural wage: \[
e\, w_U > w_R .
\]



18.3.3 Dismal dynamics
Suppose rural wages are $10 and urban wages $100, and the city starts with no unemployment. Then \(e = 1\) and the expected urban wage is $100, ten times the rural wage. People pour into the city. Because the urban wage is fixed, employers hire no more workers than before, so every newcomer joins the unemployed, and the chance of getting a job falls. Migration stops only when the expected urban wage has fallen to the rural wage:
\[
w_R = e\, w_U \quad\Longrightarrow\quad e = \frac{w_R}{w_U}.
\]
The share of urban job-seekers who are employed ends up equal to the ratio of rural to urban wages. With a wage ratio of 1 to 10, 90 percent of the urban labor force is unemployed.
Figure 18.1 shows the urban labor market. Employers hire \(E\) workers at the fixed wage; the urban labor force \(S_U\) is set by migration; the gap is urban unemployment.








Figure 18.1: Todaro’s first model. At the fixed urban wage, employers hire E workers (where the fixed wage meets urban labor demand). The urban labor force S_U is set by migration, so that the chance of a job, E / S_U, equals w_R / w_U. Right: creating urban jobs shifts demand out (dashed). Employment rises, but with w_R / w_U = 1/10, each new job draws ten more people into the city, so unemployment rises too.





What happens if the government creates jobs in the city, shifting urban labor demand to the right? Employment rises, but so does unemployment. If the ratio of urban to rural wages is 10 to 1, creating one urban job creates nine new urban unemployed. Every newly employed worker must be matched by enough additional job-seekers to keep the chance of a job at 1 in 10. And the costs of a bigger city follow: more congestion, more housing problems, more pollution.


18.3.4 Like Malthus
Todaro’s model has the same stubborn character as the Malthusian model of Chapter 3:

Any improvement in city life is erased by population growth, here through migration rather than births.
The equilibrium is very stable. In Malthus, the wage is set by \(b(w^*) = d(w^*)\). In Todaro, the unemployment rate is set by \(w_{\text{rural}}/w_{\text{urban}}\).

The policy implications of Todaro’s first theory:

It is worth trying to slow urban growth.
It is worth trying to increase rural wages.
It is worth trying to liberalize urban wages.

title: 18  Why People Move: Cities, Borders, and Development
text:
18.4 From Todaro to Todaro–Harris
In 1970, John Harris and Michael Todaro published a two-sector version of the model in the American Economic Review. It was later voted one of the top 20 articles ever published in that journal. Migration still depends on expected urban wages, and wages are still fixed in the cities. But now rural wages can vary: as people leave the countryside, the workers who remain earn more. That one change turns a dismal model into a more hopeful one.
We build it up in three steps, using a single labor market diagram (Figure 18.2). The total labor force is the width of the box. Urban workers are counted from the left, and urban labor demand (\(D_U\), blue) slopes down from the left. Rural workers are counted from the right, so rural labor demand (\(D_R\), orange) is drawn “backwards,” rising to the left.








Figure 18.2: Building the Todaro–Harris model. Urban workers are counted from the left, rural workers from the right; the width of each panel is the total labor force of 100. (1) Perfect competition: workers move until urban and rural wages are equal, with no unemployment. (2) A rigid urban wage with employment ‘enforced’: fewer urban jobs, and the extra workers crowd into the countryside, lowering the rural wage. (3) Todaro–Harris: migrants compare the rural wage with the expected urban wage (the grey curve); the gap between the employed and the urban labor force is urban unemployment. The red dashed line is the fixed urban wage of 20. Illustrative linear demand curves from lecture: urban demand N = 112 − 5w, rural demand N = 100 − 3w.





Step 1: perfect competition. If both wages are flexible, workers move until urban and rural wages are equal. In the example, 42 of the 100 workers end up in the city, both earn 14, and there is no unemployment. This allocation also maximizes total output: the last worker adds as much in the city as in the countryside. (Suppose instead we started with too few urban workers. Which way would people move, and what would happen to wages?)
Step 2: a rigid urban wage, with employment “enforced.” Now fix the urban wage at 20, above the market level. Employers hire only 12 workers. If everyone else had to stay in the countryside, the extra workers would crowd into farming and the rural wage would fall to 4. Urban and rural wages now differ, but there is still no unemployment.
Step 3: the full Todaro–Harris model. But workers don’t have to stay put. They compare the rural wage with the expected urban wage, \(w_U \times E/(E+UE)\), which falls as more job-seekers crowd into the city. Because \(E\) is fixed, the expected urban wage traces out a curve shaped like \(Y = 1/X\), a hyperbola (grey in the figure). Equilibrium is where it meets rural labor demand: \(w_R^* = w_U\, e^*\). In the example, the city has 12 employed and 14.8 unemployed, an urban unemployment rate of 55 percent, and the rural wage rises to 8.94, equal to the expected urban wage.

18.4.1 Creating jobs, revisited
Now repeat Kenya’s experiment in the Todaro–Harris world: create urban jobs, shifting urban demand to the right (panel 4). In the example, urban employment rises from 12 to 27. More people come to the city. But because they leave the countryside, the rural wage rises from 8.94 to 13.42, which makes the countryside more attractive and holds back the flood. The number unemployed in the city actually falls slightly, from 14.8 to 13.2, and the urban unemployment rate falls from 55 to 33 percent.
This is the optimistic view. If we develop the urban economy, it:

increases the number of urban workers,
increases rural wages, and
decreases the urban unemployment rate.

The Todaro–Harris model is not so gloomy. Countries can partly escape the “Todaro trap” because rising rural wages counteract the appeal of more jobs in the city.






Try it



The Todaro–Harris app is in Chapter 15. Open it in a new tab: the Todaro–Harris app ↗. Before moving any slider, predict: if you raise rural labor demand (for example, through better farming technology), what happens to the number of urban unemployed? Then check.




18.4.2 But…
Harris and Todaro still advocated keeping some barriers to rural-to-urban migration. Their idea is that total output can be higher with fewer unemployed in the cities. This is an example where a social planner would choose something different from what individuals choose. Does that mean markets are failing?
Models matter: both Todaro’s model and the Todaro–Harris model are still influential. The empirical evidence is still unclear. Newer models add an informal sector, the matching of skills to jobs, and other benefits of cities.

title: 18  Why People Move: Cities, Borders, and Development
text:
18.5 Gains from a borderless world
Todaro and Harris studied migration within countries. The same logic of expected earnings applies across borders, and there the gaps are far larger. Chapter 15 presents Michael Clemens’s argument that removing barriers to international migration could raise world GDP by 50 to 150 percent, his back-of-the-envelope calculation, and the two-country diagram of who gains and who loses. Here we add some of the evidence and objections Clemens discusses.


Added · from readings This section draws on Clemens 2011, pp. 83–84, 89–95, and 98–101. None of it is in the slides or in Chapter 15.

18.5.1 Unmet demand
How many people would move if they could? The Gallup World Poll found that “more than 40 percent of adults in the poorest quartile of countries ‘would like to move permanently to another country’ if they had the opportunity, including 60 percent or more of adults in Guyana and Sierra Leone.” The U.S. Diversity Visa Lottery received 272 applications for every available slot in 2010.
The gains can be dramatic even from today’s limited migration. Among Haitians who live either in the United States or in Haiti and who live on more than $10 a day at U.S. prices, Clemens reports, “four out of five live in the United States.” Emigration from Haiti, he argues, “may be at least as important as any economic change that has occurred within Haiti” for reducing Haitians’ poverty.


18.5.2 “Brain drain” and remittances
Discussions of emigration and development usually turn quickly to two topics: the “brain drain” of skilled workers, and the money migrants send home. Clemens argues that both are second-order compared with the gains to the migrants themselves.
On the brain drain, he objects even to the name:






In their own words



“Externalities like these are often assumed to be so pervasive that the literature refers to skilled migration with a pejorative catchphrase—‘brain drain’—embodying the assumption. (To see why economists should avoid this term, picture reading a journal article on female labor force participation that calls it the ‘family abandonment rate.’)” (Clemens 2011, p. 89)


The most common worry concerns doctors and nurses. But if their departure were a major cause of poor health, the African countries losing the most health workers should have the worst health. “In fact,” Clemens writes, “those countries have systematically better health conditions.” On remittances, which were approaching $400 billion a year, he argues that they are mostly transfers within households that happen to cross a border. What matters for welfare is the migrant’s gain in income, whether it is spent abroad or sent home.


18.5.3 Who loses, and should they be compensated?
The two-country diagram in Chapter 15 shows that workers in the rich country can lose. Clemens makes two points about this. First, the losses in practice have been small even after large openings. Wages of whites in South Africa did not fall much after apartheid ended, despite the removal of huge barriers for a population that outnumbered them six to one; and unlimited labor mobility from some Eastern European countries to Britain did not cause important declines in British wages. In the other direction, mass emigration may have raised wages in Mexico by about 8 percent between 1970 and 2000.
Second, he distinguishes pecuniary externalities, which work through prices (such as lower wages from more competition), from technical externalities, such as pollution. Standard welfare economics doesn’t justify restricting a decision because of its pecuniary effects: “no economist would argue” for taxing people who move between cities, or women entering the labor force, because they modestly lower others’ wages. That doesn’t mean helping low-wage workers is undesirable, only that the case rests on equity rather than efficiency. Several economists have proposed ways to compensate those who lose, such as charging immigrants a fee ($50,000 is a figure that often comes up) or auctioning work permits.


18.5.4 Politics
Clemens wrote in 2011 that a large expansion of emigration “may thus seem politically impractical, and within a time frame of a few years, this objection holds some force.” In lecture we asked: was this writing before Trump? (His reminder about Poland and the German border, quoted in Chapter 15, is his answer to the skeptics.)
crumbs: Optional chapters
18  Why People Move: Cities, Borders, and Development

title: 18  Why People Move: Cities, Borders, and Development
text:
18.6 Does development reduce migration?

18.6.1 What is the goal?
Suppose a rich country wants fewer immigrants. Notice first that this is a different goal from the one in the last section. If the goal is to maximize the average standard of living for everyone, the answer is open borders. Why might a country want fewer immigrants instead, and what are some good and bad reasons?
If the goal is fewer immigrants, there are two broad approaches:

Walls: build a wall, or make life unpleasant for immigrants.
Aid: send development aid, or in other ways try to raise wages in the sending country.

The second approach sounds humane and sensible. Raise incomes at home, and people won’t need to leave.


Added · from readings The policy quotes are from Clemens 2014, pp. 1–3, quoting the White House (1993), the U.S. State Department (1993), and the European Commission (2005).
This idea has a long history in policy. As President Bill Clinton signed side agreements to the North American Free Trade Agreement in 1993, he predicted that “as the benefits of economic growth are spread in Mexico … there will be less illegal immigration because more Mexicans will be able to support their children by staying home.” Mexico’s president, Carlos Salinas, agreed that “higher wages in Mexico … will mean fewer migrants to the United States and Canada.” Announcing a large aid package for Africa in 2005, European Commission president José Manuel Barroso said that immigration “can only be addressed effectively in the long term through an ambitious and coordinated Development cooperation to fight its root causes.”


18.6.2 Up, then down
Throughout this course we have seen relationships that go up and then down: population size and well-being (optimum population theory), resource harvesting (the Malthusian harvest model), optimal fertility (Lee and government tax and benefit profiles), and the demographic transition itself. Migration may be another.
In the demographic transition, population growth rises and then falls because growth is births minus deaths, and births respond with a lag. In a mobility transition, migration rises and then falls because migration depends on push, pull, and costs. As a country develops:

the pull of better wages abroad goes down,
but push may go up, and
the costs of moving may go down.

The geographer Wilbur Zelinsky proposed a “mobility transition” in 1971, with international migration rising and then falling over the phases of development. (For Zelinsky the phases are periods of time; for Clemens, they are levels of income.) Zelinsky’s theory was complicated: phases related to development, and not just international migration but frontier settlement, rural-urban migration, urban-urban migration, and “circulation” of all kinds.


18.6.3 What the data show
Clemens (2014) assembles the best available data: World Bank counts of people living outside their country of birth for 1960–2000, and UN counts for 1990–2010.


Added · from readings Clemens 2014, pp. 3–9 and 26–30. Page numbers for Clemens 2014 refer to the IZA working-paper version (Discussion Paper 8592), a draft of the handbook chapter; the published chapter (pp. 152–185) wasn’t available.






In their own words



“In all years, there is no hint of a negative relationship between income and emigrant stock between PPP income per capita of roughly $600 (that of today’s Niger or Ethiopia) and about $7,500 (today’s Albania or Colombia). In this range of income, in fact, the relationship is positive.” (Clemens 2014, pp. 4–5)


Above about $7,000 to $8,000 per person (at purchasing power parity), the relationship turns negative. Early in the period, the middle-income countries had emigrant stocks about 3 percentage points larger than the poorest countries; by 2000 the gap had grown to 9 points. Flows show the same inverted U, turning down at about $5,000 to $6,000 per person. “In poor countries,” Clemens concludes, “more development means more migration, not less.”
How long would the up-slope last? Clemens estimates the time for a country to reach PPP$7,000 per person. Growing at a healthy 2 percent per year, a country starting at $500 (like Niger or Burundi) would take 133 years, and one starting at $2,000 (like Cambodia or Zambia) 63 years. Even at 3 percent per year, it would take 89 and 42 years. For comparison, the average country grew 1.8 percent per year in 1960–2000. “The migration transition is a process of generations.”
The 2019 lecture replicated Clemens’s cross-country pattern with World Bank data for 2000. The levels may not be exactly right, but the patterns look similar: a linear trend is nearly flat, but a quadratic or a local smoother shows the hump.


18.6.4 Six reasons migration can rise with development
Why would development increase emigration? Clemens lists six classes of theory:

The demographic transition. At the onset of development, mortality falls before fertility. Faster population growth, and a bulge of young adults, increase migration. (The number of migrants, yes, because the population is bigger. But what about the rate?)
Credit constraints. Migrants face money costs besides transportation. With perfect credit markets, they could borrow against future earnings, and poverty at the origin wouldn’t matter. Without credit, you can’t move if you can’t afford to now. Development helps through more individual savings, better credit markets, and “chain-borrowing” from family and friends who have already moved.
More information. About jobs, earnings, the cost of living, how to migrate, even marriage markets. The more immigrants there are, the more relevant information flows back, lowering costs and reducing risk. (What’s the difference between Facebook and a letter home?)
Modernization. “The onset of modernization … brings with it a great shaking loose of migrants from the countryside” (Zelinsky 1971). Development “displaces many people from traditional livelihoods and past ways of life. … Most become internal migrants, … [b]ut some always migrate internationally, seeking wider opportunities in more dynamic economies abroad” (Massey 1988).
Increasing inequality. If development raises inequality, it can raise ambitions (the “reference level of satisfactory income”) more than it improves everyday life. The desire for economic mobility translates into geographic movement.
Overcoming immigration hurdles. Destination countries set hurdles: capital, skills, diplomas. If a country doesn’t have an accredited nursing school, it is hard for it to send nurses abroad. Compare the Philippines with Rwanda.



Added · from readings The inferior-goods comparison is from Clemens 2014, p. 10.
None of this contradicts the basic economics of the wage gap. Holding everything else equal, higher wages at home do reduce the incentive to leave. But development never holds everything else equal. Clemens compares this to inferior goods: the existence of goods whose demand falls as income rises doesn’t refute the theory of consumer demand.


18.6.5 Why studies over time disagree
Studies that compare countries at a point in time consistently find the rising part of the hump. Studies that follow countries over time find no consistent pattern. Clemens’s explanation: if the transition takes a century or two, a study following countries for 15 to 25 years sees only a short, nearly straight piece of the curve, rising for some countries and falling for others (Figure 18.3).








Figure 18.3: Why a long mobility transition is hard to see over short periods (after Clemens 2014, Figure 3). The grey curve is a hypothetical transition lasting two centuries. Each colored segment is one country observed for 20 years at a different point in its transition. Across countries, the hump is clear; within any one country over 20 years, the trend looks nearly straight, rising for some and falling for others.







18.6.6 An example: Japanese emigration to Brazil
Japan, once a major sending country, shows the down-slope as it grew rich. Figure 18.4 shows the number of Japanese immigrants to Brazil by period, from the table shown in lecture (taken from Wikipedia).


Show the R code
jb <- data.frame(
  period = c("1906–10", "1911–15", "1916–20", "1921–25", "1926–30", "1931–35", "1936–41",
             "1952–55", "1956–60", "1961–65", "1966–70", "1971–75", "1976–80", "1981–85",
             "1986–90", "1991–93"),
  n = c(1714, 13371, 13576, 11350, 59564, 72661, 16750, 7715, 29727, 9488, 2753, 1992,
        1352, 411, 171, 48))
op <- par(mar = c(5.5, 4.5, 0.5, 0.5))
bp <- barplot(jb$n / 1000, names.arg = jb$period, las = 2, cex.names = 0.75,
              col = "grey60", border = NA, ylab = "Immigrants (thousands)")
par(op)








Figure 18.4: Japanese immigration to Brazil by period, 1906–1993. Periods are mostly five years long (a few are four or six), and there is a gap during World War II. Source: lecture slide (2019), from Wikipedia.







Added · new The interpretation of the Japan series is mine; the lecture slide shows only the table.
Migration peaked in the late 1920s and early 1930s, revived briefly after the war, and dwindled to almost nothing as Japan became one of the world’s richest countries.


18.6.7 Implications
Will faster development in Sub-Saharan Africa reduce migration to Europe? Will sending aid to Central America reduce the “caravans”? The first answer is that it depends on where in the transition a country is. Fostering economic growth in the Czech Republic or Canada might reduce emigration. Fostering economic growth in a poor country might increase it.
Do Clemens’s six reasons apply to Sub-Saharan Africa? To Central America? That is a good exercise to work through, reason by reason.
The conclusions from lecture:

The effect of economic growth on migration depends on the level of development. In rich countries, further growth tends to reduce migration. In poor countries, growth increases migration. In the middle there’s a shift (Mexico? Turkey?).
Unintended consequences. More aid may increase migration. That doesn’t mean a “wall” would work. Perhaps we need to rethink our goals, and focus on maximizing the benefits of migration in both origin and destination.
An unintended consequence of walls. Increased border enforcement under Presidents Bush and Obama increased the stock of undocumented immigrants in the United States. Why? It didn’t discourage the first border crossing, but it greatly discouraged circular, back-and-forth migration. Immigrants became permanent instead of temporary.







In their own words



“To state a fact bluntly, much of the research interest in the mobility transition has been spurred by a broad policy interest in finding ways to deter poor people from turning up at airports and beaches in rich countries. … There is no empirical economic basis for this view, after decades of testing, at least on a timescale that is meaningful to most politicians. The weight of our current evidence is that this view is generally false.” (Clemens 2014, p. 28)

title: 18  Why People Move: Cities, Borders, and Development
text:
18.7 Key ideas

People migrate when life is better there than here, but networks, proximity, costs, and policy shape who actually moves.
In Todaro’s first model, migrants respond to expected urban earnings. In equilibrium the employment rate in the city equals \(w_R/w_U\), and creating urban jobs can raise urban unemployment. Like Malthus, it is a stubborn equilibrium.
In the Todaro–Harris model, rural wages rise as people leave. Creating urban jobs then raises rural wages and lowers the urban unemployment rate: a more optimistic picture.
The gains from international migration go mostly to migrants. Clemens argues that “brain drain,” remittances, and wage effects at the destination are second-order by comparison.
Across countries, emigration rises with income until about PPP$7,000–8,000 per person and falls only after that: a mobility transition. For poor countries, development is likely to increase emigration for generations.

title: 18  Why People Move: Cities, Borders, and Development
text:
18.8 Check your understanding


Added · new The questions are mine. Q1 and Q4 restate questions posed on the 2024 and 2019 slides.

Todaro’s arithmetic. In Todaro’s first model, suppose urban wages are $60 and rural wages $20. What share of the urban labor force is unemployed in equilibrium? If the government creates 1,000 new urban jobs, about how many people move to the city?
Predict, then check. In the Todaro–Harris model, predict what happens to urban unemployment and to rural wages if the fixed urban wage is lowered. Then check your prediction with the app.
Two policies. A government can either subsidize urban employers to hire more workers, or invest in rural roads that raise farm productivity. Compare their effects on urban unemployment in Todaro’s first model and in the Todaro–Harris model.
Migration Malthus? Treat in-migration like births and out-migration like deaths. What plays the role of the wage on the horizontal axis? Would the relationship between a sending country’s income and its net emigration be up-then-down, just up, or just down?
Pecuniary or technical? Classify each as a pecuniary or a technical externality, and explain: (a) immigrants lower the wages of workers with similar skills; (b) a doctor’s emigration leaves a rural clinic without care; (c) newcomers add to traffic congestion.
Reading a hump. A study follows Mexico from 1990 to 2010 and finds that emigration fell as Mexican incomes rose. Does this contradict Clemens’s mobility transition? Why or why not?

title: 19  Fertility and the Economy: The Great Recession and Beyond
text:
19.1 A question from spring 2020
In the spring of 2020, as COVID-19 closed schools and offices, journalists began to speculate about a coming baby boom: couples stuck at home together, with little else to do. Before reading on, make your own prediction. As a result of the pandemic, will fertility
A. go up,
B. go down, or
C. stay about the same, with some people having more children and others fewer?
Economists Melissa Kearney and Phillip Levine thought the “baby boom” story got the mechanism wrong. Such speculation, they wrote, “is based on persistent myths about birth spikes occurring nine months after blizzards or major electricity blackouts,” which “tend not to hold up to statistical examination.” The pandemic was not a long weekend indoors. It was “leading to tremendous economic loss, uncertainty, and insecurity. That is why birth rates will tumble.”
As your slides put it, there’s more to having kids than sex. The economist’s question is what a pandemic does to the costs and benefits of a child. In the language of the cost-of-time model (Chapter 10), a downturn has two effects that pull in opposite directions:
Which one wins is an empirical question, and, as we’ll see, the answer has changed over time. In the longer run, other forces matter too: worries about climate, politics, and now pandemics might mean fewer children; renewed attention to family and the meaning of life might mean more; uncertainty about long-term economic prospects might mean fewer.

title: 19  Fertility and the Economy: The Great Recession and Beyond
text:
Added · from readings Kearney and Levine (2020). The blizzard and blackout myths, and the reference to Udry (1970), are theirs.



An income effect. Families have less income, and if children are a normal good, they want fewer.
A substitution (price) effect. When wages are low or jobs are scarce, the time spent raising a child costs less in forgone earnings, so children become relatively cheaper.




Added · from readings Kearney and Levine (2020).






In their own words



“As any parent will tell you, children come at a cost. They require outlays of money, time, and energy. Certainly, they are also a source of joy and love. In the analytical terms of economic modeling, adults ‘choose’ the quantity of children that maximizes their lifetime well-being subject to the costs associated with childbearing.” (Kearney and Levine 2020)

title: 19  Fertility and the Economy: The Great Recession and Beyond
text:
19.2 Income and substitution effects, revisited

19.2.1 A history that points both ways
Over the long run, U.S. fertility fell from about 7 children per woman in 1800 to about 2 today, with one great exception, the postwar baby boom. In lecture we mark different stretches of this history according to which effect seems to dominate, and ask what was happening to the economy in each. The point is that the sign of the relationship between good times and births has not been constant.


Added · from readings Karaman Örsal and Goldstein (2018), p. 109. The 1948–1975 period of Butz and Ward’s study is from the 2010 working-paper version, p. 3. The study is not on the reading list; it is the source of your slides 15–16.
In the 1970s and 1980s, careful studies found that fertility was, if anything, counter-cyclical. In a classic analysis of the United States from 1948 to 1975, Butz and Ward “concluded that fertility was counter-cyclical, with fertility falling in good times, as the opportunity costs of childbearing rose” (Karaman Örsal and Goldstein 2018, p. 109). In the language of the model, the substitution effect dominated. Good times were the most expensive times to have a child.


19.2.2 The sign flips
Since then, the relationship has flipped. Your slides show results from a study of developed countries by Deniz Karaman Örsal and Joshua Goldstein, published in Population Studies in 2018. In the United States and Austria from 1957 to 1974, years with higher unemployment tended to be followed by higher fertility. From 1975 to 2014, higher unemployment was followed by lower fertility.


Added · from readings Karaman Örsal and Goldstein (2018), pp. 109–115. The plain-language explanations of fixed effects and semi-elasticities are mine.
Here is what the study did:

Data. Each country’s total fertility rate, mostly from the Human Fertility Database, and its unemployment rate, from the OECD. Unemployment is measured the year before the births, “to account for the time between conception and birth” (p. 110).
Countries and years. The main analysis uses the 15 OECD countries with data back to 1957: Austria, Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, the UK, and the USA, for 1957–2014. A check uses 22 countries over a shorter period, 1976–2014.
Method. A regression of (the log of) each country’s TFR on its unemployment rate the year before, comparing each country with itself over time. The coefficient is a semi-elasticity: the percent change in the TFR when unemployment rises by one percentage point. A negative number means pro-cyclical fertility (more unemployment, fewer births); a positive number means counter-cyclical fertility.

Over the whole period, the estimate is −0.048: “when the unemployment rate increases by about one unit (one percentage point) then the fertility rate declines by about 4.8 per cent” (p. 114). When the authors also control for each year’s conditions common to all countries (year fixed effects), the decline is about 1.5 percent.
The key result is what happens when the effect is allowed to differ across periods of four or five years. Your slide 16 is the paper’s Figure 3(a). The estimates are positive, about +0.05 to +0.08, in 1957–60, 1961–65, and 1966–70. They turn slightly negative in 1971–75 (not statistically different from zero), and are clearly negative, about −0.03 to −0.05, in every period since. In the authors’ words, the figure “provides eye-catching evidence of fertility being counter-cyclical until the beginning of the 1970s and pro-cyclical thereafter” (p. 115). The 22-country check, for 1976–2014, finds clearly pro-cyclical fertility from the early 1980s on, and the same holds for women’s and for men’s unemployment separately. Fertility has become pro-cyclical: good times, more children; bad times, fewer.


Added · from readings Karaman Örsal and Goldstein (2018), p. 117. The values above for each period are read off Figure 3(a), so they are approximate.
How big is the effect today? The authors’ summary is that a one-point rise in unemployment “on average reduces the period TFR by about 1.3 per cent according to the fixed effects model and 0.5 per cent according to the first-differenced model when year fixed effects are also taken into account” (p. 117). (The paper writes “a 1 per cent increase in the unemployment rate” here, but it means one percentage point.) Their verdict on the older finding: “the prominent (and controversial) counter-cyclical fertility result found by Butz and Ward (1979) no longer holds in the industrialized world” (p. 117).


Added · from readings On slide 16’s note (“+0.06 means a 1% increase in UE reduces TFR by 6% (e.g., from 2.0 to 1.88)”): the published paper settles it. A negative coefficient means pro-cyclical: β = −0.0477 means a one-point rise in unemployment lowers fertility by about 4.8 percent (p. 114). So the early-period +0.06 means a one-point rise in unemployment raised the TFR by about 6 percent (2.0 to about 2.12). The slide’s example, 2.0 to 1.88, would need a coefficient of −0.06, more negative than any post-1970 estimate. The note has the direction reversed, and “1%” should be “1 percentage point.” Suggested wording: “+0.06 means a 1-point rise in UE raises TFR by 6% (2.0 to 2.12); −0.03 means it lowers TFR by 3% (2.0 to 1.94).”


19.2.3 Why might income effects now dominate?
Your slides suggest several explanations within our models:

Rising fixed costs of children (a higher \(p\)). If the money costs of children rise relative to the time costs, the income effect gains weight. (Recall from Chapter 10: the substitution effect is strongest when the time cost of children is large compared with their money cost.)
Paid childcare, which turns time costs into money costs, shifting \(c\) toward \(p\). Or, equivalently, families think of children as paid for out of income \(I\) rather than out of the mother’s time.
Ratcheting quality. If parents’ standards for what each child should have (the \(q\) of the quantity–quality model) rise in good times and don’t fall in bad times, a downturn squeezes the number of children.

And explanations outside them:

Jobs versus careers for women. The opportunity cost of a child is not just wages forgone today but a career penalty. A recession may lower current wages without lowering the long-run career penalty at all.
A “tempo” artifact, which we take up below.



Added · from readings Karaman Örsal and Goldstein (2018), p. 117, and the 2010 working-paper version, pp. 1–3. The published paper does not discuss parental leave.
The Karaman Örsal–Goldstein study adds two more. The published paper ends with the first: “in the new world of dual-earning couples, economic conditions matter more than ever in the decision to have children” (p. 117). When the household depends on two incomes, losing either job is a blow to income, not a cheap moment to stay home. The second, from the 2010 working-paper version, is the spread of earnings-related parental leave. If benefits depend on prior earnings, it may have “encouraged women who have yet to find permanent positions to postpone childbearing” until they have a stable job. That makes fertility more sensitive to job prospects.

title: 19  Fertility and the Economy: The Great Recession and Beyond
text:
19.3 The Great Recession

19.3.1 A recession, and no rebound
Figure 19.1 shows U.S. fertility and unemployment since 1960, with recessions shaded.


Show the R code
yrs <- 1960:2024
r1 <- rm[rm$t >= 1960, ]
starts <- r1$t[r1$USREC == 1 & c(0, head(r1$USREC, -1)) == 0]
ends <- r1$t[r1$USREC == 1 & c(tail(r1$USREC, -1), 0) == 0] + 1 / 12
shade <- function(ylim) rect(starts, ylim[1], ends, ylim[2], col = col_rec, border = NA)
op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 1), mar = c(2, 4.5, 1, 1), oma = c(2, 0, 0, 0), las = 1)
yl <- c(1.4, 3.8)
plot(wb$year, wb$tfr, type = "n", ylim = yl, xlim = range(yrs),
     xlab = "", ylab = "TFR (children per woman)")
shade(yl)
lines(wb$year, wb$tfr, col = col_tfr, lwd = 2.5)
abline(h = 2.1, lty = 3, col = col_grey)
text(1986, 2.1, "replacement (about 2.1)", pos = 3, col = col_grey, cex = 0.8)
for (y in c(2007, 2024)) {
  points(y, tfr_in(y), pch = 19, col = col_tfr, cex = 0.8)
  if (y == 2024) text(y, tfr_in(y) - 0.06, sprintf("%d: %.2f", y, tfr_in(y)), adj = c(1, 1), cex = 0.8)
  else text(y, tfr_in(y), sprintf("%d: %.2f", y, tfr_in(y)), pos = 3, cex = 0.8)
}
u <- ue[ue$year %in% yrs, ]
yl2 <- c(2, 11)
plot(u$year, u$unemployment_rate, type = "n", ylim = yl2, xlim = range(yrs),
     xlab = "", ylab = "Unemployment rate (%)")
shade(yl2)
lines(u$year, u$unemployment_rate, col = col_ue, lwd = 2.5)
mtext("Year", side = 1, outer = TRUE, line = 0.5)
par(op)








Figure 19.1: U.S. total fertility rate (top) and unemployment rate (bottom; annual averages), 1960–2024. Grey bands mark NBER-dated recessions. Sources: World Bank (TFR); Bureau of Labor Statistics and NBER via FRED (unemployment, recessions).





The Great Recession officially began in December 2007. Unemployment rose from 4.6 percent in 2007 to 9.6 percent in 2010, and the TFR fell from 2.12 in 2007 to 1.93 in 2010. That much fits a pro-cyclical story. The surprise came next. By 2015 unemployment was back to about 5 percent, and by 2019 it was the lowest in half a century. But fertility never came back. As your slides note, the TFR kept drifting down: 1.85 in 2013, 1.86 in 2014, 1.84 in 2015, 1.82 in 2016, 1.77 in 2017, and 1.73 in 2018.


Added · new The figure uses the World Bank TFR series and FRED unemployment, extended to 2024. The slides’ figure (1933–2015) and table (2013–2018) use slightly different TFR estimates. The 2013–2018 values in the text are the slides’.


19.3.2 What the first studies found


Added · from readings Livingston (2011), pp. 1–6.
Within a few years of the recession’s onset, a Pew Research Center analysis by Gretchen Livingston reported that “a sharp decline in fertility rates in the United States that started in 2008 is closely linked to the souring of the economy that began about the same time.” Its main findings:

A record, then a fall. The year 2007 saw a record 4,316,233 births in the United States. The general fertility rate (births per 1,000 women aged 15–44) fell from 69.6 in 2007 to 66.7 in 2009, and provisionally to 64.7 in 2010.
Harder-hit states saw bigger drops. Six of seven state-level economic indicators were linked to subsequent changes in fertility. The strongest was the change in the unemployment rate from 2007 to 2008, correlated −0.72 with the change in the fertility rate from 2008 to 2009. North Dakota, “which experienced one of the nation’s lowest unemployment rates (3.1%) in 2008, was the only state to show even a slight increase (0.7%) in births from 2008 to 2009.”
Harder-hit groups saw bigger drops. Hispanic households, which lost the most in employment and wealth, saw birth rates fall 5.9 percent from 2008 to 2009, compared with 2.4 percent for black women and 1.6 percent for white women.
Younger women cut back most. Fertility fell for every age group except women 40 and older.

Livingston was careful: “This does not conclusively prove that the economic changes led to fertility changes.” But in 48 of 51 states (including the District of Columbia), fertility declines came within one to two years of the start of economic declines, about the time it takes to act on a decision about a pregnancy.


Added · from readings Kearney and Levine (2020). The studies cited in this paragraph are as they describe them.
A decade later, Kearney and Levine summarized the case in similar terms. The birth rate fell from 69.1 per 1,000 women in 2007 to 63.0 in 2012: “That nine percent drop meant roughly 400,000 fewer births.” Across metropolitan areas, “a one percentage-point increase in the unemployment rate is associated with a 1.4 percent decrease in birth rates.” The evidence goes beyond recessions. Marital births tracked earnings in coal-producing areas during the coal boom and bust of the 1970s and 1980s. Births rose in counties that got richer from fracking. Births fell in places that lost jobs to import competition from China.






In their own words: income and price effects in the housing market



“Increases in house prices lead to increases in births among existing home owners, consistent with a positive wealth or home equity effect, while … increases in house prices lead to reductions in births among renters, consistent with a negative price effect.” (Kearney and Levine 2020, describing Dettling and Kearney 2014)
The same rise in house prices makes owners richer (an income effect) but makes the extra bedroom more expensive for renters (a price effect). The model predicts opposite responses, and that’s what the data show.




Added · new The two sentences after the quote are my gloss.
crumbs: Optional chapters
19  Fertility and the Economy: The Great Recession and Beyond

title: 19  Fertility and the Economy: The Great Recession and Beyond
text:
19.4 Data in action: comparing states
If the economy drives fertility, states hit harder by the recession should have seen bigger declines. Your slides summarize the finding: places with the biggest increases in unemployment and the most housing foreclosures had the biggest drops, and places with a fracking boom, like North Dakota, actually saw an increase. Figure 19.2 shows the comparison using the state data from the recession lab.


Show the R code
w <- reshape(st[, c("state.name", "year", "tfr", "ue")], idvar = "state.name",
             timevar = "year", direction = "wide")
w$dUE <- 100 * (w$ue.2010 - w$ue.2007)
w$dT  <- 100 * (log(w$tfr.2011) - log(w$tfr.2008))
fit <- lm(dT ~ dUE, data = w)
op <- par(mar = c(4.2, 4.5, 1, 1), las = 1)
plot(w$dUE, w$dT, pch = 19, col = "grey35", cex = 0.85,
     xlab = "Change in unemployment rate, 2007–2010 (percentage points)",
     ylab = "Change in TFR, 2008–2011 (%)")
abline(h = 0, lty = 3, col = col_grey)
abline(fit, lwd = 2, col = col_tfr)
lab_pos <- c("North Dakota" = 4, "Nevada" = 2, "Montana" = 4)
k <- match(names(lab_pos), w$state.name)
text(w$dUE[k], w$dT[k], names(lab_pos), pos = lab_pos, cex = 0.8)
par(op)
slope <- coef(fit)[2]; r <- cor(w$dUE, w$dT)








Figure 19.2: Change in unemployment (2007 to 2010, percentage points) and change in the total fertility rate (2008 to 2011, percent) by state, from the recession lab’s American Community Survey estimates. Fertility is measured a year later than unemployment, to allow for the time from decision to birth. The line is a least-squares fit.





On average, each additional percentage point of unemployment goes with a fall in fertility of about 1.6 percent, close to Kearney and Levine’s estimate of 1.4 percent. North Dakota, the only state where unemployment fell, saw fertility rise. But notice how much scatter there is (the correlation is only -0.24). Nevada had the largest rise in unemployment but only a small fall in fertility. Some of the scatter is real, but some is noise. These TFRs are estimated from a survey, and in small states a year’s estimate can bounce around. Montana’s estimated TFR “rose” by 30 percent in three years, which no real population does.


Added · new The calculation, the comparison with Kearney and Levine, and the comment on survey noise are mine. The lab’s ACS-based TFRs run higher than official vital-statistics TFRs, so use them for comparisons across states, not for levels.






In the lab



In the recession lab (2017–2018 versions) you plot fertility and unemployment for the United States and for every state, arranged in the shape of a map, and look for the states where the recession hit hardest. Then you ask whether the recession affected some groups more than others, and what the trends since the recession suggest about why fertility hasn’t recovered.
